checks.source: Kligfield P et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part I: The electrocardiogram and its technology. Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324 (PMID 17322457); IEC 60601-2-25:2011
checks.current_value: Standard gain 10 mm/mV (1 mm = 0.1 mV), shown by a 1 mV, 10 mm calibration pulse at the start of the tracing. Half gain (5 mm/mV) and double gain (20 mm/mV) are legitimate settings that must be read off the pulse and corrected for before applying voltage criteria. Many machines show half gain on the precordial leads only, and the pulse is then stepped.
checks.note: Gain and rescaling are correct. Fix the wording 'rounded corners = miscalibration'. On analog pen recorders a rounded pulse meant over-damping and an overshoot meant under-damping. That is a problem of frequency response, not of gain. On digital machines the pulse is generated electronically, and its shape mainly shows the filter settings. Teach students to check the gain on the pulse first. A low-frequency filter that is too aggressive is a separate problem (see missing criteria).

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I (Circulation 2007;115:1306); IEC 60601-2-25:2011
checks.current_value: At 25 mm/s: 1 mm = 0.04 s (40 ms), 5 mm = 0.20 s, 25 mm = 1 s, so 1500 small and 300 large squares per minute. The standard 12-lead layout is 10 s long: a 3x4 grid with 2.5 s per lead plus one or more 10 s rhythm strips.
checks.note: The arithmetic is correct. Add that 50 mm/s is routine in some European countries (e.g. Germany). Students should check paper speed as well as gain before measuring, because at 50 mm/s intervals look twice as long and the rate looks half as fast. The statement about Holter at 12.5 mm/s and 5 mm/mV is fine as a typical print setting, but it is not a standard.

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I (Circulation 2007;115:1306)
checks.current_value: I = LA - RA; II = LL - RA; III = LL - LA. The right-leg electrode is the reference / driven-right-leg electrode.
checks.note: Polarity is correct. Small updates: (1) On modern machines the right-leg electrode drives an active common-mode rejection circuit (right-leg drive) and is not a passive ground. (2) AHA 2007 discourages the strict 'bipolar vs unipolar' split, because every lead is a potential difference between an exploring electrode and a reference.

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I (Circulation 2007;115:1306)
checks.current_value: II = I + III at every instant. Related identities: aVR + aVL + aVF = 0; aVR = -(I+II)/2; aVL = I - II/2 = (I-III)/2; aVF = II - I/2 = (II+III)/2. A 12-lead ECG therefore holds only 8 independent signals (I, II, V1-V6).
checks.note: The law is correct. As a quality check its value is limited today. Digital electrocardiographs normally record I and II and compute III, aVR, aVL and aVF, so the law holds automatically and cannot detect a cable reversal. It is still useful for teaching, for checking hand-drawn or mislabelled tracings, and for spotting a lead that was pasted in the wrong position. For the app, the synthetic-ECG one-source rule enforces it by construction.

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I (Circulation 2007;115:1306); Goldberger E. Am Heart J 1942;23:483
checks.current_value: Wilson's central terminal (WCT) is the average of the RA, LA and LL potentials. It is a reference, not a true zero: its potential changes a little through the cardiac cycle. Goldberger's augmented leads compare one limb with the average of the other two, and they are exactly 1.5 times (+50%) the corresponding WCT-referenced limb potential (aVR = 3/2 VR, and so on). The 5000-ohm resistor network is Wilson's historical hardware; modern machines compute these leads digitally with high-input-impedance amplifiers.
checks.note: Change 'up to 50% larger' to 'exactly 50% larger (factor 3/2)'. Present the 'approximately zero potential' idea as a historical simplification, not a fact. AHA 2007 also advises against calling the augmented and precordial leads 'unipolar'.

checks.source: IEC 60601-2-25:2011 (IEC colour code); ANSI/AAMI EC53 (AHA colour code); Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I
checks.current_value: IEC (Europe, Spain, China): RA red, LA yellow, LL green, RL black. AHA/AAMI (USA, Canada): RA white, LA black, LL red, RL green. Precordial leads: IEC C1-C6 = red, yellow, green, brown, black, violet; AHA V1-V6 = red, yellow, green, blue, orange, purple.
checks.note: Correct for the IEC code only. The app has zh/en/es users and the two codes reuse the same colours for different limbs (red = RA in IEC but LL in AHA), which is a known source of reversals. Teach both codes and label which one is which.

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I (Circulation 2007;115:1306); SCST Clinical Guidelines by Consensus: Recording a standard 12-lead ECG (2017, rev. 2020)
checks.current_value: V1: 4th ICS, right sternal border. V2: 4th ICS, left sternal border. V3: midway between V2 and V4. V4: 5th ICS, left midclavicular line. V5: left anterior axillary line, same horizontal level as V4. V6: left midaxillary line, same horizontal level as V4 and V5. Do not follow the 5th ICS laterally. Find the ICS by palpation, starting from the sternal angle (Louis), which marks the 2nd rib.
checks.note: The book's 'V6 in the 5th ICS' is superseded: V5 and V6 now go on the horizontal line through V4. Also teach the most common real-world error: V1 and V2 placed one or two spaces too high (2nd-3rd ICS). This produces rSr' or an incomplete-RBBB look, negative P waves in V1-V2, apparent poor R progression or pseudo-anterior Q waves, and a Brugada-like pattern. For women, SCST recommends V4-V6 under the breast, on the chest wall.

checks.source: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (Thygesen K et al., Eur Heart J 2019;40:237 / Circulation 2018;138:e618); Wagner GS et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part VI: Acute ischemia/infarction, Circulation 2009;119:e262; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines (Byrne RA et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720)
checks.current_value: V7 at the left posterior axillary line, V8 at the tip of the left scapula (mid-scapular line), V9 at the left paravertebral border, all on the same horizontal plane as V6. Right-sided leads mirror V3-V6 (V3R-V6R); V4R (5th right ICS, midclavicular line) is the key one. Modern thresholds: ST elevation >=0.5 mm in V7-V9 (>=1 mm in men <40 y) for posterior (inferobasal) MI; ST elevation >=0.5 mm in V3R/V4R (>=1 mm in men <30 y) for RV involvement.
checks.note: V7-V9 and the right-sided leads are current, but describe their level as 'the horizontal plane of V6' rather than '5th ICS'. Medrano leads (MD, ME, MI) are a regional Spanish/Latin American tradition and are not part of any current international guideline or consensus. Teach them, if at all, as optional or historical. Right-sided precordials and reversed limb leads are still used to confirm dextrocardia.

checks.source: Fletcher GF et al. Exercise standards for testing and training: AHA scientific statement. Circulation 2013;128:873-934; Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; Mason RE, Likar I. Am Heart J 1966;71:196
checks.current_value: Use a full 12-lead recording with Mason-Likar torso placement. Arm electrodes go in the infraclavicular fossae, medial to the deltoid; leg electrodes go on the lower torso, between the costal margin and the iliac crest. Precordial leads stay in the standard positions. CM5 belongs to older limited-lead monitoring systems and is not part of current standards.
checks.note: The torso placement and the warning about non-comparability are correct. Mason-Likar shifts the frontal axis to the right, increases inferior-lead voltage and can hide or mimic inferior Q waves. AHA 2007 says a resting ECG taken with torso electrodes must be labelled as such and must not be read as a standard tracing. The statement that '12 leads + CM5 is best' is outdated.

checks.source: Batchvarov VN, Malik M, Camm AJ. Incorrect electrode cable connection during electrocardiographic recording. Europace 2007;9:1081-1090; Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I
checks.current_value: Full LA/RA reversal signature: lead I fully inverted (negative P, QRS and T); II and III swapped; aVR and aVL swapped (so P and QRS turn positive in aVR); aVF unchanged; V1-V6 normal, with normal R-wave progression.
checks.note: Correct but incomplete. The key test against true mirror-image dextrocardia (situs inversus) is the precordial leads. With a cable reversal R-wave progression in V1-V6 is normal. In dextrocardia R waves get smaller from V1 to V6, and the right-sided leads become normal. Also add 'P positive in aVR' to the general rule that a sinus P wave is never positive in aVR.

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; Surawicz B et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part III: Intraventricular conduction disturbances, Circulation 2009;119:e235 (definitions of notching and slurring)
checks.current_value: R = first positive deflection. Q = negative deflection before the first R. S = negative deflection after an R. QS = an entirely negative complex. R' and S' (and R'', S'') = later waves of the same polarity. Lowercase = a relatively small wave, uppercase = a large one. Notching and slurring are described in words, not with a letter code.
checks.note: The core rules are current. Two parts need review: (1) The 5 mm cut-off between lowercase and uppercase is only one convention; many sources use size relative to the other waves in the same complex. Present it as a convention, not a rule. (2) Using 'm' for a notched wave is not international notation and should not be taught as standard. Use 'notched' / 'slurred' (Spanish: 'melladura' / 'empastamiento') in words.

checks.source: Nerbonne JM, Kass RS. Molecular physiology of cardiac repolarization. Physiol Rev 2005;85:1205-1253; Macfarlane PW et al. Comprehensive Electrocardiology, 2nd ed. (Springer 2011)
checks.current_value: Phase 0 = QRS; phase 1 = J point; phase 2 (plateau) = ST segment; phase 3 = T wave; phase 4 = electrical diastole (TQ).
checks.note: Correct as a teaching map. Make clear that the ECG shows voltage differences between regions: the ST segment is isoelectric because all cells are in plateau at a similar level, and the T wave comes from timing differences in phase 3 (transmural and apex-base gradients). It is not the action potential of a single cell.

checks.source: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14th ed. (2020), ch. 9-10; Mangoni ME, Nargeot J. Genesis and regulation of the heart automaticity. Physiol Rev 2008;88:919-982; Nerbonne & Kass, Physiol Rev 2005;85:1205
checks.current_value: Fast response (atrial and ventricular myocardium, His-Purkinje): resting potential about -85 to -90 mV, overshoot about +20 to +30 mV, conduction about 0.3-1 m/s in working myocardium and 2-4 m/s in Purkinje fibres. Slow response (SA and AV node): maximum diastolic potential about -55 to -65 mV, take-off threshold about -40 mV (L-type Ca2+ current), conduction about 0.02-0.05 m/s. Phase-4 depolarization comes from the funny current (If, HCN4) together with the intracellular Ca2+ 'clock'.
checks.note: The general fast/slow distinction is correct. The nodal numbers in the book (rest about -70 mV, threshold about -55 mV) are more negative than current physiology texts. 5 m/s is at the very top of the Purkinje range. The PR delay comes mainly from slow AV-nodal conduction, not SA-nodal conduction.

checks.source: Zipes DP, Jalife J et al. Cardiac Electrophysiology: From Cell to Bedside, 8th ed. (2022); Braunwald's Heart Disease, 12th ed. (2022), chapter on mechanisms of arrhythmias
checks.current_value: Absolute/effective refractory period: from QRS onset to about the T-wave apex. Relative refractory period: about the descending limb of the T wave; it contains the vulnerable period, a narrow window near the T apex where an extra stimulus (R-on-T) can trigger VF/VT. Supernormal period: a short window at the very end of T or just after it.
checks.note: Roughly correct. Move the end of the absolute period from 'end of ST' to 'around the T apex', and place the vulnerable window near the apex and early downslope of T. Supernormal excitability and conduction are shown in Purkinje tissue but have little clinical role; teach them briefly.

checks.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; Macfarlane PW et al. Comprehensive Electrocardiology, 2nd ed. (2011)
checks.current_value: A depolarization front moving toward the positive pole of a lead gives a positive deflection; moving away gives a negative one; moving perpendicular gives an isodiphasic (equiphasic) deflection.
checks.note: Correct. Add the counterpart for repolarization: a repolarization front moving toward the electrode gives a negative deflection. That is why T waves normally share the QRS polarity even though repolarization runs from epicardium to endocardium. In vector terms, the deflection is proportional to the projection of the heart vector on the lead axis.

checks.source: Durrer D et al. Total excitation of the isolated human heart. Circulation 1970;41:899-912; Macfarlane PW et al. Comprehensive Electrocardiology, 2nd ed. (2011)
checks.current_value: Vector 1: septal, from left to right and anterior. Vector 2: free walls, dominated by the LV, pointing left, inferior and posterior. Vector 3: basal / posterobasal, pointing up, posterior and slightly right. Together they give rS in V1-V2, RS near the transition (V3-V4) and qRs or qR in V5-V6, I and aVL.
checks.note: Current; Durrer 1970 is still the primary source. The transition zone varies normally between V2 and V5.

checks.source: Yan GX, Antzelevitch C. Cellular basis for the normal T wave and the electrocardiographic manifestations of the long-QT syndrome. Circulation 1998;98:1928-1936; Rautaharju PM et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part IV: ST segment, T and U waves, and the QT interval. Circulation 2009;119:e241
checks.current_value: Epicardial action potentials are shorter than endocardial ones, so repolarization runs from epicardium to endocardium and the subendocardium repolarizes last. The T wave therefore usually has the same polarity as the main QRS deflection.
checks.note: Correct. Normal exceptions: T may be negative in aVR, often in V1, sometimes in III; persistent juvenile T inversion in V1-V3 is common in children and some adolescents. Apex-to-base gradients add to the transmural one.

checks.source: Sapin PM et al. Identification of false positive exercise tests with use of electrocardiographic criteria: a possible role for atrial repolarization waves. J Am Coll Cardiol 1991;18:127-135; Macfarlane PW et al. Comprehensive Electrocardiology, 2nd ed. (2011)
checks.current_value: The atrial repolarization wave (Ta) has the opposite polarity to the P wave and is usually hidden in the PR segment and the QRS.
checks.note: Correct. Add when Ta becomes visible or important: (1) in complete AV block or with non-conducted P waves, where it follows the P wave; (2) during exercise or sinus tachycardia, where a deep Ta causes downsloping PR depression and false-positive inferior ST depression; (3) PR-segment deviation in pericarditis and atrial infarction.

missing_criteria.value: Diagnostic ECG: low-frequency cut-off 0.05 Hz, or up to 0.67 Hz only with zero-phase-distortion (linear-phase/bidirectional) digital filters. High-frequency cut-off at least 150 Hz in adults and at least 250 Hz in children. 'Monitor' or 'muscle' settings (about 0.5-40 Hz) distort ST segments (false ST elevation or depression), shrink QRS amplitude and can hide pacemaker spikes and notches.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I (Circulation 2007;115:1306)

missing_criteria.value: At least 500 samples/s for diagnostic 12-lead ECGs. Pacemaker-spike detection needs much higher internal sampling or dedicated spike detection, and machine-added pacing markers can be artefacts.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: Regular fine oscillation at 50 Hz (Spain, Europe, China) or 60 Hz (USA, parts of Latin America) that thickens the baseline. Causes: poor skin contact, a broken lead wire, nearby equipment. Fix the electrode contact rather than relying on the notch filter alone.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; IEC 60601-2-25:2011

missing_criteria.value: Tremor (e.g. Parkinsonian, 4-6 Hz), shivering or tapping can mimic atrial flutter or fibrillation and even VT. Clues: the real QRS complexes keep 'marching through' at the underlying R-R interval; the artefact is missing or minimal in at least one lead; the patient's condition does not change. Misreading has led to unnecessary procedures.
missing_criteria.source: Knight BP et al. Clinical consequences of electrocardiographic artifact mimicking ventricular tachycardia. N Engl J Med 1999;341:1270-1274; Baranchuk A et al. Electrocardiography pitfalls and artifacts: the 10 commandments. Crit Care Nurse 2009;29:67-73

missing_criteria.value: A limb-electrode artefact appears in the two bipolar leads that use that electrode and is nearly absent from the third. RA artefact: I and II, not III. LA artefact: I and III, not II. LL artefact: II and III, not I. It is largest in the augmented lead named after that electrode.
missing_criteria.leads: I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF
missing_criteria.source: Aslanger E, Yalin K. Electromechanical association: a subtle electrocardiogram artifact. J Electrocardiol 2012;45:15-17; Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: Slow drift with respiration or movement. It can mimic or hide ST deviation. Correct it with skin preparation, a relaxed supine patient and proper (zero-phase) high-pass filtering, not by raising the cut-off in non-linear-phase filters.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: LA/LL: I and II swapped, aVL and aVF swapped, III inverted, aVR unchanged. Subtle clue: the P wave is larger in I than in II, or III shows a terminally positive P. RA/LL: I, II and III inverted (II inverted, I and III swap with inversion), aVR and aVF swapped, aVL unchanged; looks like inferior Q waves or an ectopic atrial rhythm. RA/RL: lead II almost a flat line. LA/RL: lead III almost a flat line. Bilateral arm-leg reversals cause other near-flat or bizarre patterns. In all limb reversals V1-V6 are unaffected.
missing_criteria.leads: I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF
missing_criteria.source: Batchvarov VN, Malik M, Camm AJ. Europace 2007;9:1081-1090; Harrigan RA, Chan TC, Brady WJ. Electrocardiographic electrode misplacement, misconnection, and artifact. J Emerg Med 2012;43:1038-1044

missing_criteria.value: Swapped precordial cables break the smooth R-wave progression and T-wave evolution (for example, an isolated 'jump' in one lead). V1-V2 placed too high gives rSr', negative P in V1-V2, pseudo-septal Q waves and a Brugada-like ST. V1-V2 placed too low can hide a true pattern. Before serial comparison, check that electrode placement is identical.
missing_criteria.source: Batchvarov 2007 Europace; SCST Clinical Guidelines: Recording a standard 12-lead ECG (2017/2020); Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: Recording V1-V2 in the 2nd and 3rd ICS increases sensitivity for the type 1 Brugada pattern. The diagnosis needs coved ST elevation >=2 mm in >=1 right precordial lead in the 2nd, 3rd or 4th ICS. Students must be able to tell deliberate high placement apart from accidental misplacement.
missing_criteria.source: Zeppenfeld K et al. 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of SCD. Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126; Antzelevitch C et al. J-Wave syndromes expert consensus conference report. Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295

missing_criteria.value: Find landmarks by palpation and place V4-V6 on the chest wall, under the breast, at the standard horizontal level, rather than on top of breast tissue. Document any deviation from standard placement.
missing_criteria.source: SCST Clinical Guidelines by Consensus: Recording a standard 12-lead ECG (2017, rev. 2020); Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: I 0 deg, II +60 deg, III +120 deg, aVF +90 deg, aVL -30 deg, aVR -150 deg (or +210 deg). The Cabrera (orderly) display aVL, I, -aVR, II, aVF, III makes the frontal-plane sequence continuous and is an AHA-endorsed option.
missing_criteria.leads: I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: Regular rhythm: 300 / number of large squares, or 1500 / number of small squares, between consecutive R waves (at 25 mm/s). Irregular rhythm: count the QRS complexes in the 10 s strip and multiply by 6. Paper speed and gain must be checked first.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; Mason JW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part II: Electrocardiography diagnostic statement list. Circulation 2007;115:1325

missing_criteria.value: On digital ECGs, global PR, QRS and QT are measured from the earliest onset to the latest offset across the simultaneously recorded leads. This makes them systematically longer than single-lead manual measurements, which explains differences between machine and manual values.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; Rautaharju PM et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part IV. Circulation 2009;119:e241

missing_criteria.value: The automated statement must always be confirmed by a qualified reader. Its errors cluster in rhythm diagnosis (e.g. AF vs artefact, pacemaker rhythms), and it does not recognize electrode reversals reliably.
missing_criteria.source: Schläpfer J, Wellens HJ. Computer-interpreted electrocardiograms: benefits and limitations. J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;70:1183-1192; Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I

missing_criteria.value: Patient supine and relaxed, with skin preparation (clean, dry, shaved if needed). Limb electrodes go on the limbs, not the torso, for a resting diagnostic ECG. Any non-standard condition (sitting, torso limb electrodes, extra leads, modified gain or speed) is written on the tracing, because posture and electrode position change axis, voltages and T waves.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield 2007 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I; SCST Clinical Guidelines: Recording a standard 12-lead ECG (2017/2020)

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part II: Diagnostic statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325-1332); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline (Page RL et al., Circulation 2016;133:e506-e574) for sinus P morphology; normal P axis 0 to +75 deg per Surawicz B, Knilans TK, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed., 2008
checks.current_value: Sinus P is upright in I, II and aVF, inverted in aVR, upright in V3-V6. In III and aVL it may be upright, flat, biphasic or inverted depending on the P axis (normal 0 to +75 deg). In V1 it is often biphasic (+/-), and V2 may be biphasic too.
checks.note: The only error is requiring a positive P in III and aVL. A vertical P axis (about +75 deg) gives a negative P in aVL; a leftward P axis (about 0 to +15 deg) gives a flat or negative P in III. Both are still sinus. The rest of the rule (I, II, aVF positive; aVR negative; V1 +/-) is correct. A grader using the book's rule would wrongly reject normal sinus rhythm.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay (Kusumoto FM et al., Circulation 2019;140:e382-e482; JACC 2019;74:e51-e156); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline (Page RL et al.); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part II statement list (Mason JW et al.)
checks.current_value: Sinus rhythm is defined by where the P wave comes from (sinus P axis and morphology) and a regular P-P interval. It does not require a normal PR: sinus rhythm with first-degree or second-degree AV block is still sinus rhythm. Rate: 60-100 bpm remains the usual ECG-reading range, and sinus tachycardia is >100 bpm. The 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline uses 50-100 bpm as normal and <50 bpm as clinically significant sinus bradycardia, while ECG reports often still flag <60. Sinus arrhythmia is judged on P-P intervals, not R-R: variation >0.12 s, or >10% of mean P-P, is commonly used, and older texts use >0.16 s. There is no single guideline value. It may be respiratory (phasic) or non-respiratory.
checks.note: Teach both rate thresholds and say which context each belongs to. Take 'every P conducted with constant PR 0.12-0.20 s' out of the definition of sinus rhythm, because it mixes rhythm origin with AV conduction.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part V: ECG changes associated with cardiac chamber hypertrophy (Hancock EW et al., Circulation 2009;119:e251-e261); Bayes de Luna A et al., Interatrial blocks consensus, J Electrocardiol 2012;45:445-451
checks.current_value: P axis 0 to +75 deg. P duration <120 ms: >=120 ms means interatrial block or left atrial abnormality, and >=120 ms with a biphasic (+/-) P in II, III and aVF means advanced interatrial block. P amplitude <2.5 mm (0.25 mV) in II; >=2.5 mm suggests right atrial abnormality. In V1 the positive part should be <1.5 mm, and a P-terminal force >=0.04 mm*s suggests left atrial abnormality. Look in lead II and V1.
checks.note: The book's upper limit of 0.10 s is too strict; current cut-offs use 120 ms. Its axis range of +30 to +60 deg is narrower than today's normal range.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline (Kusumoto FM et al.): first-degree AV block = PR >200 ms; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline / 2019 ESC SVT guideline (Brugada J et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720) for pre-excitation; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al., Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324) for global interval measurement
checks.note: 120-200 ms in adults is still correct. Measure the PR globally, from the earliest P onset to the earliest QRS onset across simultaneous leads. For a short PR (<120 ms), teach this differential: pre-excitation (delta wave, wide QRS), ectopic or low atrial rhythm, junctional rhythm, and enhanced AV nodal conduction or normal variant. Lown-Ganong-Levine is no longer treated as a separate syndrome; call it 'short PR with normal QRS'. Children have shorter normal PR intervals.

checks.source: Rijnbeek PR et al., New normal limits for the paediatric ECG, Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711; Davignon A et al., Pediatr Cardiol 1979/80;1:123-131; ESC Task Force guidelines for interpretation of the neonatal ECG (Schwartz PJ et al., Eur Heart J 2002;23:1329-1344); 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline (adult PR >200 ms)
checks.current_value: Adults: one cut-off, PR >200 ms = first-degree AV block, with no heart-rate-specific upper limits. In trained athletes, PR up to 399 ms is treated as a normal training effect (2017 International athlete criteria). Children: use age-specific percentile tables (Rijnbeek 2001; Davignon 1979) or the ESC neonatal ECG guideline for infants.
checks.note: These tables are mid-20th-century nomograms and are no longer used. The book's own column headers are misprinted. The adult value of 0.21 s at heart rate <=70 also contradicts the 0.20 s cut-off used everywhere else. Do not use this table to grade.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I: The ECG and its technology (Kligfield P et al., Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324), standard 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, 10-s 12-lead recording; standard ECG texts (e.g., Goldberger's Clinical Electrocardiography, 10th ed., 2023)
checks.note: Correct. '(each small square 0.2)' means a small square counts as 0.2 of a large square in the 300 rule. Make that explicit so learners do not confuse it with time: one small square is 0.04 s (1 mm), and one large square is 0.20 s (5 mm). Add the equivalent rule: rate = 1500 / number of small squares between R waves. A standard 12-lead lasts 10 s, so QRS count x 6 is the method of choice for irregular rhythms. At 50 mm/s, use 3000 / large squares or 3000 / small squares... more simply, double the square counts.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline (Kusumoto FM et al.); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline (junctional rhythms); Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed.
checks.note: These match current teaching. Junctional escape is usually taught as 40-60 bpm; the book's lower bound of 35 is unusual but harmless. Ventricular (idioventricular) escape is 20-40 bpm. Also teach the 'accelerated' forms: accelerated junctional rhythm is about 60-100 (up to about 130) bpm, and accelerated idioventricular rhythm is about 40/50-110 bpm. Normal sinus rate at rest is 60-100 bpm, or 50-100 bpm per the 2018 guideline.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III: Intraventricular conduction disturbances (Surawicz B et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240; JACC 2009;53:976-981); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al.) for global measurement
checks.current_value: Adults: QRS is usually 80-100 ms, and the upper limit of normal is <110 ms. 110-119 ms = incomplete RBBB/LBBB or non-specific intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD). >=120 ms = complete bundle branch block or wide QRS. Children have lower, age-specific limits: non-specific IVCD at >90 ms (8-16 y) and >80 ms (<8 y). Measure globally, from the earliest QRS onset to the latest QRS offset across simultaneous leads.
checks.note: The book's range fits normal values, but a 100 ms upper limit would wrongly call 100-109 ms abnormal. The app needs the AHA 110 and 120 ms thresholds for grading. 'Widest lead' is close to global measurement but not the same.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV: The ST segment, T and U waves, and the QT interval (Rautaharju PM et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241-e250; JACC 2009;53:982-991); AHA/ACCF Scientific Statement on prevention of torsade de pointes in hospital settings (Drew BJ et al., Circulation 2010;121:1047-1060); 2022 ESC VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld K et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126)
checks.current_value: QT runs from the earliest QRS onset to the end of the T wave. Measure it in the lead with the longest QT (often II or V2-V5), use the tangent method, and leave out the U wave. QTc limits are sex-specific: prolonged at >=450 ms in men and >=460 ms in women; short at <=390 ms (AHA 2009 Part IV). QTc >500 ms, or a rise of >60 ms on a drug, means high risk of torsade de pointes. Bazett over-corrects at fast heart rates (and under-corrects at slow ones). Linear corrections such as Framingham (QTc = QT + 0.154 x (1 - RR)) or Hodges, or Fridericia (QT / RR^(1/3)), are preferred, especially above about 90 bpm. When QRS >=120 ms, use the JT interval or a QRS-adjusted QT.
checks.note: The single 0.44 s cut-off and the 'predicted QT = 0.39 x sqrt(RR) + 0.04 s' rule are obsolete. The way QT is measured from QRS onset to T end is still correct.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju PM et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241-e250); 2022 ESC VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld K et al.)
checks.current_value: Do not use a lookup table of maximum QT by heart rate. Correct the QT for rate (linear or Fridericia formula preferred) and compare it with sex-specific QTc limits. Normal: <450 ms in men and <460 ms in women. Borderline/prolonged: >=450 or >=460 ms. Marked: >500 ms. LQTS diagnosis: >=480 ms. Short: <=390 ms on the AHA standard, and <=360 ms for short QT syndrome (SQTS).
checks.note: These values come from old Ashman/Hull-style nomograms. They are internally consistent with QTc of about 0.42-0.44 s, but they are not in current guidelines. You can keep them as historical context, but do not grade against them.

checks.source: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (Thygesen K et al., Eur Heart J 2019;40:237-269; Circulation 2018;138:e618-e651); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju PM et al.); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part VI (Wagner GS et al., Circulation 2009;119:e262-e270); 2023 ESC ACS guidelines (Byrne RA et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720-3826)
checks.note: Correct as a general description, but 'isoelectric' must be qualified. Normal J-point elevation has upper limits. In V2-V3: <2 mm in men >=40 y, <2.5 mm in men <40 y, and <1.5 mm in women. In other leads: <1 mm. New horizontal or downsloping ST depression >=0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads is abnormal. T inversion is normal in aVR, often in V1, and sometimes in III, aVL or aVF when the QRS in that lead is small or negative. Young adults can also show T inversion in V2. T inversion >1 mm in leads with a dominant R wave (R/S >1) is abnormal. T is usually concordant with the net QRS. The U wave is normally small (about 25% or less of T), upright and best seen in V2-V3; an inverted U is abnormal.

checks.source: International Recommendations for Electrocardiographic Interpretation in Athletes (Sharma S, Drezner JA et al., JACC 2017;69:1057-1075; Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466-1480); Malhotra A et al., Anterior T-wave inversion in young white athletes and nonathletes, JACC 2017;69:1-9; ESC neonatal ECG guideline (Schwartz PJ et al., Eur Heart J 2002;23:1329-1344)
checks.current_value: Children: T in V1 turns negative after the first week of life. T inversion in V1-V3 is normal through childhood, and in athletes it is accepted as the 'juvenile pattern' under 16 years (2017 International criteria). Adults (>=16 y): T inversion in V1 alone is normal. T inversion in V2 is sometimes seen. Inversion extending to V3 or beyond is uncommon (about 2% overall; more common in women, roughly 4%) and needs evaluation. Exception: Black athletes may show J-point elevation with convex ST elevation followed by T inversion in V1-V4, which is a normal variant. T inversion >=1 mm in >=2 contiguous leads outside aVR, III and V1 (other than these exceptions) is abnormal.
checks.note: The '25% of women' figure is not supported by modern population data; the real prevalence is a few percent. The age limit should be 16 years, not 6-12 years. The Black-individual variant has a specific shape (J-point elevation and convex ST elevation before the T inversion) that should be taught.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al., Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324) lead definitions; Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed.
checks.note: The angles and perpendicular pairs are correct. You could also teach the Cabrera (orderly) display aVL, I, -aVR, II, aVF, III. It shows the angles in sequence at 30 deg steps; note that -aVR is at +30 deg.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz B et al.) axis categories; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part II statement list (Mason JW et al.) including 'indeterminate axis'
checks.note: Both methods are still valid. Add the quick quadrant check: look at the net QRS polarity in I and aVF first (and in II, to tell normal from left axis deviation in the 0 to -30 deg band), then refine using the lead closest to isodiphasic. Indeterminate axis (all limb leads isodiphasic) is still a standard statement.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III: Intraventricular conduction disturbances (Surawicz B et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240; JACC 2009;53:976-981)
checks.current_value: Normal adult QRS axis is -30 deg to +90 deg. Left axis deviation is beyond -30 deg: moderate from -30 to -45 deg, marked from -45 to -90 deg (marked LAD with qR in aVL and QRS <120 ms suggests left anterior fascicular block). Right axis deviation is beyond +90 deg: moderate from +90 to +120 deg, marked from +120 to +180 deg. -90 to +/-180 deg is a right superior ('extreme', northwest) axis. Children have age-dependent, more rightward normal limits.
checks.note: The book's upper limit of +105/+110 deg is out of date. Axes from +90 to +110 deg in tall, thin young adults are common, but standard terminology now labels them right axis deviation. Teach that this is often a benign finding.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part II statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325-1332) and 2009 Part III (Surawicz B et al.), which describe the frontal plane only by QRS axis categories; Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed.
checks.current_value: Describe the frontal plane by QRS axis only: normal, LAD, RAD, right superior or indeterminate. A 'vertical axis' (about +60 to +90 deg; qR in II, III, aVF; rS/QS in aVL) is common in thin or young people and in COPD. A 'horizontal axis' (about 0 to +30 deg; qR in I and aVL; rS in III) is common in obesity, pregnancy, ascites and older age. These are descriptive terms and do not prove anatomical heart position.
checks.note: Wilson's 'electrical heart positions' are a historical concept and are not part of the current standard statement lists. The axis values and QRS patterns in the criterion are internally consistent, so they can be kept as a description of positional variants, renamed as axis terms.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al.) on precordial electrode placement; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part II statement list (Mason JW et al.) on R-wave progression and transition; Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed.
checks.note: Correct. Normal transition (R = S) is in V3-V4. Modern teaching says 'early transition' (R >= S by V2) and 'late transition' (R < S still in V5) and treats 'clockwise/counterclockwise rotation' as electrical description only. Teach the differential. Early transition: normal variant, RVH, posterior MI, RBBB, pre-excitation, or V1-V2 placed too low or too far right. Late transition or poor R-wave progression (R in V3 <=3 mm): anterior MI, LVH, LBBB/LAFB, COPD, or electrodes placed too high.

missing_criteria.value: Paper speed is 25 mm/s and gain is 10 mm/mV, so a small square is 0.04 s and 0.1 mV, and a large square is 0.20 s and 0.5 mV. Check the calibration pulse before reading; half-standard gain makes voltages look smaller. Bandwidth: high-pass 0.05 Hz (or 0.67 Hz with a zero-phase filter); low-pass >=150 Hz in adults and 250 Hz in children. Recording is 10 s.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I: The ECG and its technology (Kligfield P et al., Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324)

missing_criteria.value: Rate = 1500 / number of small squares between R waves at 25 mm/s. For irregular rhythms, count QRS complexes on the 10-s ECG and multiply by 6.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al.); Goldberger's Clinical Electrocardiography, 10th ed., 2023

missing_criteria.value: Measure PR, QRS and QT from the earliest onset in any lead to the latest offset in any lead on simultaneously recorded leads. Computer-measured intervals must be over-read by a physician.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al., Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324)

missing_criteria.parameter: bradycardia, pause, tachycardia, inappropriate sinus tachycardia
missing_criteria.value: Sinus bradycardia: <50 bpm in the 2018 guideline (<60 bpm by convention). A sinus pause >=3 s is significant. Sinus tachycardia: >100 bpm. Inappropriate sinus tachycardia: resting sinus rate >100 bpm with a mean 24-h rate >90 bpm and no primary cause. Sinus arrhythmia: P-P variation >0.12 s or >10%, either respiratory or non-respiratory.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline (Kusumoto FM et al., Circulation 2019;140:e382-e482); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline (Page RL et al., Circulation 2016;133:e506-e574); 2019 ESC SVT guidelines (Brugada J et al.)

missing_criteria.entity: Ectopic atrial rhythm / wandering atrial pacemaker / MAT
missing_criteria.value: Ectopic atrial rhythm: P axis outside the sinus range, at <100 bpm (e.g. a low atrial focus gives a negative P in II, III and aVF with PR >=120 ms). Wandering atrial pacemaker: >=3 different P morphologies at <100 bpm. Multifocal atrial tachycardia: >=3 P morphologies with variable PP/PR at >100 bpm.
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF, I, aVL, V1
missing_criteria.source: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline (Page RL et al.); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part II statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325-1332)

missing_criteria.value: Partial interatrial block: P duration >=120 ms. Advanced interatrial block: P >=120 ms with a biphasic (+/-) P in II, III and aVF. Advanced block is linked to atrial fibrillation and stroke (Bayes syndrome).
missing_criteria.source: Bayes de Luna A et al., Interatrial blocks: a separate entity from left atrial enlargement - a consensus report, J Electrocardiol 2012;45:445-451

missing_criteria.parameter: RAD, right superior axis, fascicular blocks
missing_criteria.value: Right axis deviation: +90 to +180 deg (moderate +90 to +120, marked +120 to +180). Right superior ('extreme') axis: -90 to +/-180 deg. Indeterminate axis: all limb leads isodiphasic. Left anterior fascicular block: axis -45 to -90 deg, qR in aVL, R-peak time in aVL >=45 ms, QRS <120 ms. Left posterior fascicular block: axis +90 to +180 deg in adults (after excluding other causes), rS in I/aVL, qR in III/aVF, QRS <120 ms. Children have age-specific normal ranges (neonates are normally right-axis).
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz B et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240)

missing_criteria.value: Adults: QRS <110 ms normal; 110-119 ms = incomplete RBBB/LBBB or non-specific IVCD; >=120 ms = complete bundle branch block or wide QRS. Children have lower, age-specific thresholds: non-specific IVCD at >90 ms (8-16 y) and >80 ms (<8 y), with corresponding RBBB limits.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz B et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240)

missing_criteria.value: Measure from QRS onset to T end using the tangent method, in the lead with the longest QT. Do not include the U wave. In atrial fibrillation, average over about 10 beats. Prefer Fridericia or linear corrections (Framingham, Hodges) to Bazett at heart rates far from 60 bpm. With QRS >=120 ms, use JT or a QRS-adjusted QT. Prolonged: >=450 ms in men, >=460 ms in women. Short: <=390 ms.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju PM et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241-e250)

missing_criteria.value: QTc >500 ms, or a rise of >60 ms from baseline, marks a high risk of torsade de pointes. Stop or review QT-prolonging drugs, correct potassium and magnesium, and monitor.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF Scientific Statement: Prevention of torsade de pointes in hospital settings (Drew BJ et al., Circulation 2010;121:1047-1060)

missing_criteria.value: LQTS: QTc >=480 ms on repeated 12-lead ECGs, or LQTS (Schwartz) score >3. Consider LQTS at QTc >=460 ms with unexplained syncope. Short QT syndrome: QTc <=360 ms plus a supporting feature (pathogenic variant, family history, or survived VT/VF); consider it at QTc <=320 ms.
missing_criteria.source: 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death (Zeppenfeld K et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126)

missing_criteria.value: V2-V3: <2 mm in men >=40 y, <2.5 mm in men <40 y, <1.5 mm in women. All other leads: <1 mm. Exceeding these in 2 contiguous leads (new) meets the STEMI ECG threshold. Lead-specific limits apply to V7-V9 and V3R-V4R.
missing_criteria.source: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (Thygesen K et al., Eur Heart J 2019;40:237-269); 2023 ESC ACS guidelines (Byrne RA et al.)

missing_criteria.value: Normal septal q waves in I, aVL, V5-V6 are narrow (<30-40 ms) and small. An isolated Q in III, and a Q in aVR, can be normal. Pathological Q: any Q >=20 ms (or QS) in V2-V3; or Q >=30 ms and >=1 mm deep (or QS) in 2 contiguous leads of the I/aVL/V6, V4-V6 or II/III/aVF groups; or R >=40 ms with R/S >=1 in V1-V2 (posterior equivalent).
missing_criteria.leads: I, aVL, V5-V6, III, aVR, V1-V3
missing_criteria.source: Fourth Universal Definition of MI (Thygesen K et al., Eur Heart J 2019;40:237-269)

missing_criteria.value: J-point elevation (Jp) >=0.1 mV in >=2 contiguous inferior and/or lateral leads, with a notch or slur at the end of the QRS and QRS <120 ms. It is a common benign variant (young, male, athletes). 'Early repolarization syndrome' requires documented VF or polymorphic VT.
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF, I, aVL, V4-V6
missing_criteria.source: Macfarlane PW et al., The early repolarization pattern: a consensus paper, JACC 2015;66:470-477; 2022 ESC VA/SCD guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Normal training-related findings: sinus bradycardia >=30 bpm, sinus arrhythmia, ectopic atrial or junctional escape rhythm, first-degree AV block (PR <400 ms), Mobitz I, incomplete RBBB, isolated QRS voltage criteria for LVH/RVH, early repolarization, the Black-athlete V1-V4 repolarization pattern, and juvenile T inversion V1-V3 under 16 y. Abnormal (needs evaluation): T inversion >=1 mm in >=2 contiguous leads outside aVR, III and V1 (except the variants above); ST depression; pathological Q; complete LBBB; QRS >=140 ms; QTc >=470 ms (men) or >=480 ms (women); PR >=400 ms; sinus rate <30 bpm or pauses >=3 s.
missing_criteria.source: International Recommendations for Electrocardiographic Interpretation in Athletes (Sharma S, Drezner JA et al., JACC 2017;69:1057-1075; Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466-1480)

missing_criteria.value: PR <120 ms, a delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), QRS usually >=110-120 ms, and secondary ST-T changes. The delta-wave polarity helps localize the accessory pathway.
missing_criteria.leads: All 12; delta wave best in leads with a dominant R
missing_criteria.source: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline (Page RL et al.); 2019 ESC SVT guidelines (Brugada J et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720)

missing_criteria.value: LA/RA reversal: inverted P, QRS and T in I, and upright P/QRS in aVR, while the precordial leads look normal (this is how it differs from dextrocardia). Any reversal involving RL gives an almost flat line in one limb lead. V1-V2 placed too high (2nd-3rd intercostal space) gives a pseudo-incomplete RBBB pattern (rSr'), a negative P and poor R-wave progression.
missing_criteria.leads: I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF, V1-V2
missing_criteria.source: Batchvarov VN, Malik M, Camm AJ, Incorrect electrode cable connection during ECG recording, Europace 2007;9:1081-1090; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part I (Kligfield P et al.)

missing_criteria.value: Low voltage: all limb-lead QRS amplitudes <5 mm, and/or all precordial QRS amplitudes <10 mm. Causes include pericardial effusion, obesity, COPD, infiltrative cardiomyopathy and hypothyroidism.
missing_criteria.leads: I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF; V1-V6
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007 Part II statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325-1332); Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed.

missing_criteria.parameter: age-dependent axis, R in V1, T in V1
missing_criteria.value: Newborns normally have a rightward QRS axis (often +90 to +180 deg) and a dominant R in V1. The T in V1 becomes negative after about the first week; an upright T in V1 after that and before adolescence suggests RVH. Children also have shorter PR and QRS intervals and higher precordial voltages. Use age-specific percentile tables.
missing_criteria.source: ESC Task Force Guidelines for interpretation of the neonatal ECG (Schwartz PJ et al., Eur Heart J 2002;23:1329-1344); Rijnbeek PR et al., Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711

checks.source: Hancock EW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part V: ECG changes associated with cardiac chamber hypertrophy. Circulation 2009;119:e251-e261 / JACC 2009;53:992-1002 (atrial abnormality section: RA activation forms the early P, LA activation starts later via Bachmann's bundle and forms the late P); Surawicz B, Knilans T. Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed. 2008
checks.current_value: RA activation first (roughly the first two-thirds of P), LA activation starts about 20-30 ms later and finishes the P wave; total adult P duration <120 ms
checks.note: The values are approximate and fine for teaching. Keep the conceptual message: RA abnormality changes the early P and its amplitude, LA abnormality changes the late P and its duration. Use the adult upper limit of 120 ms for P duration (not 110 ms) throughout the app.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part V (thresholds of >2.5 mm in II and >1.5 mm initial P positivity in V1/V2 confirmed via a 2009 SA Heart Journal ECG-quiz summary citing Part V); Kaplan JD et al. JACC 1994;23:747-752; Sharma S, Drezner JA et al. International recommendations for ECG interpretation in athletes, Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466-1480 (JACC 2017;69:1057-1075)
checks.current_value: Right atrial abnormality: P amplitude >2.5 mm (0.25 mV) in II (or III/aVF); initial positive P in V1 or V2 >1.5 mm (0.15 mV); rightward P axis (>+75°); P duration normal (<120 ms). Peaked shape is typical but not required
checks.note: Book axis cut-off (+54°) is not used today. The >+75° value is the one usually given (Chou's) and attributed to Part V, but it was not checked against Part V's full text (paywalled). Duration limit is now <120 ms, not ≤110 ms. Use the term 'right atrial abnormality'. P-pulmonale criteria are specific but very insensitive: Kaplan 1994 found P pulmonale in only 6% of echo-proven RAE. In athletes, P ≥2.5 mm in II/III/aVF is a 'borderline' finding. Treat the congenital leftward-P-axis variant ('P congenitale') as a historical aside only.

checks.source: Reeves WC et al. Two-dimensional echocardiographic assessment of ECG criteria for right atrial enlargement. Circulation 1981;64:387-391; Kaplan JD et al. JACC 1994;23:747-752
checks.current_value: Supportive QRS signs of RA enlargement: qR in V1 without infarction (Sodi-Pallares sign); small QRS in V1 with a much larger QRS in V2 (Peñaloza-Tranchesi sign). Echo-validated thresholds: V1 total QRS ≤6 mm with V2/V1 ≥3 (PPV ~48%); V2/V1 ≥4 gave sensitivity ~85%, specificity ~60%. Kaplan: QRS axis >+90°, R/S V1 >1 (no RBBB) and P in V2 >1.5 mm were the best predictors
checks.note: Still taught as indirect signs, but the evidence comes from small studies. The book's numbers (V2/V1 ≥4; >5 with V1 ≤4 mm) roughly match Reeves but are not identical; the app should cite Reeves 1981. These are supportive signs only, with low specificity for the ratio criterion.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (P ≥120 ms, notch interpeak ≥40 ms, V1 terminal negativity; corroborated via SA Heart J 2009 summary and e-cardiogram.com summaries of Part V); Morris JJ et al. Circulation 1964;29:242-252; Sharma/Drezner 2017 International athlete criteria (LAE = P >120 ms in I or II with V1 terminal negative ≥1 mm and ≥40 ms); Bayés de Luna A et al. J Electrocardiol 2012;45:445-451
checks.current_value: Left atrial abnormality: P duration ≥120 ms (lead II); notched/bifid P with peak-to-peak ≥40 ms; V1 terminal negative P ≥1 mm deep and ≥40 ms (P terminal force ≥0.04 mm·s); leftward P axis (-30° to -45°) is a minor, rarely used sign
checks.note: The book's >0.11 s duration threshold is superseded by ≥120 ms. A 'second hump >2.5 mm' is not a standard criterion; drop it. Preferred term is 'left atrial abnormality': a prolonged notched P may come from interatrial conduction delay (interatrial block) as well as LA dilatation. Sensitivity against echo/MRI is low; specificity is moderate.

checks.source: Waggoner AD et al. Left atrial enlargement: echocardiographic assessment of ECG criteria. Circulation 1976;54:553-557 (coarse vs fine f waves unreliable for predicting LAE); later f-wave amplitude studies give conflicting results, some showing smaller f waves with larger LA
checks.current_value: f-wave amplitude (coarse >1 mm vs fine ≤1 mm in V1) should not be taught as a marker of LA size; LA size in AF is judged by imaging (echo LA volume index)
checks.note: Coarse vs fine can still be described as an f-wave feature (it matters when telling AF from flutter or artefact), but it should not be graded as LA enlargement.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (biatrial abnormality = features of both; corroborated by SA Heart J 2009 summary citing Part V); Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice 6th ed.
checks.current_value: Biatrial abnormality = RAA plus LAA signs together, e.g. P in II >2.5 mm AND ≥120 ms; or biphasic V1 P with initial positive >1.5 mm AND terminal negative ≥1 mm and ≥40 ms; or tall limb-lead P (>2.5 mm) with LAA-type V1 terminal negativity; or broad notched limb-lead P (≥120 ms) with tall initial V1 positivity
checks.note: The book's 0.10 s duration cut-off is internally inconsistent and below the current LAA limit. Use 120 ms. The combination approach (limb-lead sign of one atrium plus V1 sign of the other) is still valid.

checks.source: Sokolow M, Lyon TP. Am Heart J 1949;37:161-186; Hancock 2009 Part V; Williams B et al. 2018 ESC/ESH hypertension guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021-3104 and McEvoy JW et al. 2024 ESC hypertension guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912-4018 (ECG LVH: Sokolow-Lyon >35 mm, RaVL ≥11 mm, Cornell voltage/product)
checks.current_value: Sokolow-Lyon: S V1 + the larger of R V5 or R V6 >35 mm (≥3.5 mV). Companion criterion R aVL ≥11 mm. Left axis deviation (≥ -30°) is not an LVH voltage criterion; it is a supportive item (2 points in Romhilt-Estes) and usually means LAFB
checks.note: The book's R V6-only version underestimates the index. LAD should not be presented as an LVH criterion on its own. Sokolow-Lyon is unspecific in young adults (<35-40 y), athletes and thin people, and insensitive in obesity and in women.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (no single criterion; use validated criteria); Pewsner D et al. BMJ 2007;335:711 (limb-lead indexes such as Gubner have median sensitivity ~10%)
checks.current_value: Not part of current core teaching. Historical value: Lewis index >+17 mm suggests LVH and < -14 mm suggests RVH. Teach Sokolow-Lyon, Cornell voltage/product, R aVL and Peguero-Lo Presti instead
checks.note: The numbers are historically correct (Lewis 1914). Keep it at most as an optional historical footnote; do not grade learners on it.

checks.source: Surawicz B et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part III: Intraventricular conduction disturbances. Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240 (uses 'R-wave peak time'); Romhilt DW, Estes EH. Am Heart J 1968;75:752-758
checks.current_value: R-wave peak time (QRS onset to R peak): normal <35 ms in V1 and <45 ms in V5-V6; ≥50 ms in V5/V6 supports LVH (Romhilt-Estes 1 point); >60 ms in V5-V6 is part of LBBB; >50 ms in V1 is part of RBBB
checks.note: Values are current. Rename it in the app: 'R-wave peak time' is the standard term, and 'intrinsicoid deflection' should appear only as a synonym.

checks.source: Surawicz B, Knilans T. Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice 6th ed. 2008 (LVH: deep S V1-V3, possible poor R progression/pseudo-infarct QS in V1-V2); MacKenzie R. Poor R-wave progression. J Insur Med 2005;37:58-62 (LVH as a cause); ESC 2023 cardiomyopathy guidelines, Arbelo E et al. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503-3626 (deep narrow Q in HCM)
checks.current_value: Mainstream teaching: LVH gives deep S in V1-V3 and tall R in V5-V6/aVL; R progression may be poor and the transition delayed (QS/rS in V1-V2 can mimic anterior MI). Deep narrow q in V5-V6 (and inferior leads) suggests septal hypertrophy (e.g. HCM); septal q may also be absent with LVH and incomplete left-sided conduction delay
checks.note: The book's 'transition shifted right (RS in V1-V2, qRs in V3-V4)' conflicts with the usual description. It may reflect a different rotation convention (Mexican/Spanish school) or apply only to septal-dominant/volume-overload forms. Check the original wording before teaching. The deep-q part is acceptable.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (prefers 'secondary ST-T abnormality' to 'strain'; corroborated by SA Heart J 2009 summary of Part V); Okin PM et al. LIFE study, JAMA 2004;292:2343-2349 (prognostic value of strain pattern)
checks.current_value: LVH with secondary ST-T (repolarization) abnormality: downsloping/horizontal ST depression with asymmetric T inversion opposite the dominant R in I, aVL, V5-V6 (often with reciprocal ST elevation and upright T in V1-V3)
checks.note: The morphology is correct. Use 'secondary repolarization abnormality' rather than 'strain' or 'systolic overload'. The pattern does not reliably separate pressure from volume load. Digoxin, ischemia and LBBB mimic it. It carries adverse prognosis.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (discourages inferring hemodynamic type and labels such as 'strain'/'overload'; exact wording on 'systolic/diastolic overload' not verified against the paywalled full text); Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice 6th ed.
checks.current_value: Do not teach a distinct 'diastolic (volume) overload' ECG. Describe as LVH voltage with or without repolarization abnormality. Prominent narrow q waves and tall upright T in V5-V6 can be seen in chronic AR/MR but are nonspecific and do not reliably identify volume overload
checks.note: The Cabrera-Monroy systolic/diastolic overload split correlates poorly with hemodynamics or echo. If kept, label it as a historical concept. Tall, peaked symmetric T waves must also be told apart from hyperkalemia and hyperacute T waves.

checks.source: Pewsner D et al. Accuracy of electrocardiography in diagnosis of LVH in arterial hypertension: systematic review. BMJ 2007;335:711 (median sensitivity 10.5% Gubner to 21% Sokolow-Lyon; median specificity 89-99%); Peguero JG et al. JACC 2017;69:1694-1703
checks.current_value: Classic voltage criteria: sensitivity ~10-25% (median; individual studies up to ~50%), specificity ~85-99% vs echo. Peguero-Lo Presti: ~45-62% sensitivity at ~90% specificity. A normal ECG does not exclude LVH
checks.note: The book's ~50% sensitivity is too optimistic for single criteria. Factors that lower voltage: obesity, female sex, older age, COPD/emphysema, pericardial/pleural effusion, coexisting RVH. Factors that raise it: young age, male sex, Black race, thin chest wall, athletic training.

checks.source: Romhilt DW, Estes EH Jr. A point-score system for the ECG diagnosis of LVH. Am Heart J 1968;75:752-758; Hancock 2009 Part V
checks.current_value: Voltage (any: largest limb-lead R or S ≥20 mm; S V1 or V2 ≥30 mm; R V5 or V6 ≥30 mm) 3 pts; typical ST-T opposite QRS: 3 pts without digitalis, 1 pt with digitalis; LA abnormality (V1 terminal P negativity ≥1 mm deep and ≥40 ms) 3 pts; left axis ≥ -30° 2 pts; QRS duration ≥90 ms 1 pt; R-wave peak time V5/V6 ≥50 ms 1 pt. Max 13: ≥5 = LVH, 4 = probable LVH
checks.note: Teach the original table, not the scanned variant with the missing axis item and different QRS scoring. Sensitivity in modern echo studies is low (~15-35%) with high specificity.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (per SA Heart J 2009 summary: R V1 >7 mm, S V1 <2 mm, qR V1, RAD >+110°, secondary right precordial T inversion, R V1 + S V5/V6 >10.5 mm; no single criterion recommended); Chou's 6th ed.
checks.current_value: RVH constellation: RAD ≥+110° (adults); R V1 ≥7 mm; R/S V1 >1 (Cabrera R/(R+S) ≥0.5 is equivalent); S V1 <2 mm; qR in V1 (most specific); S V5/V6 ≥7 mm with R/S V5/V6 ≤1; R V1 + S V5/V6 >10.5 mm; R-wave peak time V1 ≥35 ms; R aVR ≥5 mm; secondary ST-T in V1-V3. Exclude RBBB, posterior MI, WPW, HCM, dextrocardia/lead error and normal youth
checks.note: These are still the taught criteria, but each has low sensitivity. Teach them as a constellation. A tall R in aVR is a general RVH sign, not specific to outflow obstruction. Isolated RAD may be LPFB, lateral MI, lean habitus or COPD. In athletes, RAD >120° is only 'borderline'.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V ('secondary ST-T abnormality' preferred to 'strain'; via SA Heart J 2009 summary)
checks.current_value: RVH with secondary ST-T abnormality: asymmetric T inversion ± ST depression in V1-V3 (sometimes to V4 and in II/III/aVF) in leads with tall R
checks.note: The morphology is correct. Use 'RVH with secondary repolarization abnormality' instead of 'systolic overload'/'strain'. Teach the differential with ischemic T inversion and with acute RV overload (PE).

checks.source: Flowers NC, Horan LG. In: Schlant RC, Hurst JW (eds). Advances in Electrocardiography. Grune & Stratton 1972; Hancock 2009 Part V (no single criterion or score recommended for RVH); Butler PM et al. Am J Cardiol 1986;57:639-643
checks.current_value: Not part of current teaching. Teach the Part V RVH constellation. If a formula is wanted, use Butler-Leggett: A + R - PL ≥0.70 mV (A = largest R or R' in V1/V2; R = largest S in I or V6; PL = S in V1)
checks.note: The point table could not be verified against a primary source and one item is illegible in the scan, so do not publish an incomplete score. Leave it out or mark it as historical.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (RAD with LVH voltage, or large biphasic RS in several precordial leads, suggests BVH; via e-cardiogram.com summary); Katz LN, Wachtel H. Am Heart J 1937;13:202-206
checks.current_value: BVH suggested by LVH voltage plus RVH signs: LVH criteria with RAD (>+90°); or LVH with tall R in V1-V2 or deep S in V5-V6; or large equiphasic RS in V2-V4 with R+S ≥50-60 mm (Katz-Wachtel, mainly in children with congenital disease); LA abnormality plus RVH signs also raises suspicion
checks.note: The book's pattern is acceptable. Add the 'LVH + RAD' rule. Sensitivity is very low because opposing forces cancel. The Katz-Wachtel threshold is pediatric. Deep q in V5-V6 is supportive only.

checks.source: Hancock 2009 Part V; Heller J et al. 'Crochetage' (notch) on R wave in inferior limb leads: a new independent ECG sign of atrial septal defect. Circulation 1996;93:1440-1446; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines for adult congenital heart disease, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645
checks.current_value: Chronic RV volume load (classically secundum ASD): rsR'/rSR' in V1 (incomplete RBBB pattern) with rightward axis; often with crochetage notch on R in II, III, aVF and first-degree AV block. Primum ASD: rsR' with LEFT axis deviation
checks.note: The pattern is correct. Add the crochetage sign and the primum-ASD contrast. Prefer 'RV volume load' to 'diastolic overload'.

missing_criteria.value: S V3 + R aVL >28 mm in men, >20 mm in women
missing_criteria.source: Casale PN et al. Circulation 1985;72:565-573; Hancock 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part V; 2018 ESC/ESH and 2024 ESC hypertension guidelines

missing_criteria.value: (R aVL + S V3, adding 6 mm in women) × QRS duration >2440 mm·ms
missing_criteria.source: Molloy TJ et al. JACC 1992;20:1180-1186; Okin PM et al. (LIFE) JAMA 2004;292:2343-2349; 2018 ESC/ESH and 2024 ESC hypertension guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Deepest S in any lead + S V4 ≥28 mm in men, ≥23 mm in women (sensitivity ~45-62%, specificity ~90%)
missing_criteria.source: Peguero JG et al. J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1694-1703

missing_criteria.value: R aVL ≥11 mm (Sokolow); R I + S III >25 mm (Gubner-Ungerleider): high specificity, very low sensitivity
missing_criteria.source: Hancock 2009 Part V; 2024 ESC hypertension guidelines (R aVL ≥11 mm); Pewsner D et al. BMJ 2007;335:711

missing_criteria.value: LAFB: R-wave criteria in I/aVL are unreliable; use S-wave-based criteria (e.g. S III + max precordial R+S ≥30 mm men / ≥28 mm women). LBBB: voltage criteria unreliable, so diagnose LVH only with great caution. RBBB: standard criteria lose sensitivity
missing_criteria.source: Hancock 2009 Part V (LAFB caveat quoted in Ann Noninvasive Electrocardiol 2013 reexamination); Gertsch M et al. Am J Cardiol 1988;61:1098-1101

missing_criteria.value: 'Right/left/biatrial abnormality' instead of enlargement/hypertrophy/overload/strain. 'LVH/RVH with secondary ST-T (repolarization) abnormality' instead of 'strain'. Do not infer pressure vs volume load from the ECG
missing_criteria.source: Hancock 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS Part V (corroborated by SA Heart J 2009;6(4):258-259 summary)

missing_criteria.value: Partial IAB: P ≥120 ms. Advanced IAB: P ≥120 ms with biphasic (+/-) P in II, III and aVF. A conduction disorder distinct from LA enlargement, linked to AF and stroke (Bayés syndrome)
missing_criteria.source: Bayés de Luna A et al. Interatrial blocks: a separate entity from left atrial enlargement. Consensus report. J Electrocardiol 2012;45:445-451

missing_criteria.parameter: P-terminal force in V1 (Morris index), quantitative
missing_criteria.value: Depth (mm) × duration (s) of the terminal negative P in V1 ≥0.04 mm·s (e.g. ≥1 mm deep and ≥40 ms); abnormal PTFV1 is also linked to AF and stroke risk
missing_criteria.source: Morris JJ et al. Circulation 1964;29:242-252; Hancock 2009 Part V; Romhilt & Estes 1968

missing_criteria.value: Isolated QRS voltage criteria for LVH or RVH = normal training-related finding (no work-up unless T inversion, ST depression, pathological Q or symptoms). LAE, RAE, LAD (-30° to -90°) and RAD (>120°) = 'borderline': one alone needs no work-up; two or more warrant evaluation
missing_criteria.source: Sharma S, Drezner JA et al. International recommendations for ECG interpretation in athletes. Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466-1480 / J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057-1075

missing_criteria.value: Voltage is higher in young adults, men, Black individuals and thin chests, and lower in women, older age, obesity, COPD and effusion. Use sex-specific criteria (Cornell) and interpret voltage-only LVH in people under ~35-40 y with caution
missing_criteria.source: Hancock 2009 Part V; Pewsner D et al. BMJ 2007;335:711

missing_criteria.value: R ≥ S in V1: RVH vs RBBB (wide QRS), posterior MI (inferior Q, upright T V1), WPW with left-sided pathway (delta wave, short PR), HCM, dextrocardia/lead misplacement, Duchenne dystrophy, normal in children. Check axis, QRS width, PR/delta and T direction before calling RVH
missing_criteria.source: Surawicz B, Knilans T. Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice 6th ed. 2008; SA Heart J 2009;6(4):258-259 (ECG quiz review based on Part V)

missing_criteria.value: Low limb-lead voltage, tall P in inferior leads with vertical/rightward P axis, rightward or indeterminate QRS axis (S1S2S3), rS complexes across the precordium with poor R progression; classic RVH criteria are insensitive here
missing_criteria.source: Hancock 2009 Part V; Chou's 6th ed.

missing_criteria.value: Sinus tachycardia; new complete/incomplete RBBB; S1Q3T3; T inversion in V1-V4 (± inferior); right axis shift; qR in V1; ST elevation in aVR/V1. Low sensitivity, but RV-overload signs carry prognostic weight
missing_criteria.source: Konstantinides SV et al. 2019 ESC Guidelines for acute pulmonary embolism. Eur Heart J 2020;41:543-603

missing_criteria.value: LVH causes discordant ST elevation in V1-V3 opposite deep S waves. Suspect superimposed STEMI if ST elevation ≥25% of the preceding QRS (S) amplitude, if ST elevation is convex, or if it is new
missing_criteria.source: Armstrong EJ et al. Am J Cardiol 2012;110:977-983; Thygesen K et al. Fourth Universal Definition of MI. Circulation 2018;138:e618-e651 (LVH listed as an ST-elevation confounder)

missing_criteria.entity: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and infiltrative LV thickening
missing_criteria.value: HCM: LVH voltage with repolarization abnormality, deep narrow Q waves (inferolateral), giant negative T waves (≥10 mm) in V2-V5 in apical HCM, LA abnormality. Amyloidosis: increased wall thickness with LOW or normal QRS voltage (voltage-mass discordance), pseudo-infarct Q waves
missing_criteria.leads: V2-V6, I, aVL, II, III, aVF
missing_criteria.source: Arbelo E et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies. Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503-3626; Garcia-Pavia P et al. ESC position statement on cardiac amyloidosis. Eur Heart J 2021;42:1554-1568

missing_criteria.value: RV dominance is normal in neonates and infants, so use age-specific percentile tables. An upright T in V1 between ~1 week of age and late childhood suggests RVH. qR in V1 is abnormal at any age
missing_criteria.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. New normal limits for the paediatric ECG. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711; Hancock 2009 Part V (pediatric criteria differ)

missing_criteria.value: A + R - PL ≥0.70 mV, where A = largest R or R' in V1/V2, R = largest S in I or V6, PL = S in V1
missing_criteria.source: Butler PM, Leggett SI et al. Am J Cardiol 1986;57:639-643

checks.current_value: Complete RBBB or LBBB in adults: QRS ≥120 ms (use ≥, not >). Incomplete RBBB or LBBB in adults: QRS 110–119 ms, with the matching morphology. Children: complete BBB means QRS >100 ms at 4–16 y and >90 ms under 4 y. Incomplete RBBB: 90–100 ms at 8–16 y and 86–90 ms under 8 y. Incomplete LBBB: 90–100 ms at 8–16 y and 80–90 ms under 8 y.
checks.note: The ≥120 ms cutoff for complete BBB is still current. Two parts need fixing. First, the book's Table 6.1 uses '>0.12 s', which conflicts with its own intro; use ≥120 ms. Second, 'incomplete <0.12 s' has no lower bound. A pattern with QRS under 110 ms, such as rSr' in V1, is usually a normal variant and should not be called incomplete BBB. The app's grading should also make the cutoff age-dependent.
checks.source: Surawicz B et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part III: Intraventricular Conduction Disturbances. Circulation 2009;119:e235–e240; J Am Coll Cardiol 2009;53:976–981.

checks.current_value: QRS ≥120 ms. V1 or V2 shows rsr', rsR' or rSR', with R' usually wider than the first R; a minority show a broad, often notched R. In I and V6 the S wave lasts longer than the R wave or more than 40 ms. R-peak time is normal in V5–V6 and >50 ms in V1. Criteria 1–3 are required. When V1 has a pure dominant R, the V1 R-peak criterion is also required. Secondary ST-T changes run opposite the terminal QRS deflection, so T is negative in V1–V2 and upright in I and V6.
checks.note: The book's morphology description agrees with current teaching. The axis remark beyond +80° (in the context field) should not be taught as a feature of RBBB. Isolated RBBB barely changes the frontal axis, which is usually normal. A clearly right axis (≥+90° to +180°) with RBBB suggests added LPFB, or RVH. A clearly left axis (−45° to −90°) suggests added LAFB. Add the AHA quantitative criteria (S-wave duration in I/V6, R-peak time in V1) to make grading reproducible.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235–e240).

checks.current_value: Same QRS morphology as complete RBBB, but QRS 110–119 ms in adults (90–100 ms at 8–16 y; 86–90 ms under 8 y). An rSr' in V1 with QRS <110 ms is a common normal variant and should not be labelled incomplete RBBB.
checks.note: The book sets only an upper limit (<120 ms). Without the 110 ms lower limit, students will over-call normal rSr' patterns. Incomplete RBBB is also classed as a normal, training-related finding in athletes. Teach the differential of rSr' in V1: normal variant, Brugada type 2, ASD/RV volume overload, pectus excavatum, and high placement of V1–V2.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III; Drezner JA et al. International recommendations for ECG interpretation in athletes, J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057–1075 / Br J Sports Med 2017;51:704–731.

checks.current_value: QRS ≥120 ms. Broad R waves, notched or slurred, in I, aVL, V5 and V6; V5–V6 may occasionally show RS because the transition is displaced. No q waves in I, V5 or V6, though a narrow q in aVL can be normal. R-peak time >60 ms in V5–V6 and normal in V1–V3 when a small initial r is present. V1–V2 show QS or rS. ST-T is usually discordant to the QRS. Positive concordance (upright T where the QRS is upright) can be normal. Negative concordance (ST depression or T inversion where the QRS is negative) is abnormal. LBBB may shift the frontal axis right, left or superiorly, sometimes depending on rate, so the axis is not a diagnostic criterion.
checks.note: The precordial morphology and the discordant, asymmetric negative T in V5–V6 are still current. The outdated part is listing an axis of −15° to −60° (or 0° to −60°) as a defining feature. Most LBBB has a normal or mildly left axis. Marked left axis deviation is a separate marker of more extensive conduction disease or LV disease. Also correct the absolute 'no q in aVL' (a narrow q in aVL is allowed) and add the R-peak time and ST-T concordance rules. For CRT selection, the stricter Strauss definition is used (see missing criteria).
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz et al.); Strauss DG, Selvester RH, Wagner GS. Am J Cardiol 2011;107:927–934.

checks.current_value: Grading incomplete LBBB into grades I–II is no longer used. Current adult criteria for incomplete LBBB: QRS 110–119 ms, an LVH pattern, R-peak time >60 ms in V4–V6, and no q wave in I, V5 and V6.
checks.note: Losing the septal q in V5–V6 on its own is nonspecific. It occurs with LVH, lead placement, rotation and normal variants, so a 'grade I' diagnosis is not reproducible. Teach incomplete LBBB with the AHA four-part definition, or as nonspecific IVCD when it does not fit. The Sodi-Pallares grades can stay as a historical or mechanistic note only.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz et al.).

checks.current_value: Frontal QRS axis −45° to −90°; qR in aVL; R-peak time in aVL ≥45 ms; QRS <120 ms. rS in II, III and aVF follows from the axis and is the usual supporting finding. These criteria do not apply to infants with congenital heart disease who have left axis deviation.
checks.note: The book's axis range is wrong at both ends. The −75° upper limit is too narrow, because LAFB extends to −90°. The text's 'beyond −30°' is too loose: an axis between −30° and −44° is left axis deviation, not LAFB. The delayed intrinsicoid deflection in I/aVL is correct and matches the aVL R-peak time ≥45 ms. Also teach the pitfalls. LAFB can hide or imitate an inferior MI. It can produce small q waves or poor R progression in V1–V3. It lowers inferior R waves and raises aVL voltage, which affects LVH criteria.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz et al.).

checks.current_value: Frontal axis +90° to +180° in adults (in children up to 16 y, use only when a distinct rightward axis shift is documented); rS in I and aVL; qR in III and aVF; QRS <120 ms. This is a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out RVH, lateral MI, a vertical heart or slender build, acute RV strain/PE, emphysema, and limb-lead reversal.
checks.note: The book's +90° to +120° range is narrower than the current +90° to +180°. Some textbooks require ≥+100° or ≥+120° to improve specificity, so the app should state which threshold it uses. A prolonged R-peak time in the inferior leads (aVF) is an acceptable supporting sign, but it is not one of the AHA criteria. Excluding other causes is mandatory and is missing from the book's list.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz et al.).

checks.current_value: RBBB plus LAFB: RBBB morphology with a frontal axis −45° to −90° (qR in aVL, rS in the inferior leads), with a broad terminal S inferiorly and a terminal R in aVR. RBBB plus LPFB: RBBB morphology with a frontal axis of +90° to +180° (rS in I/aVL, qR in III/aVF), after other causes of right axis deviation are excluded. Many guideline documents also count complete LBBB as a bifascicular lesion.
checks.note: The concept and the morphologies described are current. Diagnose the fascicular component with the same axis cutoffs as isolated LAFB/LPFB, not the book's 'about −60°'. Clinical teaching should add three points. Asymptomatic bifascicular block is not an indication for pacing. Unexplained syncope with bifascicular block calls for an EP study, and pacing is indicated if HV ≥70 ms or infra-Hisian block is induced. RBBB with LPFB is less common and carries a higher risk of progression than RBBB with LAFB.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III; Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427–3520; Kusumoto FM et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia and conduction delay guideline, Circulation 2019;140:e382–e482.

checks.current_value: Do not use 'trifascicular block' for bifascicular block plus PR >200 ms. Describe each component instead, e.g. 'RBBB + LAFB + first-degree AV block'. The PR prolongation is usually AV nodal, and the risk of progression is close to that of bifascicular block alone. Reserve the idea of three-fascicle disease for evidence actually seen on the ECG. Alternating BBB (RBBB and LBBB on the same or successive ECGs, or RBBB+LAFB alternating with RBBB+LPFB) is a Class I pacing indication even without symptoms. Complete AV block with a wide infranodal escape is another such case.
checks.note: Both of the book's definitions are problematic. 'RBBB + both left fascicles' block persistently would itself produce complete AV block. 'Bifascicular block + long PR' is the misnomer that current standards advise against, because the surface ECG cannot locate the PR delay.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (recommends against the term 'trifascicular block'); 2021 ESC pacing/CRT guidelines (alternating BBB: Class I pacing); 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline.

checks.current_value: Masquerading BBB, standard (limb-lead) form: RBBB pattern in the precordial leads (dominant, wide R' in V1). The limb leads look like LBBB: broad R with no or tiny S in I/aVL, rS/QS inferiorly, and marked left axis deviation. Mechanism: RBBB plus severe LAFB, often with LVH or a lateral/anterior infarct, which hides the terminal S in I/aVL. A precordial form also exists, with LBBB-like V5–V6 despite RBBB in V1. It marks advanced conduction-system and myocardial disease with a poor prognosis.
checks.note: The pattern described matches current descriptions. It is rare and specialist-level; teach it as a recognition pattern rather than core material. The AHA 2009 statement does not cover it.
checks.source: Elizari MV, Baranchuk A, Chiale PA. Masquerading bundle branch block: a variety of right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block. Expert Rev Cardiovasc Ther 2013;11:69–75; original description Richman JL, Wolff L. Am Heart J 1954;47:383–393.

checks.current_value: Intermittent BBB can be acceleration-dependent: it appears when the heart rate rises above a critical rate (cycle length shortens) and usually resolves only at a slower rate than the onset rate, a hysteresis effect. It can also be deceleration-dependent: it appears after long pauses or at slow rates. BBB can occur in a 2:1 pattern, with every other beat conducted with BBB. Related phenomenon: Ashman aberrancy after a long-short cycle in AF.
checks.note: The book's statement is correct but incomplete. Add the deceleration-dependent form and the hysteresis effect. Keep 2:1 rate-related BBB, the same block appearing on every other beat, clearly separate from alternating BBB (RBBB ↔ LBBB). Alternating BBB is a different entity and a Class I pacing indication. Rate-related LBBB can also shift the frontal axis.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (rate-dependent change of QRS and axis in LBBB); 2021 ESC pacing/CRT guidelines (alternating BBB).

missing_criteria.value: QRS >110 ms in adults (>90 ms at 8–16 y; >80 ms under 8 y) that does not meet RBBB or LBBB morphology criteria. In athletes, profound nonspecific IVCD ≥140 ms is abnormal and needs evaluation.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III (Surawicz et al.); 2017 International criteria for ECG interpretation in athletes (Drezner et al.).
missing_criteria.leads: All 12 leads; morphology in V1 and V6 decides between RBBB, LBBB and IVCD.

missing_criteria.value: RBBB: >50 ms in V1 (normal in V5–V6). LBBB: >60 ms in V5–V6 (normal in V1–V3). Incomplete LBBB: >60 ms in V4–V6. LAFB: ≥45 ms in aVL.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III.

missing_criteria.value: Discordant ST-T is expected. Upright T with upright QRS (positive concordance) may be normal. ST depression or T inversion in leads with a negative QRS (negative concordance) is abnormal.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III.
