missing_criteria.leads: V1–V3 (negative QRS), I, aVL, V5–V6 (positive QRS)

missing_criteria.entity: Acute MI in LBBB or ventricular paced rhythm
missing_criteria.value: Any of: concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm in a lead with positive QRS; concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3; excessively discordant ST elevation. The original Sgarbossa threshold for discordant elevation is ≥5 mm. Smith's modification uses an ST/S ratio ≤ −0.25 (ST elevation ≥1 mm divided by the depth of the preceding S), which is more sensitive.
missing_criteria.source: Sgarbossa EB et al. N Engl J Med 1996;334:481–487; Smith SW et al. Ann Emerg Med 2012;60:766–776; Thygesen K et al. Fourth Universal Definition of MI 2018 (Circulation 2018;138:e618–e651); Byrne RA et al. 2023 ESC ACS guidelines (Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826).
missing_criteria.leads: Every lead; V1–V3 for concordant ST depression.

missing_criteria.entity: Bundle branch block in suspected ACS
missing_criteria.value: LBBB or RBBB (new or previously known) with ongoing symptoms suggestive of myocardial ischaemia should prompt a primary-PCI (STEMI-equivalent) strategy. LBBB on its own is not diagnostic of MI. RBBB does not hide pathological Q waves, because initial activation is preserved, and new RBBB in acute MI signals extensive (often proximal LAD) involvement.
missing_criteria.source: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes (Byrne RA et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826); Fourth Universal Definition of MI 2018.

missing_criteria.parameter: Strauss criteria and CRT QRS thresholds
missing_criteria.value: Strict LBBB requires all of: QRS ≥140 ms (men) or ≥130 ms (women); QS or rS in V1 and V2; mid-QRS notching or slurring in ≥2 of V1, V2, V5, V6, I, aVL. Guideline CRT thresholds in sinus rhythm with LVEF ≤35%: LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms is Class I; LBBB 130–149 ms is IIa; non-LBBB ≥150 ms is IIa; non-LBBB 130–149 ms is IIb. CRT is not indicated for QRS <130 ms.
missing_criteria.source: Strauss DG, Selvester RH, Wagner GS. Am J Cardiol 2011;107:927–934; 2021 ESC pacing/CRT guidelines (Glikson et al.); 2021 ESC heart failure guidelines (McDonagh et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42:3599–3726).
missing_criteria.leads: V1, V2, V5, V6, I, aVL

missing_criteria.value: ECG evidence of block in all three fascicles on the same or successive tracings: RBBB and LBBB, or RBBB+LAFB and RBBB+LPFB. Permanent pacing is indicated (Class I) even without symptoms.
missing_criteria.source: 2021 ESC pacing/CRT guidelines; 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia and conduction delay guideline (Kusumoto et al.).
missing_criteria.leads: V1, V6, frontal axis (I, II, III, aVF) compared across ECGs

missing_criteria.value: Asymptomatic bifascicular block, with or without first-degree AV block, does not need pacing. Unexplained syncope with bifascicular block calls for an EP study. Pacing is indicated if HV ≥70 ms, second- or third-degree intra- or infra-Hisian block appears with incremental atrial pacing, or a pharmacological challenge is abnormal.
missing_criteria.source: 2021 ESC pacing/CRT guidelines; 2018 ESC syncope guidelines (Brignole et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883–1948).
missing_criteria.leads: Rhythm strip (PR) plus V1/V6 and the frontal axis

missing_criteria.value: Incomplete RBBB is a normal, training-related finding. Complete RBBB, left axis deviation (−30° to −90°) and right axis deviation (>120°) are 'borderline': one alone needs no work-up, but two or more need evaluation. Complete LBBB and nonspecific IVCD ≥140 ms are abnormal and need evaluation.
missing_criteria.source: Drezner JA, Sharma S et al. International recommendations for electrocardiographic interpretation in athletes. J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057–1075.

missing_criteria.entity: rSr' in V1 / incomplete RBBB vs Brugada pattern
missing_criteria.value: Brugada type 1 (diagnostic): coved ST elevation ≥2 mm followed by a negative T in ≥1 right precordial lead (V1–V2, including leads recorded in the 2nd–4th intercostal spaces). Type 2 (saddleback) vs incomplete RBBB: in type 2 the r' is broad and rounded, with a β angle >58° and a wide r' triangle base about 5 mm below its peak (≥3.5–4 mm). The r' of RBBB is narrow and sharp. In Brugada, V6 lacks a matching wide S.
missing_criteria.source: Bayés de Luna A et al. Current electrocardiographic criteria for diagnosis of Brugada pattern: a consensus report. J Electrocardiol 2012;45:433–442; Wilde AAM et al. 2022 EHRA/HRS/APHRS/LAHRS expert consensus on inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes (Europace 2022;24:1307–1367); 2022 ESC VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al.).
missing_criteria.leads: V1, V2 (including high intercostal placement), V6

missing_criteria.value: Typical RBBB or LBBB morphology during tachycardia supports aberrancy. VT is favored by AV dissociation, fusion or capture beats, absent RS in all precordial leads, R-to-S nadir >100 ms in any precordial lead, initial R or Q in aVR (Vereckei), and precordial concordance. When in doubt, treat as VT.
missing_criteria.source: Zeppenfeld K et al. 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of SCD, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126; Brugada P et al. Circulation 1991;83:1649–1659; Vereckei A et al. Heart Rhythm 2008;5:89–98.

missing_criteria.value: Standard voltage criteria lose accuracy in BBB and fascicular block. LAFB lowers inferior R and raises R in aVL, so aVL-based criteria over-call LVH. Adding the S wave in lead III (e.g., S(III) plus the largest precordial R+S ≥30 mm, Gertsch) has been proposed. With LBBB, LVH is very common, and voltage criteria are unreliable and should be read with caution.
missing_criteria.source: Hancock EW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part V: ECG changes associated with cardiac chamber hypertrophy (Circulation 2009;119:e251–e261); Gertsch M et al. Am J Cardiol 1988;61:1098–1101.

checks.source: Josephson ME, Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology (6th ed., 2021); 2021 ESC Guidelines on Cardiac Pacing and CRT (Glikson et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-3520), HV threshold in syncope + bifascicular block
checks.current_value: Normal HV 35-55 ms (unchanged). AH is usually quoted as about 50-120/125 ms and varies with autonomic tone. The book's 140 ms upper limit is generous but acceptable. His deflection is about 15-25 ms. PA is rarely used today. Clinical cut-off: in syncope with bifascicular block, baseline HV >=70 ms makes pacing a Class I indication (ESC 2021).
checks.note: These are intracardiac (EP-lab) values, not surface-ECG criteria. Ranges vary by laboratory, so teach them as approximate. The HV interval is the part most worth teaching because it links infranodal disease to the pacing decision. Optional or advanced content only.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay (Kusumoto et al., JACC 2019;74:e51), Table 3 definitions and Figure 3/7; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 ECG standardization recommendations (age-dependent normal limits)
checks.current_value: PR >200 ms with 1:1 AV conduction. The 2018 guideline says 'AV delay' is the more accurate name, because no P waves are blocked. Pediatric limits depend on age and heart rate: use age-specific tables rather than one 0.18 s cut-off. Marked first-degree block (PR >300 ms) with a narrow QRS usually means delay in the AV node. If symptoms correlate with it (pseudo-pacemaker syndrome), permanent pacing is Class IIa.
checks.note: The adult threshold is correct. The heuristic that a variable PR means a vagal cause and a fixed PR means a structural cause is not guideline teaching. Teach the vagal signature instead: PR lengthens together with sinus slowing and improves with exercise or atropine. Very long PR can bury the P in the preceding T (correct). In athletes, first-degree block is a normal training-related finding; PR >=400 ms needs evaluation (see missing criteria).

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 (Mobitz type I definition) and Figure 3 footnote (narrow-QRS Mobitz I localizes to the AV node); Denes P et al., Am J Cardiol 1975 (frequency of atypical Wenckebach periodicity)
checks.current_value: Constant P rate (<100 bpm). A single non-conducted P, with an inconstant PR before and after the blocked beat. The most reliable sign is that the first PR after the pause is shorter than the last PR before it. RR shortening and a pause <2xPP describe only the typical pattern. Atypical sequences are frequent, especially in long cycles, and may even be the majority. With a narrow QRS the block is almost always in the AV node. With bundle branch block an infranodal Wenckebach is possible.
checks.note: The definition is correct. Present RR shortening as typical but not required, so learners do not miss atypical sequences. The '75% nodal' figure is not a standard quoted number. Teach instead that narrow QRS means very likely nodal, and wide QRS means the site is uncertain. Nocturnal Mobitz I, and Mobitz I in athletes, is usually physiologic (vagal).

checks.source: Classic Wenckebach periodicity analysis, e.g. Surawicz B, Knilans T, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice (6th ed.); Barold SS, Hayes DL, Mayo Clin Proc 2001;76:44-57 (Second-degree AV block: a reappraisal)
checks.current_value: Checked: PR increments are 160, 120 and 80 ms. Each RR equals PP plus that increment: 960, 920 and 880 ms. Pause = 2xPP - (last PR - first PR) = 1600 - 360 = 1240 ms. The book's example is internally consistent and the formula is correct.
checks.note: This holds only for typical Wenckebach (decreasing increments, constant PP). Label it 'typical'. A synthetic generator should also produce atypical sequences (largest increment late, irregular RR) and sinus arrhythmia, so learners do not learn to rely on RR shortening.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 and take-home message 5 (pacing regardless of symptoms); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (Class I pacing for type II second-degree block); Barold SS, Hayes DL, Mayo Clin Proc 2001
checks.current_value: Constant P rate (<100 bpm). A single non-conducted P, with a constant PR in the P waves before and after the block. 2:1 block is excluded from this definition. The block is infranodal (His-Purkinje), usually with a wide QRS. Narrow-QRS Mobitz II implies an intra-Hisian site. Once reversible causes are excluded, permanent pacing is Class I regardless of symptoms.
checks.note: Two refinements are needed. (1) Constant PP is mandatory: a non-conducted premature P (blocked PAC) must be excluded, and so must vagal 'pseudo-Mobitz II', where sinus slowing comes with the dropped beat. (2) 'Always structural' should read 'true Mobitz II indicates His-Purkinje disease'. Sudden progression to complete block is correct teaching.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 (2:1 AV block; advanced/high-grade AV block definitions) and Figure 3 (2:1 = site unclear, use exercise testing or EPS); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines
checks.current_value: Ratios are written as P waves : QRS complexes. 3:2 means one P blocked in every three. 3:1 means two consecutive P waves blocked for each conducted beat, which is high-grade block. High-grade (advanced) AV block: >=2 consecutive P waves at a constant physiologic rate fail to conduct, with evidence of some AV conduction. 2:1 AV block: P waves at a constant rate where every other P conducts. It cannot be typed as Mobitz I or II from the 2:1 segment alone.
checks.note: The book's notation ('3:1 = one P blocked in every 3') conflicts with the standard P:QRS convention. Do not teach it; it would make students mislabel strips. A constant PR in conducted beats is not part of the 2018 definition. It is a useful sign that conduction exists (versus complete block), but it is not a defining criterion. For 2:1 block, teach the site clues. Narrow QRS with long PR points to the AV node. Wide QRS with normal PR points to infranodal block. Block that improves with atropine or exercise is nodal; block that worsens is infranodal. Look in a longer strip for 3:2 Wenckebach periods.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 (third-degree AV block: no evidence of AV conduction); Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography (ventriculophasic sinus arrhythmia)
checks.current_value: No evidence of AV conduction. Atria and ventricles are independent, the atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate, the PR varies at random, and the escape rhythm is regular. P waves must be seen falling at all points of the cycle, including outside the refractory period, without conducting.
checks.note: The criteria are correct. Add these points. (a) An apparent 'complete' block with occasional captures is high-grade block, not complete block. (b) Ventriculophasic sinus arrhythmia: PP intervals that contain a QRS are shorter. (c) In atrial fibrillation, complete AV block shows as a slow, regular ventricular rhythm.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline (site-of-block evaluation, Figure 3); Josephson, Clinical Cardiac Electrophysiology (2021); Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography
checks.current_value: A narrow-QRS escape at about 40-60 bpm suggests block in the AV node or the His bundle (junctional escape). A wide-QRS escape at about 20-40 bpm suggests infranodal block (fascicular or ventricular escape). Infranodal block is the commonest site in acquired adult complete AV block. Escape morphology: an LV focus gives an RBBB-like QRS and an RV focus gives an LBBB-like QRS.
checks.note: This is acceptable teaching, with caveats. A narrow escape does not exclude intra-Hisian block. A wide escape can be a junctional escape conducted with pre-existing bundle branch block, so compare with a previous ECG. The 30-40% vs 60-70% split is approximate. Escape rate and stability matter for prognosis.

checks.source: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes (Byrne et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines, section on pacing after acute MI (permanent pacing only if block persists after a waiting period, at least 5 days); 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Table 8 (aminophylline for AV block in inferior MI); Gang UJ et al., Europace 2012 (HAVB ~3% in primary-PCI STEMI); Kosmidou I et al., Am J Cardiol 2017;119:1295 (HORIZONS-AMI: HAVB linked to higher 1-year mortality, adjusted HR 2.45); Korean multicenter registry, Korean Circ J 2016 (HAVB independently predicts in-hospital death in anterior but not inferior STEMI)
checks.current_value: The site distinction still holds. Inferior MI (usually RCA): AV-nodal block that progresses gradually through Wenckebach, with a narrow escape. It often has vagal or ischemic causes, is usually transient and resolves after reperfusion. Treat with atropine, and aminophylline if atropine fails. Anterior MI: infranodal block from extensive septal necrosis, often preceded by new bundle branch or bifascicular block. Onset is sudden with a slow wide escape; it marks a large infarct and carries high mortality. In primary-PCI STEMI, high-grade AV block occurs in roughly 2-5% of patients. It raises early mortality, most strongly in anterior MI.
checks.note: The mortality figures (20-25% inferior, 70-80% anterior) come from the pre-reperfusion era. Do not present them as current. One recent single-centre primary-PCI cohort reported in-hospital mortality of about 13% (inferior) vs about 53% (anterior) with complete AV block. Use relative risk wording rather than fixed percentages. Permanent pacing is deferred unless high-grade or complete block persists after the waiting period. Temporary pacing is used for haemodynamically significant bradycardia.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Figure 3 (exercise testing, Class IIa, to localize unclear block such as 2:1); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (exercise testing for exertional symptoms; exercise-induced second- or third-degree block implies infranodal disease and is a pacing indication)
checks.current_value: Exercise normally shortens the PR. Nodal block (Mobitz I, nodal 2:1) improves with sympathetic drive. Infranodal block worsens as the atrial rate rises. Second- or third-degree AV block that appears during exercise is almost always infranodal and warrants pacing.
checks.note: The core teaching is current. The statement that complete block in recovery is serious is less established. AV block appearing only in early recovery is more often vagally mediated, but infranodal disease must still be excluded. The strongest red flag is block that appears or worsens during exercise.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 (sinoatrial exit block with group beating; sinus pause >3 s; sinus node arrest); Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography
checks.current_value: Second-degree SA exit block, type II: the pause is about an exact multiple of the basic PP (within sinus-arrhythmia tolerance). Type I SA Wenckebach: PP intervals progressively shorten, then a pause shorter than 2xPP, giving group beating. Sinus arrest: no relation to the PP. First-degree SA block is invisible on the surface ECG. Third-degree SA block looks the same as sinus arrest. A sinus pause >3 s is the guideline definition of a significant pause.
checks.note: Correct. Add three things. (1) 'Exact multiple' should be 'approximately', because sinus arrhythmia makes the multiple imprecise. (2) Add the type I SA Wenckebach pattern. (3) The first step is to look for a non-conducted premature P' in the preceding T wave. This is correct and is the commonest cause of an unexpected pause.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, take-home message 4, Figure 2 (evaluation: ambulatory monitoring Class I chosen by symptom frequency, exercise test Class IIa, EPS not primarily for SND Class IIb) and Figure 6 (pacing Class I if symptoms correlate; pacing in asymptomatic SND Class III: Harm); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (SND and reflex-syncope recommendations)
checks.current_value: No minimum heart rate or pause length on its own triggers pacing in SND. Pacing is Class I when symptoms correlate with bradycardia, and for symptomatic tachy-brady syndrome. Pacing for asymptomatic SND is Class III (Harm) in the 2018 guideline. ESC 2021: in patients over 40 with recurrent unpredictable syncope, dual-chamber pacing is indicated for a documented symptomatic pause >3 s or an asymptomatic pause >6 s due to sinus arrest or AV block. Diagnosis: match the monitor to symptom frequency. Use 24-48 h Holter for daily symptoms, 2-4 week patch or event recorder for less frequent ones, and an implantable loop recorder for rare ones. Use an exercise test for chronotropic incompetence (failure to reach 80% of expected heart-rate reserve).
checks.note: 'Pauses >3 s' as a pacing trigger without symptoms is outdated. The atropine test (rate rise <20-25% or failure to exceed about 90 bpm) is a historical test that current guidelines do not recommend. Atropine now appears only as acute treatment: 0.5-1 mg IV every 3-5 min, up to 3 mg.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 (isorhythmic dissociation: atrial rate slower than the AV-nodal, His or ventricular rate); 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of SCD (AV dissociation, capture and fusion beats as VT criteria); Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography
checks.current_value: AV dissociation describes independent atrial and ventricular activity; it is not a diagnosis. Mechanisms: (1) slowing of the sinus node with a junctional or ventricular escape; (2) acceleration of a subsidiary pacemaker (accelerated junctional rhythm, VT); (3) AV block; or a combination. In AV dissociation without block, the ventricular rate equals or exceeds the atrial rate. Variants are complete, incomplete (with capture beats) and isorhythmic.
checks.note: The book's narrow usage (ventricular rate > atrial rate, i.e. dissociation without block) is a recognized convention (Marriott school) and is pedagogically useful: 'AV dissociation is not the same as complete heart block'. Many current texts also describe complete AV block as 'AV dissociation due to block'. Teach both usages explicitly. Add that AV dissociation in a wide-QRS tachycardia is close to diagnostic of VT.

checks.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 9 (degenerative causes: Lev's and Lenègre's diseases; genetic causes such as SCN5A; iatrogenic causes including TAVR); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (progressive cardiac conduction disease, genetic forms); Baruteau AE et al., Eur J Pediatr / Nat Rev Cardiol reviews on progressive cardiac conduction disease
checks.current_value: Grouped as degenerative progressive cardiac conduction disease (Lev–Lenègre). Lev disease is age-related sclerocalcific degeneration of the left side of the cardiac fibrous skeleton: mitral annulus, central fibrous body, aortic ring and crest of the muscular septum. It encroaches on the His bundle and the proximal bundle branches, causing bundle branch block that progresses to AV block. Lenègre disease is diffuse fibrosis of the distal conduction system in younger patients. Hereditary forms are recognized (SCN5A, TRPM4, LMNA, NKX2-5).
checks.note: The book's statement is only partly right. It narrows Lev disease to calcific aortic valve disease, which is one contributor, not the definition. A modern course should also mention TAVR, alongside calcific aortic stenosis, as a common contemporary cause of new LBBB or AV block.

missing_criteria.value: The guideline definition is a sinus rate <50 bpm, versus the traditional <60 bpm. Rates of 40-50 bpm at rest or during sleep are often physiologic, especially in the young and in athletes. Treatment depends on symptom correlation, not the number alone.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3

missing_criteria.value: Sinus pause = the sinus node fires >3 s after the previous atrial depolarization. Sinus arrest = no evidence of sinus node depolarization.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3

missing_criteria.value: The heart rate cannot rise to match demand. In practice this means failing to reach 80% of the expected heart-rate reserve on exercise testing; predicted maximum HR = 220 - age. Exercise ECG testing is Class IIa when symptoms are exercise-related.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 and Figure 2

missing_criteria.value: Sinus bradycardia, ectopic atrial bradycardia or sinus pauses alternate with atrial tachycardia, flutter or AF. A pause of variable length often follows the end of the tachycardia (post-conversion pause). Pacing is Class I when symptomatic, both to relieve symptoms and to allow rate- or rhythm-control drugs. AF ablation is an alternative.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3; 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines

missing_criteria.value: From 2:1 conduction alone the block cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II. Clues pointing to the AV node: narrow QRS, long PR in conducted beats, 3:2 Wenckebach periods elsewhere on the strip, improvement with atropine or exercise. Clues pointing to infranodal block: wide QRS or BBB, normal PR, worsening with exercise or atropine, improvement with carotid sinus massage. If the site is still unclear, use exercise testing (IIa) or an EP study (IIb).
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 and Figure 3; 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines
missing_criteria.leads: Long rhythm strip (II, V1); full 12-lead for QRS width

missing_criteria.value: Ratios are written as P waves : QRS complexes (P : conducted beats). 3:2 = one blocked P in three. 3:1, 4:1 or longer runs of consecutive blocked P waves = high-grade (advanced) AV block, defined as >=2 consecutive non-conducted P waves at a constant physiologic rate with some AV conduction still present.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3

missing_criteria.value: Before diagnosing Mobitz I or II, confirm a constant P rate (<100 bpm). Exclude: (a) non-conducted premature atrial complexes (the early P' is often buried in the T); (b) vagal block, in which sinus slowing occurs together with PR prolongation or a dropped beat; (c) concealed junctional extrasystoles (advanced).
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 3 (Mobitz definitions require a constant P rate; vagally mediated AV block); Barold SS, Hayes DL, Mayo Clin Proc 2001;76:44-57
missing_criteria.leads: Rhythm strip; compare T-wave shapes for hidden P'

missing_criteria.entity: Vagally mediated AV block and nocturnal bradycardia
missing_criteria.value: Recognize vagal block by simultaneous sinus slowing and PR lengthening, mostly at night or at rest, and resolution with activity. Nocturnal bradycardia or AV block is not in itself an indication for pacing. Screen for sleep apnea.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, take-home message 2 and Table 3

missing_criteria.value: Acquired Mobitz II, high-grade or third-degree AV block without a reversible or physiologic cause: permanent pacing is Class I regardless of symptoms. Alternating bundle branch block: pacing is Class I. Syncope with bifascicular block and HV >=70 ms on EP study: pacing is Class I (ESC 2021). In other AV block, pace only when symptoms correlate.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, take-home message 5 and Figure 7; 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Normal training-related findings: sinus bradycardia >=30 bpm, sinus arrhythmia, ectopic atrial or junctional escape rhythm, first-degree AV block, and Mobitz I that disappears with exercise. Need evaluation: profound sinus bradycardia <30 bpm, PR >=400 ms (>=300 ms in children/adolescents per the 2025 EAPC statement), Mobitz II, high-grade block, third-degree block, and daytime Mobitz I that persists during exercise.
missing_criteria.source: Sharma S, Drezner JA et al., International Recommendations for ECG Interpretation in Athletes, JACC 2017;69:1057 / Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466; Finocchiaro G et al., EAPC consensus on abnormal ECG findings in athletes, Eur Heart J 2025

missing_criteria.parameter: must exclude before labelling intrinsic disease
missing_criteria.value: Drugs: beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, antiarrhythmics. Other causes: hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism, acute MI or ischaemia, Lyme carditis, sleep apnea, hypothermia, raised intracranial pressure. Treat the cause first (Class I).
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Tables 4, 7 and 9, Figures 2-3
missing_criteria.leads: 12-lead (e.g. peaked T in hyperkalaemia, scooped ST in digoxin effect)

missing_criteria.entity: Unexplained AV block in younger adults
missing_criteria.value: Second- or third-degree AV block without a clear cause in patients under about 60 should prompt a search for infiltrative or inflammatory disease, especially cardiac sarcoidosis, as well as Lyme, myocarditis, amyloid and laminopathy (LMNA). Advanced imaging (CMR, FDG-PET) is Class IIa.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Figure 3 and Table 9; 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines; 2014 HRS Expert Consensus on Cardiac Sarcoidosis

missing_criteria.value: New LBBB and high-degree AV block are common after TAVR. Compare pre- and post-procedure ECGs for new or worsening PR or QRS prolongation. Persistent complete or high-grade block needs pacing; new LBBB needs monitoring.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, TAVR recommendations (take-home message 7); 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (pacing after TAVI)

missing_criteria.entity: Complete AV block in atrial fibrillation
missing_criteria.value: In AF, a slow and perfectly regular ventricular rhythm, with a junctional or ventricular escape, means complete AV block. Classic causes are digoxin toxicity and conduction disease.
missing_criteria.source: Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice; 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (AF with bradycardia/AV block)

missing_criteria.value: Sudden 1:1 conduction to complete block with a long ventricular asystole, often triggered by a PAC or PVC or by a slowing rate (phase-4 block). It suggests His-Purkinje disease. An idiopathic low-adenosine form also exists. It is a cause of syncope even when the resting ECG is near-normal (often with BBB).
missing_criteria.source: 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (paroxysmal AV block; adenosine-sensitive syncope); Aste M, Brignole M, Europace reviews on paroxysmal AV block

missing_criteria.value: Congenital complete AV block is linked to maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (maternal SLE or Sjögren) and to congenital heart disease such as congenitally corrected TGA. The escape is usually a narrow junctional rhythm.
missing_criteria.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Bradycardia Guideline, Table 9; 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines (congenital AV block)

missing_criteria.value: P waves dissociated from QRS complexes, or capture or fusion beats, in a wide-QRS tachycardia strongly favour VT.
missing_criteria.source: 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of sudden cardiac death (Zeppenfeld et al.)

checks.current_value: Name the T-wave shape, not a guessed layer of the wall. Hyperacute T waves (broad-based, bulky, symmetric, large relative to the QRS, in 2 or more contiguous leads) are an early sign of acute coronary occlusion and can appear before ST elevation: repeat the ECG and compare with old tracings. Ischaemic T inversion means more than 1 mm in 2 contiguous leads with a prominent R or R/S >1. Deep symmetric or biphasic inversion in V2-V3 after pain (Wellens) points to evolving or reperfused ischaemia from a critical proximal LAD stenosis, not ongoing 'subepicardial ischaemia'. A narrow, tented, peaked T suggests hyperkalaemia, not ischaemia.
checks.note: The 'subendocardial = tall T / subepicardial = negative T' labels come from an experimental electrophysiological model taught mainly in the Spanish school. International guidelines do not use them. The book's 'peaked/pointed' wording also overlaps with the hyperkalaemic T. Keep the shapes but teach them in clinical context. Negative T waves in coronary patients usually mean post-ischaemic or reperfused myocardium.
checks.source: Thygesen K et al. Fourth Universal Definition of MI (UDMI) 2018, Eur Heart J 2019;40:237-269, section 27 (hyperacute T waves before ST elevation; T inversion criterion); Byrne RA et al. 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720-3826, section 3.2 (hyperacute, inverted, biphasic, flat and pseudo-normalised T; Wellens sign); Wagner GS et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization Part VI, Circulation 2009;119:e262-e270

checks.current_value: Ischaemia limited to the subendocardium gives ST depression. Transmural ischaemia (acute occlusion) gives ST elevation in the leads facing the ischaemic zone, often with reciprocal depression. Measure at the J point against the PR/TP baseline and apply the UDMI/ESC thresholds.
checks.note: The physiology is still taught, with three caveats. (1) UDMI 2018 now uses 'myocardial injury' for a troponin above the 99th percentile, so the old ECG phrase 'injury current' clashes with it; prefer 'ST elevation' or 'ST depression (ischaemia)'. (2) ST depression does not localise the culprit artery. (3) ST depression in V1-V3 can be the mirror of a posterior STEMI rather than subendocardial ischaemia. The criterion needs numeric thresholds (see missing_criteria).
checks.source: UDMI 2018 (Thygesen et al.), sections 3 and 27; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1

checks.current_value: Prior MI (UDMI 2018, no LBBB/LVH/WPW): any Q >0.02 s or a QS complex in V2-V3. Elsewhere, Q ≥0.03 s and ≥1 mm deep (or QS) in I, II, aVL, aVF or V4-V6, in 2 or more leads of one contiguous group (I/aVL, V1-V6, II/III/aVF). Q-wave equivalent of a posterior/lateral MI: R ≥0.04 s in V1-V2 with R/S ≥1 and an upright T, with no conduction defect. Normal variants: QS in V1; small septal q (<0.03 s and <25% of R) in I, aVL, aVF, V4-V6; Q in III <0.03 s and <25% of R when the axis is −30° to 0°.
checks.note: Two parts are superseded. The '>25% of R and/or ≥0.04 s' rule survives only inside the normal-q exclusion. 'QS = transmural, Qr/QR = surviving tissue' has not held up: cardiac MRI shows Q waves track infarct size more than transmurality. Q waves can be transient after reperfusion. Non-infarct causes of Q waves: pre-excitation, LBBB, LVH, hypertrophic or other cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, hyperkalaemia. Septal q in V5-V6 is normal (current).
checks.source: UDMI 2018 sections 30-31 and Table 3; Moon JC et al. J Am Coll Cardiol 2004;44:554-560 (CMR: Q waves vs transmurality)

checks.current_value: Natural history of an unreperfused STEMI. Minutes: hyperacute T. Minutes to hours: ST elevation. Hours (about 1-12 h): R loss and Q waves. Hours to days: T inversion starts while the ST is still elevated. Days to about 2 weeks: ST returns to baseline (sooner in inferior MI). Weeks to months: T may normalise; Q usually persists.
checks.note: The sequence is fine as approximate teaching, but add the hyperacute-T stage first. 'About 24 h ST falls' is early for unreperfused MI: resolution usually takes days. Reperfusion compresses the sequence (fast ST fall, early T inversion, Q waves sometimes transient). ST elevation that persists for weeks suggests a large dyskinetic scar or aneurysm.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 section 27 (hyperacute T, transient Q, ST fall with reperfusion); Wagner GS et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part VI 2009

checks.current_value: Inferior: II, III, aVF. Anterior/anteroseptal: V1-V4 (septal V1-V2). Extensive anterior: V1-V6 ± I/aVL. Lateral: I, aVL, V5-V6. Posterior/inferobasal: mirror changes in V1-V3, direct changes in V7-V9. Right ventricle: V3R-V4R (± V1).
checks.note: The groupings are still used for contiguity (UDMI, ESC 2023). Caveats: (a) CMR studies (ISHE 2006) show that Q in I/aVL without V6 often means a mid-anterior (diagonal-territory) infarct rather than 'high lateral', and that Q in V1-V2 alone is often not purely septal. (b) ISHE proposed renaming 'posterior' to lateral/inferobasal, but ESC 2023 and UDMI still use 'posterior'. (c) 'V2 or V3 = apical' is not a standard grouping; drop it or present it as approximate. (d) ECG localisation matches imaging only moderately.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 (contiguous lead groups); 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1; Bayés de Luna A et al. ISHE consensus on CMR-based infarct terminology, Circulation 2006;114:1755-1760; Wagner GS et al. Part VI 2009

checks.note: Correct. In inferior STEMI, aVL is the most sensitive reciprocal lead and its ST depression can come before obvious inferior elevation. In anterior STEMI, inferior ST depression implies occlusion proximal to D1 (high lateral involvement). A 'wraparound' distal LAD gives inferior ST elevation instead. Posterior involvement gives ST depression in V1-V3, often deepest in V2-V4, with an upright terminal T. Reciprocal change helps separate STEMI from pericarditis and early repolarisation.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 section 27 (reciprocal changes vs pericarditis/early repolarisation); 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1; Wagner GS et al. Part VI 2009

checks.note: Still taught. RCA: ST elevation III > II plus ST depression in I and aVL; ST elevation in V1 and/or V4R adds proximal RCA with RV involvement. Circumflex: ST elevation II ≥ III, I/aVL isoelectric or elevated, often ST elevation in V5-V6 and ST depression in V1-V3. Accuracy is moderate and depends on coronary dominance. Circumflex occlusions are often electrically silent on the standard 12 leads, so record V7-V9.
checks.source: Zimetbaum PJ, Josephson ME. Use of the ECG in acute MI. N Engl J Med 2003;348:933-940; Wagner GS et al. Part VI 2009; UDMI 2018 section 28

checks.current_value: In every inferior STEMI, record right-sided leads (V3R, V4R). RV involvement: ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V3R/V4R (≥1 mm in men <30 y). ST elevation in V1 (and sometimes aVR ≥1 mm) can accompany it.
checks.note: Add the numeric threshold. ST depression in I/aVL marks an RCA culprit and is not itself an RV criterion. V4R elevation is short-lived (often gone within about 12 h), so record early; a normal V4R does not exclude RV infarction. RV involvement in roughly a third to half of inferior MIs is consistent with the literature.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 section 28 (V3R/V4R ≥0.5 mm, ≥1 mm men <30; changes may be transient); 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1 (ST elevation in V3R/V4R highly suggestive of ongoing RV ischaemia); Zehender M et al. N Engl J Med 1993;328:981-988

checks.current_value: Acute: isolated ST depression ≥0.5 mm in V1-V3 (especially with an upright terminal T) should prompt V7-V9. ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V7-V9 (≥1 mm in men <40 y) confirms posterior occlusion. Old: R ≥0.04 s in V1-V2 with R/S ≥1 and an upright T (no RBBB/WPW/RVH).
checks.note: The mirror and direct images are correct; add these thresholds. Treat isolated posterior STEMI like STEMI. ISHE proposed calling this wall lateral/inferobasal, but current guidelines keep 'posterior'.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 section 28 and Table 3; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1 (ST depression V1-V3 with positive terminal T and ST elevation V7-V9 highly suggestive of posterior occlusion); Bayés de Luna A et al. Circulation 2006;114:1755-1760

checks.current_value: The Q/non-Q split has been replaced at presentation by STEMI vs NSTE-ACS (NSTEMI or unstable angina). MI requires a rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin (preferably high-sensitivity) with at least one value above the 99th-percentile URL, plus evidence of ischaemia. NSTE-ACS ECG findings: new horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads and/or T inversion >1 mm with a prominent R or R/S >1, or transient ST elevation. The ECG is normal in more than a third of NSTE-ACS.
checks.note: 'Enzyme rise' is now troponin. 'ECG normalises' is not a diagnostic criterion. Q waves can develop in NSTEMI and may be absent after a reperfused STEMI. A normal ECG does not exclude ACS.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 (criteria for type 1 MI; ECG ischaemia thresholds); 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines sections 3.2.2 and 1 (STEMI/NSTE-ACS classification; ECG normal in >1/3 of NSTE-ACS)

checks.current_value: ST depression ≥1 mm in 6 or more leads (inferolateral), with ST elevation in aVR and/or V1, suggests multivessel ischaemia or left main (or equivalent) obstruction, especially with haemodynamic compromise. It is a high-risk pattern needing urgent invasive assessment, not a classic STEMI.
checks.note: The book's '>8 leads' matches the older ESC 2017 wording; ESC 2023 and UDMI 2018 use 6 or more leads with a 1 mm threshold. Teach that this pattern can also come from severe supply-demand ischaemia (anaemia, tachyarrhythmia), not only left main thrombosis.
checks.source: 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1; UDMI 2018 section 27 (ST depression ≥1 mm in six leads suggests multivessel or left main disease)

checks.current_value: Vasospastic angina (COVADIS): nitrate-responsive angina, typically at rest, with transient ischaemic ECG changes during the episode (ST elevation ≥1 mm, ST depression ≥1 mm, or new negative U waves in 2 or more contiguous leads) and/or spasm proven on provocation testing (>90% vasoconstriction).
checks.note: Transient ST elevation in one territory that resolves is still the classic picture. Add that spasm can cause ST depression, AV block or ventricular arrhythmias, and that troponin can rise (MINOCA), so 'normal enzymes afterwards' is not required. Ambulatory ECG can capture episodes.
checks.source: Beltrame JF et al. (COVADIS) International standardization of diagnostic criteria for vasospastic angina, Eur Heart J 2017;38:2565-2568; Vrints C et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for chronic coronary syndromes, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3415-3537 (ANOCA/INOCA section)

checks.current_value: '1×1×1' rule: horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥1 mm at J+80 ms (J+60 ms at fast rates), lasting ≥1 min, separated from other episodes by ≥1 min.
checks.note: Add 'horizontal/downsloping' and the separation rule. A stable baseline is needed, and positional or rate-related artefacts must be excluded. LBBB, LVH strain and digoxin make the analysis unreliable. Holter ST analysis now has a limited clinical role.
checks.source: Crawford MH et al. ACC/AHA Guidelines for Ambulatory Electrocardiography, Circulation 1999;100:886-893; Steinberg JS et al. ISHNE-HRS expert consensus on ambulatory ECG, Heart Rhythm 2017;14:e55-e96

checks.note: Persistent ST elevation over Q waves weeks after an MI is valid teaching. It reflects a large transmural scar or dyskinesia, not only a true aneurysm, and echo or CMR confirms it. More useful to teach: telling old aneurysmal ST elevation from a new STEMI. A large T wave relative to the QRS in V1-V4 favours acute STEMI (T/QRS ratio rule, Klein 2015). The 'rsR′ in V5-V6' remark has no current guideline or evidence support; omit it.
checks.source: UDMI 2018 section 31 (confounders); Klein LR, Shroff GR, Beeman W, Smith SW. Am J Emerg Med 2015;33:786-790 (T/QRS ratio, LV aneurysm vs acute STEMI)

checks.note: A classic sign: a qR/QR premature ventricular beat with a wide Q in leads facing the infarct supports an old MI, while a QS ectopic beat is non-diagnostic. It rests on small, old observational series and is absent from UDMI 2018, AHA/ACCF/HRS Part VI and ESC guidelines. If kept, present it as a supportive clue of low sensitivity and uncertain specificity. Exclude aVR, and exclude V1 in RBBB-morphology ectopy.
checks.source: Surawicz B, Knilans TK. Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed., Saunders/Elsevier 2008 (MI chapter); no current guideline addresses it

checks.current_value: Failed fibrinolysis: ST-segment resolution <50% (in the lead with the most elevation) within 60-90 min, which triggers rescue PCI. Prognostic bands: complete ≥70%, partial 30-70%, none <30%. Other reperfusion signs: pain relief, accelerated idioventricular rhythm, early terminal T inversion. After primary PCI, persistent ST elevation suggests microvascular obstruction.
checks.note: The book's '<25% at 1 h = no reperfusion' and 'about 50% suffices in anterior MI' come from older single studies. The current operational rule is <50% at 60-90 min. The ≥70% 'complete resolution' band is still valid prognostically.
checks.source: 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 5.3.1.2 (ST resolution <50% within 60-90 min = failed fibrinolysis); Schröder R et al. J Am Coll Cardiol 1994;24:384-391 (ST resolution categories)

checks.note: The patterns come mainly from Engelen et al. 1999, a single-centre angiographic study. Signs of occlusion proximal to S1: ST elevation in aVR, new RBBB, ST depression in V5, and ST elevation >2.5 mm in V1 (very specific but only about 12-14% sensitive). Proximal to D1: aVL elevation with inferior depression (III > II). Inferior ST elevation suggests a distal 'wraparound' LAD. Teach these as probabilistic clues. Present the '100% specific' figures as 'highly specific in a small series'. They do not change acute management.
checks.source: Engelen DJ et al. Value of the ECG in localizing the occlusion site in the LAD in acute anterior MI, J Am Coll Cardiol 1999;34:389-395; Zimetbaum PJ, Josephson ME. N Engl J Med 2003;348:933-940; Wagner GS et al. Part VI 2009

checks.note: Consistent with angiographic and CT anatomy data. Sinus-node artery from the RCA in about 55-60% (circumflex about 40%). Right dominance about 70-85%, codominance about 5-20%, left dominance about 5-10%, so the PDA arises from the RCA in about 80-90%. The AV-nodal artery comes from the dominant artery (RCA in about 80-90%). The LAD wraps the apex in most hearts, which explains inferior ST elevation in some anterior MIs. Present these as approximate ranges.
checks.source: Kini S et al. Normal and variant coronary arterial and venous anatomy on high-resolution CT angiography, AJR Am J Roentgenol 2007;188:1665-1674; Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed., Elsevier 2020

checks.current_value: Positive test: horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥1 mm measured 60-80 ms after the J point, relative to the PQ junction. With resting ST depression, count only the additional depression. Exercise ST elevation ≥1 mm in leads without Q waves (excluding aVR, aVL, V1) localises transmural ischaemia from severe proximal stenosis (rarely spasm). ST elevation over old Q waves reflects dyskinesia, not ischaemia.
checks.note: The book's 'horizontal or downsloping ST for >80 ms' misstates the measurement: the reading is taken at 60-80 ms after J, not over a duration. Upsloping depression ≥2 mm at 80 ms is borderline/abnormal for some authors.
checks.source: Fletcher GF et al. AHA Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, Circulation 2013;128:873-934; Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 Guideline Update for Exercise Testing, Circulation 2002;106:1883-1892

checks.current_value: Predicted maximal HR: 220 − age is still used but varies by ±10-12 bpm. Better equations: Tanaka 208 − 0.7 × age (healthy adults); Gulati 206 − 0.88 × age (women); 164 − 0.72 × age (CAD patients on β-blockers). Reaching ≥85% of predicted max HR marks a diagnostically adequate test; <85% without ischaemia is non-diagnostic. Do not use 85% by itself as a reason to stop; symptom-limited testing is preferred.
checks.note: '210 − age for women' is not a validated formula.
checks.source: Fletcher GF et al. Circulation 2013;128:873-934 (HR response; revised prediction equations); Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 exercise testing guideline

checks.current_value: High-risk ('early positive') markers: ST depression ≥1 mm appearing in Bruce stage I-II (low workload); ST depression ≥2 mm at low workload or persisting into recovery (commonly ≥5 min); downsloping depression in many leads; exercise-induced ST elevation (not aVR); exercise-induced hypotension; sustained VT/VF; Duke score ≤ −11. Low risk: reaching Bruce stage III-IV or more without ischaemia.
checks.note: The book's cut-offs (>3 mm, >8 min into recovery) are stricter than current high-risk thresholds (≥2 mm, persistence into recovery).
checks.source: Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 Guideline Update for Exercise Testing (prognosis section: early positive test ≥1 mm in first two Bruce stages; ST duration into recovery; number of leads); Fihn SD et al. 2012 ACCF/AHA SIHD Guideline, Circulation 2012;126:e354-e471 (high-risk exercise findings); Fletcher GF et al. Circulation 2013

checks.note: Formula and cut-offs are correct. The score is Bruce minutes − 5 × ST deviation in mm (measured 60-80 ms after J; deviation <1 mm scores 0) − 4 × angina index (0 none, 1 non-limiting, 2 test-limiting). ≤ −11 is high risk (≥5%/year cardiovascular mortality); −10 to +4 is moderate; ≥ +5 is low (about 0.5%/year). It is valid for the Bruce protocol (or a MET-equivalent nomogram) and has been validated in women. Few elderly patients were studied. Exercise capacity is its most robust component.
checks.source: Mark DB et al. N Engl J Med 1991;325:849-853; Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 exercise testing guideline (risk bands); Fletcher GF et al. Circulation 2013

checks.current_value: Absolute stop criteria: ST elevation >1.0 mm in leads without pre-existing Q waves (other than aVR, aVL, V1); sustained VT, or other arrhythmia (including 2nd/3rd-degree AV block) that compromises cardiac output; SBP fall >10 mmHg despite rising workload with other evidence of ischaemia; moderate-to-severe angina; CNS symptoms; poor perfusion; technical failure; patient request. Relative criteria: horizontal or downsloping ST depression >2 mm (60-80 ms after J); arrhythmias other than sustained VT (multifocal ectopy, triplets, SVT, bradyarrhythmias); new bundle-branch block that cannot be told from VT; SBP >250 or DBP >115 mmHg; increasing chest pain.
checks.note: The book's thresholds (ST depression >4 mm, ST elevation >2 mm) are looser than current standards (>2 mm relative, >1 mm absolute). New LBBB is a relative criterion.
checks.source: Fletcher GF et al. AHA Exercise Standards for Testing and Training, Circulation 2013;128:873-934 (indications for terminating exercise testing); Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 exercise testing guideline

checks.current_value: The exercise ECG cannot be read for ischaemia with LBBB, ventricular pacing, pre-excitation, or resting ST depression >1 mm (including LVH with repolarisation abnormality and digoxin): use stress imaging. In RBBB, ignore exercise ST depression in V1-V3; depression in V5-V6 or II/aVF keeps normal accuracy. Accuracy: meta-analysis mean sensitivity 68% and specificity 77%; a newer pooled estimate gives about 58% / 62%. Sensitivity rises with disease extent.
checks.note: The baseline-confounder list is correct. The RBBB rule is narrower than current teaching (inferior leads also count), and 85-90% specificity is optimistic. ESC chronic-coronary-syndrome guidelines now prefer CT coronary angiography or functional imaging for diagnosis. The exercise ECG is kept for exercise capacity and prognosis, or when imaging is unavailable.
checks.source: Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 exercise testing guideline (LBBB, RBBB V1-V3 vs V5-V6/II/aVF, LVH, digoxin); Fletcher GF et al. Circulation 2013 (sensitivity 68%, specificity 77%); Knuuti J et al. Eur Heart J 2018;39:3322-3330; Vrints C et al. 2024 ESC CCS Guidelines

checks.current_value: Exaggerated BP response: peak SBP ≥210 mmHg in men or ≥190 mmHg in women; a DBP rise >10 mmHg above rest or DBP ≥90 mmHg is abnormal. SBP >250 or DBP >115 mmHg is a relative reason to stop. Exercise hypotension (SBP falling below baseline or by >10 mmHg despite rising workload) marks severe CAD (left main / 3-vessel) or LV dysfunction. R-wave amplitude changes (Brody effect, Ellestad R score) have no independent diagnostic value; do not teach them as positivity criteria.
checks.note: The book's 'SBP rise >70 mmHg / DBP rise >15 mmHg' definition and the R-wave index are not current. The falling-BP concept is still current.
checks.source: Fletcher GF et al. Circulation 2013;128:873-934 (BP response; R-wave amplitude changes have not consistently improved accuracy); Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 exercise testing guideline (R-wave response has no diagnostic significance)

missing_criteria.value: New ST elevation at the J point in 2 or more contiguous leads: ≥1 mm in all leads except V2-V3. In V2-V3: ≥2 mm in men ≥40 y, ≥2.5 mm in men <40 y, ≥1.5 mm in women of any age (no LVH or LBBB). Measure against the PR/TP baseline and compare with prior ECGs.
missing_criteria.source: UDMI 2018 (Thygesen et al.) section 27; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1

missing_criteria.value: New horizontal or downsloping ST depression ≥0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads and/or T inversion >1 mm in 2 contiguous leads with a prominent R or R/S >1. The ECG is normal in more than a third of NSTE-ACS, so a normal ECG never rules out ACS.
missing_criteria.source: UDMI 2018 section 27; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.2

missing_criteria.value: V7-V9 at the V6 horizontal level (posterior axillary, mid-scapular and left paravertebral lines): ST elevation ≥0.5 mm (≥1 mm in men <40 y) indicates posterior occlusion. V3R/V4R (mirror of V3/V4; V4R at the 5th intercostal space, right midclavicular line): ST elevation ≥0.5 mm (≥1 mm in men <30 y) indicates RV involvement. Indications: isolated ST depression V1-V3, and every inferior STEMI.
missing_criteria.source: UDMI 2018 section 28; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1; Kligfield P et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part I, Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324

missing_criteria.value: Isolated ST depression ≥0.5 mm in V1-V3 (often deepest in V2-V4) with an upright terminal T and growing R waves suggests posterior (often circumflex) occlusion, not subendocardial ischaemia. Record V7-V9 and manage as STEMI.
missing_criteria.source: 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1; UDMI 2018 section 28

missing_criteria.value: Record a 12-lead ECG within 10 min of first medical contact. If it is non-diagnostic and symptoms persist or suspicion is high, repeat serially (for example every 15-30 min in the first hour) and with any change in symptoms; compare with old tracings. Hyperacute T waves can be the only early sign of occlusion.
missing_criteria.source: 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines; Amsterdam EA et al. 2014 AHA/ACC NSTE-ACS Guideline, Circulation 2014;130:e344-e426; Gulati M et al. 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline, Circulation 2021;144:e368-e454

missing_criteria.value: Upsloping ST depression >1 mm at the J point in the precordial leads, running into tall, symmetric T waves, usually with no precordial ST elevation and often slight ST elevation in aVR. It indicates acute proximal LAD occlusion: manage as STEMI.
missing_criteria.source: de Winter RJ et al. N Engl J Med 2008;359:2071-2073; UDMI 2018 section 27 (upsloping J-point depression with large T waves associated with LAD occlusion)

missing_criteria.parameter: T wave in the pain-free state
missing_criteria.value: After an angina episode, while pain-free: biphasic (type A) or deep symmetric inverted (type B) T waves in V2-V3 (± V1-V6), with preserved R waves, no Q waves and minimal ST elevation. It indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis: avoid stress testing and arrange early angiography.
missing_criteria.source: de Zwaan C et al. Am Heart J 1982;103:730-736; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.2 (Wellens sign)

missing_criteria.entity: MI with LBBB or ventricular pacing
missing_criteria.value: Sgarbossa criteria: concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm in any lead; concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1-V3; discordant ST elevation ≥5 mm. The Smith-modified rule replaces the last criterion with a disproportionate discordant ST/S ratio. The Barcelona criteria are an alternative. ESC 2023: BBB or paced rhythm prevents accurate assessment, and a patient with ongoing ischaemic symptoms should be managed like STEMI.
missing_criteria.source: Sgarbossa EB et al. N Engl J Med 1996;334:481-487; Smith SW et al. Ann Emerg Med 2012;60:766-776; Di Marco A et al. J Am Heart Assoc 2020;9:e015573; UDMI 2018 section 32; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1

missing_criteria.value: RBBB does not hide ST elevation: apply the standard criteria (ST/T changes in V1-V3 can be secondary). New or presumed-new RBBB with ischaemic symptoms often means an occluded artery (TIMI 0-2 flow): high risk, consider immediate angiography.
missing_criteria.source: UDMI 2018 section 32; 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines section 3.2.1

missing_criteria.value: Benign early repolarisation; acute pericarditis (widespread concave ST elevation, PR depression, PR elevation in aVR, no reciprocal depression except aVR/V1); LVH; LBBB/paced rhythm; Brugada pattern; hyperkalaemia; Takotsubo syndrome; old aneurysm. Reciprocal depression and dynamic evolution favour STEMI.
missing_criteria.source: UDMI 2018 sections 27 and 31; Adler Y et al. 2015 ESC Guidelines on pericardial diseases, Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921-2964; Ghadri JR et al. InterTAK consensus on Takotsubo syndrome, Eur Heart J 2018;39:2032-2046; Macfarlane PW et al. J Am Coll Cardiol 2015;66:470-477 (early repolarisation)

missing_criteria.entity: Subtle anterior occlusion vs early repolarisation
missing_criteria.value: When V2-V4 show modest ST elevation, a validated formula combining QTc, R amplitude in V4, QRS amplitude in V2 and ST elevation 60 ms after J in V3 helps separate subtle LAD occlusion from normal-variant ST elevation. Use it only as a supplement to serial ECGs and clinical judgement.
missing_criteria.source: Driver BE et al. J Electrocardiol 2017;50:561-569 (4-variable formula); Smith SW et al. Am J Cardiol 2012;110:1696-1701

missing_criteria.entity: Acute coronary occlusion without STEMI criteria
missing_criteria.value: STEMI millimetre criteria miss a sizeable minority of acute occlusions, especially circumflex occlusions, which are often silent on the 12 leads. NSTE-ACS with refractory pain, haemodynamic instability, life-threatening arrhythmia or dynamic ECG changes needs an immediate invasive strategy (<2 h). Patterns that should alert: hyperacute T, de Winter, isolated V1-V3 ST depression, subtle reciprocal changes.
missing_criteria.source: 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines (immediate invasive strategy criteria); Meyers HP et al. Int J Cardiol Heart Vasc 2021;33:100767

missing_criteria.value: ST elevation over established Q waves with small T waves relative to the QRS favours an old aneurysm. A large T/QRS amplitude ratio in any of V1-V4 favours acute anterior STEMI. Confirm with prior ECGs, troponin and echocardiography.
missing_criteria.source: Klein LR, Shroff GR, Beeman W, Smith SW. Am J Emerg Med 2015;33:786-790

missing_criteria.value: ST elevation in I, aVL and V2 with reciprocal ST depression in III (± II, aVF), and V3-V6 relatively spared (the 'South African flag' pattern). It indicates a mid-anterior / high-lateral infarct from a diagonal or proximal LAD lesion.
missing_criteria.source: Durant E, Singh A. Am J Emerg Med 2015 (South African flag sign); Bayés de Luna A et al. Circulation 2006;114:1755-1760 (mid-anterior pattern)

missing_criteria.value: Abnormal heart-rate recovery: fall ≤12 bpm in the first minute with an upright cool-down (cut-offs depend on protocol). Chronotropic incompetence: <80% of HR reserve used (<62% on β-blockers). Exercise capacity in METs is the strongest prognostic variable. Frequent ventricular ectopy in recovery carries prognostic weight.
missing_criteria.source: Fletcher GF et al. Circulation 2013;128:873-934; Cole CR et al. N Engl J Med 1999;341:1351-1357; Gibbons RJ et al. ACC/AHA 2002 exercise testing guideline

missing_criteria.parameter: current role in chronic coronary syndromes
missing_criteria.value: For diagnosing obstructive CAD, CT coronary angiography or functional imaging is preferred. The exercise ECG alone is used mainly to assess exercise capacity, symptoms, arrhythmias, BP response and prognosis, or for diagnosis only when imaging is unavailable. It is not diagnostic with resting ST depression ≥1 mm or on digoxin.
missing_criteria.source: Vrints C et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for chronic coronary syndromes, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3415-3537; Knuuti J et al. Eur Heart J 2018;39:3322-3330

checks.current_value: Adults: PR <120 ms in sinus rhythm (<90 ms in children); delta wave (slurred initial QRS); QRS >120 ms (>90 ms in children), though minimal pre-excitation can give a QRS of 100-120 ms; secondary ST-T changes directed opposite to the delta/QRS. P is normal in sinus rhythm. QT is NOT a criterion: QT only looks long because the QRS is wider (judge repolarization by JT). A delta wave with a normal PR (>=120 ms) is seen mainly with left free-wall pathways (long intra-atrial conduction to the pathway) or slow-conducting pathways, not with Mahaim fibres.
checks.note: The four core items (short PR, delta, wide QRS, secondary ST-T) are current. Two parts are factually wrong. (1) 'Long QT' as a WPW criterion: the apparent QT prolongation comes from the wide QRS, and teaching it as a sign of WPW would lead students to over-call LQTS. (2) The context says a PR >0.12 s is due to Mahaim fibres. Atriofascicular (Mahaim) pathways typically show little or no pre-excitation at rest. A normal PR with a visible delta usually means a left lateral pathway far from the sinus node. Do not teach the '12%' figure as fact, because estimates vary.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Recommendations for Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part III (Surawicz et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235 / JACC 2009;53:976) - ventricular pre-excitation criteria incl. paediatric limits; 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (Brugada J et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:655), section on WPW pattern (PR <=120 ms, delta, QRS >120 ms)

checks.current_value: LGL is no longer taught as a distinct syndrome or pathway entity. A short PR (<120 ms) with a normal P axis, narrow QRS and no delta is described as 'short PR / enhanced (accelerated) AV nodal conduction'. In an asymptomatic person it is usually a normal variant (young people, high sympathetic tone). If paroxysmal SVT occurs, it is classified by mechanism (AVNRT, AVRT over a concealed pathway, focal AT), not as 'LGL'. If a cut-off is used, it is <120 ms, not 0.11 s.
checks.note: Neither the 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS nor the 2019 ESC SVT guideline recognises an 'LGL syndrome'. The James-fibre substrate was never proven, and the label has been largely dropped in modern practice. Keep it only as a historical term if at all.
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (Eur Heart J 2020;41:655) - SVT classified by mechanism, no LGL entity; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for Adult SVT (Page RL et al., Circulation 2016;133:e506); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2007-2009 ECG standardization statements (short PR as a descriptive statement only)

checks.current_value: A sinus-rhythm ECG with pre-excitation (short PR + delta) after an SVT means a manifest AP, so AVRT is likely (WPW syndrome). A normal sinus ECG does NOT identify a concealed pathway. The commonest cause of regular narrow-QRS SVT with a normal baseline ECG is AVNRT, followed by AVRT over a concealed AP and focal AT. The mechanism is inferred from the tachycardia ECG (RP interval, pseudo-r' in V1 / pseudo-S in inferior leads, P morphology, QRS alternans, response to adenosine or vagal manoeuvres) and confirmed at EP study. A short PR without delta has no diagnostic value for mechanism.
checks.note: The 'short PR only = LGL' branch is outdated (see lgl). The 'normal ECG = concealed pathway' branch is a logical error that would systematically mislabel AVNRT, the most common paroxysmal SVT. Also note that subtle left-lateral pre-excitation can make a manifest AP look 'normal'.
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (Eur Heart J 2020;41:655) - differential diagnosis of narrow-QRS tachycardia; concealed APs invisible at rest and detected only during AVRT/EPS; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Adult SVT Guideline

checks.current_value: Pre-excited tachycardia over an atriofascicular (decremental, right-sided) pathway: LBBB-like morphology; QRS axis usually 0 to -75° (horizontal/superior; a normal axis is possible depending on fusion); QRS <=150 ms; R in I; rS in V1; precordial transition after V4; rate about 130-270 bpm. In sinus rhythm there is minimal or no pre-excitation; clues are loss of septal q in I/aVL/V5-V6, rS in III and a narrow QRS.
checks.note: The Bardy criteria are still the standard teaching set. Use modern terminology: 'Mahaim' is now split into atriofascicular, nodofascicular/nodoventricular and fasciculoventricular pathways. The 2019 ESC guideline confirms the LBBB-like pattern with a horizontal/superior axis and that the pathway is latent in sinus rhythm.
checks.source: Bardy GH et al., Circulation 1984;70:377-391 (original criteria); 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT, section on atypical (atriofascicular) pathways; Sternick EB et al., JACC 2004;44:1626 (sinus-rhythm ECG in Mahaim fibres)

checks.current_value: Arruda 1998 (first 20 ms of delta in I, II, aVF, V1; R/S in III and V1). Step 1: delta negative/isoelectric in I, or R>=S in V1, means left free wall (aVF then separates anterolateral/lateral from posterior/posterolateral). Step 2: negative delta in II means epicardial inferior (postero)septal (coronary sinus / middle cardiac vein). Step 3: negative/isoelectric delta in V1 means septal (aVF and R/S in III separate inferoparaseptal, midseptal and superoparaseptal/anteroseptal). Step 4: positive delta in V1 with none of the above means right free wall (aVF, and II, separate anterior/anterolateral from posterior/posterolateral). Valid only with maximal or near-maximal pre-excitation.
checks.note: The summary matches the published algorithm, which is still widely taught. Prospective sensitivity was about 90% overall, lower (about 75%) for anteroseptal pathways. Teach it as one of several validated algorithms: the ESC 2019 guideline illustrates the St George's algorithm, and newer ones include Pambrun 2018 and EASY-WPW 2020. Update the region names to attitudinal terms ('posteroseptal' becomes inferior paraseptal, 'anteroseptal' becomes superior paraseptal).
checks.source: Arruda MS et al., J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol 1998;9:2-12; 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (Fig. 16 St George's algorithm; Fig. 17 localization in maximal pre-excitation); Cosio FG, Anderson RH et al., Circulation 1999;100:e31 (attitudinally correct AV-junction nomenclature)

checks.current_value: Quick rules for maximal pre-excitation. V1: predominantly positive (R>=S) means left-sided pathway; negative or QS means right free-wall OR septal pathway (not only 'right-sided'). Negative delta in II, III and aVF means inferior (postero)septal / inferior paraseptal; a clearly negative delta in II specifically points to an epicardial coronary-sinus / middle-cardiac-vein pathway. Negative or isoelectric delta in I, aVL, V5-V6 means left lateral free wall. Positive inferior deltas mean superior (antero)septal or anterior pathways.
checks.note: Directionally correct and still taught, but simplified. The main pitfall is that a negative V1 does not separate right free-wall from septal pathways, so a stepwise algorithm is needed for that. Use the attitudinal names (inferoparaseptal and superoparaseptal instead of posteroseptal and anteroseptal).
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (AP localization figures; about 60% left free wall, 25% septal, 15% right free wall); Arruda 1998 J Cardiovasc Electrophysiol 9:2; Fitzpatrick AP et al., JACC 1994;23:107; Cosio/Anderson Circulation 1999 nomenclature

checks.current_value: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia (or with functional BBB), usually 150-220 bpm and rarely faster. Retrograde P after the QRS on the ST segment/T wave with a constant short RP (RP < PR, RP usually <1/2 RR but >70 ms; about 90 ms on the surface ECG separates it from typical AVNRT). ST depression and QRS alternans are common. Retrograde P polarity depends on pathway site: negative inferiorly with septal/paraseptal pathways, negative in I/aVL with left free-wall pathways. Functional BBB ipsilateral to a free-wall pathway lengthens the cycle (Coumel sign), which is diagnostic of AVRT.
checks.note: Core description is current. The 180-250 bpm range is narrower and higher than current teaching (about 150-220). 'Negative inferiorly' is an over-generalisation, because P axis depends on pathway location. Add the RP >70 ms cut-off versus AVNRT.
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT, AVRT section (RP constant, up to half the cycle length; rates 150 to rarely >220 bpm; functional BBB usually ipsilateral to the AP); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Adult SVT Guideline

checks.current_value: Regular wide-QRS tachycardia with maximal (full) pre-excitation: anterograde conduction over the AP, retrograde over the AV node (or a second AP). Retrograde P is usually buried in the ST-T, so RP is hard to assess. It is rare (a few % of AVRT) and multiple APs are common. Main differential is VT; a pre-excited tachycardia can also be AT, atrial flutter or AVNRT with a bystander AP. Findings favouring VT over pre-excited tachycardia (Steurer criteria): predominantly negative QRS in V4-V6, QR in one or more of V2-V6, AV dissociation.
checks.note: Correct as stated. Expand the differential with the Steurer/Brugada criteria and the bystander-AP concept. If in doubt, a wide-QRS tachycardia should be managed as VT.
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (antidromic AVRT: fully pre-excited QRS resembling VT; wide-QRS tachycardia differential); 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of SCD (WCT differential); Steurer G et al., Clin Cardiol 1994;17:306

checks.current_value: Irregularly irregular wide-QRS tachycardia ('FBI': fast, broad, irregular) with beat-to-beat variation in QRS width and morphology (variable fusion), often with very short RR intervals and ventricular rates that can exceed 250-300 bpm. High risk: shortest pre-excited RR interval during AF (SPERRI) <=250 ms, or AP ERP <=250 ms; multiple APs and inducible AVRT are also high-risk features. Intermittent pre-excitation, or abrupt loss of pre-excitation on exercise, suggests lower risk but is imperfect: more than one fifth of such patients have AP ERP <250 ms.
checks.note: The 220 ms threshold is outdated; current guideline cut-off is <=250 ms. 'Intermittent pre-excitation = low risk' must now be taught with the caveat that it does not reliably exclude a high-risk pathway. Pair recognition with the safety rule: no AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin) and no IV amiodarone. Use cardioversion if unstable; otherwise ibutilide or procainamide (flecainide/propafenone per ESC).
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (SPERRI <=250 ms, AP ERP <=250 ms, multiple APs, inducible AVRT as high-risk; intermittent pre-excitation is an imperfect low-risk marker; pre-excited AF drug recommendations); PACES/HRS 2012 Expert Consensus on asymptomatic young patients with WPW pattern (Cohen MI et al., Heart Rhythm 2012;9:1006); 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF Guideline (Joglar JA et al., Circulation 2024;149:e1)

checks.current_value: At the moment of successful ablation the delta wave disappears abruptly, the PR lengthens to normal, the QRS narrows and the QRS axis and morphology change. Afterwards, T-wave changes (often T inversion in the leads where the delta was most negative, e.g. inferior leads after inferoparaseptal ablation) can persist for days to weeks as 'cardiac memory'. These should not be read as ischaemia. Return of the delta wave means recurrence of pathway conduction.
checks.note: Correct. Add post-ablation cardiac memory as a teaching point, because it is a frequent source of false ischaemia calls.
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (catheter ablation of APs); Geller JC et al., Am Heart J 1999;138:987 (persistent T-wave changes after AP ablation due to cardiac memory)

missing_criteria.value: WPW pattern = ECG pre-excitation (short PR, delta, wide QRS) without symptoms or arrhythmia. WPW syndrome = pre-excitation plus symptomatic tachyarrhythmia (AVRT, pre-excited AF). The pattern is seen in about 0.15-0.25% of the population. Concealed APs conduct only retrogradely, give a normal resting ECG and are not linked to SCD.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (Eur Heart J 2020;41:655), WPW and concealed AP sections

missing_criteria.value: In children the PR is <90 ms and the QRS >90 ms. Adult cut-offs (120 ms) under-diagnose pre-excitation in children.
missing_criteria.leads: II for PR; widest QRS lead
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 ECG Standardization Part III (Surawicz et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235)

missing_criteria.entity: Pre-excitation as a mimic (pseudo-infarct, pseudo-LVH, pseudo-BBB)
missing_criteria.value: Negative delta waves create Q/QS complexes that mimic MI: an inferior 'pseudo-infarct' with inferoparaseptal APs, and a tall R in V1 with left APs mimicking posterior MI/RBBB. Secondary ST-T changes mimic ischaemia. Do not diagnose MI, LVH, BBB or fascicular block, and do not interpret the axis, on fully pre-excited beats.
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF (pseudo-Q); V1-V2 (tall R); I, aVL
missing_criteria.source: Fourth Universal Definition of MI 2018 (Thygesen K et al., Eur Heart J 2019;40:237) - pre-excitation listed among conditions causing Q/QS waves without MI; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part III

missing_criteria.value: The QRS is a fusion of AP and AV-node activation. Pre-excitation increases when AV-node conduction slows (vagal tone, adenosine, AV-nodal drugs, atrial pacing near the AP) and decreases with sympathetic tone. Left lateral APs often give subtle or minimal pre-excitation with a near-normal PR (look for a small q loss and slurring in I, aVL, V5-V6). The beat-to-beat 'concertina' effect is part of this.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (WPW section: pre-excitation may be intermittent or disappear in up to 35% over time); Eisenberger M et al., Europace 2010 (PR dispersion approach to confirm/exclude pre-excitation)

missing_criteria.value: Abrupt beat-to-beat loss of the delta wave, with the PR lengthening and the QRS normalising (on a resting ECG, Holter or exercise test), suggests an AP with a long refractory period, i.e. lower risk. This is imperfect: more than 20% still have AP ERP <250 ms. A gradual loss during exercise is NOT the same sign (it reflects enhanced AV-node conduction).
missing_criteria.leads: Rhythm strip, any lead with a clear delta
missing_criteria.source: PACES/HRS 2012 Expert Consensus on asymptomatic WPW pattern (Heart Rhythm 2012;9:1006); 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT

missing_criteria.value: High-risk features: SPERRI <=250 ms, AP ERP <=250 ms, multiple APs, inducible AVRT. EP study (with isoprenaline) is recommended (Class I) for asymptomatic people in high-risk occupations and competitive athletes, and can be considered for others. Ablation is recommended when high-risk features are found.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (asymptomatic pre-excitation recommendations); PACES/HRS 2012 Consensus

missing_criteria.value: Ventricular pre-excitation (PR <120 ms + delta wave + QRS >=120 ms) is an ABNORMAL finding that needs further evaluation even in trained athletes. An isolated short PR without a delta wave in an asymptomatic athlete is not pre-excitation and needs no work-up.
missing_criteria.source: International Recommendations for ECG Interpretation in Athletes 2017 (Sharma S, Drezner JA et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466 / JACC 2017;69:1057)

missing_criteria.value: Seeing an irregular, broad, very fast tachycardia with varying QRS width means: do NOT give adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin or IV amiodarone (risk of VF). Use synchronized cardioversion if unstable; otherwise ibutilide or procainamide (flecainide/propafenone acceptable per ESC). Then ablate the AP.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (acute therapy of pre-excited AF); 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF Guideline (AF with pre-excitation section)

missing_criteria.value: AVRT: retrograde P clearly separate from the QRS (RP >70 ms; about 90 ms on the surface ECG), on the ST segment. Typical AVNRT: P hidden in or at the end of the QRS, seen as a pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S in II/III/aVF (RP <70-90 ms). QRS alternans and ST depression are more frequent in AVRT but are not specific. Ipsilateral functional BBB that slows the tachycardia proves a free-wall AP (Coumel sign).
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (narrow-QRS tachycardia differential, RP cut-offs, functional BBB in AVRT); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Adult SVT Guideline

missing_criteria.value: Incessant long-RP narrow-QRS tachycardia (RP > PR) over a concealed, decremental, usually inferoparaseptal AP. Retrograde P waves are deeply negative in II, III and aVF, and the rate is often modest. It can cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Differential: atypical AVNRT, low atrial tachycardia.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (PJRT section)

missing_criteria.value: Minimal, fixed pre-excitation with a short or normal PR and a slightly wide QRS. The degree of pre-excitation does not change with atrial pacing or adenosine. It is benign, does not support re-entry and needs no ablation, but it mimics superoparaseptal WPW.
missing_criteria.source: Sternick EB et al., Heart Rhythm 2005;2:1-6 (ECG of fasciculoventricular pathways vs anteroseptal/midseptal APs); 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (atypical pathways)

missing_criteria.entity: Pre-excitation with structural or genetic disease
missing_criteria.value: Pre-excitation with Ebstein anomaly (right-sided, often multiple APs). Pre-excitation with LVH or a short PR in hypertrophic or storage cardiomyopathy should prompt a search for PRKAG2, Danon or Pompe disease.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT (Ebstein anomaly: 10-45% have right-sided APs, often multiple); 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies (ECG red flags: short PR/pre-excitation in storage diseases)

missing_criteria.value: Use attitudinally correct anatomical names: inferior (inferoparaseptal) instead of 'posteroseptal', superior paraseptal instead of 'anteroseptal', plus midseptal and left/right free-wall segments. These are the terms used in localization algorithms and ablation reports.
missing_criteria.source: Cosio FG, Anderson RH et al., Circulation 1999;100:e31 (Living anatomy of the AV junctions, expert consensus); 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT localization figures

missing_criteria.value: Favours VT over a pre-excited tachycardia: predominantly negative QRS in V4-V6, a QR complex in one or more of V2-V6, AV dissociation. If none are present, pre-excited tachycardia is possible. A sinus-rhythm ECG showing pre-excitation with the same QRS morphology supports the pre-excited mechanism.
missing_criteria.leads: V2-V6, rhythm strip for AV dissociation
missing_criteria.source: Steurer G et al., Clin Cardiol 1994;17:306; 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of SCD (WCT differential); 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT

checks.current_value: SVT is a tachycardia (atrial and/or ventricular rate >100 bpm at rest) whose mechanism involves tissue from the His bundle or above. Atrial flutter (macro-re-entrant AT) and MAT are INCLUDED; AF is conventionally excluded (it has its own guidelines). AVRT is included even though its circuit uses the ventricle. ≥3 consecutive beats is still the usual working threshold for calling a run a tachycardia.
checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with SVT (Brugada J et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720), section 3 Definitions and Table 5 classification; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for Adult SVT (Page RL et al., Circulation 2016;133:e471-e505), Definitions
checks.note: The 2004 definition leaves out flutter, which current classifications put inside the SVT umbrella, and it does not state the >100 bpm rate threshold. 'Above the His bifurcation' is close to the modern 'His bundle or above'. Teach that AVRT counts as SVT even though the ventricle is part of the circuit.

checks.current_value: Premature P' whose morphology differs from sinus. P'R is normal or prolonged. The QRS is usually identical to sinus, but can be aberrant (usually RBBB-type) or absent (non-conducted/blocked PAC) when very premature. The pause is usually less than compensatory because the sinus node is reset.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part II: Electrocardiography diagnostic statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325-1332), atrial premature complex statements; 2019 ESC SVT guidelines (atrial ectopy/focal AT section)
checks.note: Current term is premature atrial complex (PAC). Add two practical points: (1) a blocked PAC is the most common cause of an unexpected pause, so look for a P' deforming the preceding T wave; (2) the pause is not an absolute discriminator, because a PAC that fails to reset the sinus node can give a fully compensatory pause.

checks.current_value: Ectopic (low) atrial rhythm: rate <100 bpm, P negative in II, III, aVF (superior P axis), usually positive in aVR and positive/isoelectric in aVL, PR ≥120 ms. A PR <120 ms with the same P polarity suggests a junctional origin instead.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS Part II statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325) – 'ectopic atrial rhythm'; 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, focal AT P-wave localisation (negative inferior P waves suggest a caudal atrial origin)
checks.note: The polarity pattern is right. Teach the PR ≥120 ms condition and the rate <100 bpm limit (≥100 bpm = atrial tachycardia). Current statement lists use the term 'ectopic atrial rhythm'.
