P morphology only roughly localises the focus: low right atrium/coronary sinus os and low left atrium both give inferior-negative P waves, and a negative P in I/aVL points to a left atrial origin.

checks.current_value: Focal AT is an organized atrial rhythm ≥100 bpm (usually 100-250 bpm) from a discrete focus. P' differs from sinus and is usually separated by an isoelectric baseline. Usually a long-RP tachycardia (RP > PR), but the PR depends on AV conduction, so a short RP is possible. AV block can occur without stopping the tachycardia, which argues against AVRT/AVNRT. Warm-up at onset and cool-down at termination suggest an automatic focus. The mechanism (automatic, triggered or micro-re-entrant) cannot be reliably determined from the surface ECG.
checks.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines (Eur Heart J 2020;41:655), section 11.1.1 Focal AT ('organized atrial rhythm ≥100 b.p.m. initiated from a discrete origin'); 2014 AHA/ACC/HRS AF guideline differential table (focal AT: discrete P waves with isoelectric segment, rate typically 100-250 bpm)
checks.note: The 140-220 bpm range (100-180 automatic) is narrower than the current ≥100 (100-250) bpm. P'R lengthening up to block reflects AV nodal decremental conduction and does not identify re-entry. What matters is that the atrial rhythm continues despite AV block. Do not teach P'R < RP' as a mandatory criterion.

checks.current_value: AT with AV block: discrete P' waves separated by an isoelectric baseline, with more P' waves than QRS complexes (classically digoxin toxicity or hypokalaemia). MAT: rapid irregular rhythm with ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies, atrial rate >100 bpm, isoelectric baseline between P waves, and variable PP, PR and RR intervals.
checks.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.1.2 Multifocal AT (≥3 P morphologies, rate >100 bpm, isoelectric period between P waves) and section 11.1.1 (an isoelectric baseline does not exclude macro-re-entry, particularly with atrial scar); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline, MAT section
checks.note: The MAT definition lacks the rate >100 bpm condition. Below 100 bpm the same picture is called multifocal atrial rhythm (wandering atrial pacemaker). Stress the isoelectric baseline between P waves, which separates MAT from AF, its main mimic. Also warn that an isoelectric line between P' waves does not rule out a scar-related macro-re-entrant (atypical) flutter.

checks.current_value: Typical (CTI-dependent) counter-clockwise flutter: regular atrial activity about 250-330 bpm, negative sawtooth F waves in II, III, aVF with no isoelectric baseline in those leads, and positive F waves in V1. Reverse-typical (clockwise, still CTI-dependent) flutter: broad positive F waves inferiorly, negative/bimodal in V1. Atypical flutter means a non-CTI macro-re-entry whose morphology does not match the typical circuits, not simply 'positive in the inferior leads'. Untreated 2:1 conduction gives a ventricular rate about 150 bpm. Class IC drugs or amiodarone can slow flutter below 200 bpm and allow 1:1 conduction, often with a wide QRS that mimics VT (emergency).
checks.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.1.3 Macro-re-entrant atrial tachycardias (typical CCW flutter 250-330 b.p.m.; CW flutter morphology; atypical flutter; 1:1 risk with IC drugs/amiodarone); Saoudi N et al., EHRA/NASPE expert group classification of atrial tachycardias, Eur Heart J 2001;22:1162-1182
checks.note: Two problems. (1) The rate range 200-350 should be about 250-330 for untreated typical flutter; lower rates occur with antiarrhythmic drugs or diseased atria. (2) Labelling 'negative inferior = typical, positive inferior = atypical' is obsolete: clockwise flutter is positive inferiorly but is still typical (CTI-dependent). The 2:1 at about 150 bpm and 1:1 as an emergency points are still correct.

checks.current_value: No discernible repeating P waves. Irregular, disorganized atrial activity (f waves about 350-600/min, best seen in V1; may be coarse, fine or practically invisible). Irregularly irregular RR intervals when AV conduction is intact. Clinical AF diagnosis needs a 12-lead ECG or a single-lead tracing of ≥30 s. Untreated ventricular rate is typically 100-180 bpm. A very fast (often >250 bpm), irregular, wide QRS tachycardia with beat-to-beat changing QRS morphology indicates pre-excited AF (shortest pre-excited RR ≤250 ms = high risk). A slow ventricular rate without drugs suggests AV conduction disease. A regular slow RR in AF suggests complete AV block with an escape rhythm.
checks.source: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of AF (Van Gelder IC et al., Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314-3414), diagnostic criteria (12-lead ECG or ≥30 s single-lead); 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline (Joglar JA et al., Circulation 2024;149:e1-e156); 2019 ESC SVT guidelines section 11.3 (pre-excited AF, SPERRI ≤250 ms)
checks.note: The core criteria are correct. Two refinements: (1) '>200 bpm suggests a pathway' is too simple, because AF through a normal AV node can exceed 200 bpm in the young or during catecholamine excess. The specific clue is a very fast, irregular, broad QRS with varying degrees of pre-excitation. (2) Add the ≥30 s / 12-lead documentation rule and point out that a regular RR in AF is an abnormal finding.

checks.current_value: Favour aberrancy when a premature P' precedes the wide beat (the most reliable sign), V1 shows a triphasic rsR' RBBB-type pattern with qRs in V6, and the initial QRS vector matches the conducted beats. Favour ectopy (PVC) when there is no preceding P', the coupling interval is fixed, V1 shows a monophasic R/qR or an atypical LBBB-type pattern, and the beat is followed by a fully compensatory pause. Ashman (long-short) sequences support aberrancy but do not prove it. Concordance is a criterion for VT in wide-QRS tachycardia, not a single-beat test.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular conduction disturbances (Surawicz B et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240), aberrant conduction; 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 8.2 wide QRS tachycardia (Brugada 1991, Vereckei 2008 criteria); 2022 ESC VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld K et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997)
checks.note: The qualitative discriminators match current teaching. The numerical 'RP <0.11 s vs >0.20 s' cut-offs are not part of any current standard, and their meaning (which R to which P) is ambiguous, so they should not be used for grading. Caveats to teach: PVCs also tend to follow long cycles (rule of bigeminy), so Ashman is weak evidence; an interpolated PVC has no pause; a PVC with retrograde atrial capture can reset the sinus node and give a non-compensatory pause.

checks.current_value: Junctional escape rhythm 40-60 bpm; accelerated junctional rhythm about 60-100 bpm; junctional tachycardia >100 bpm (non-paroxysmal junctional tachycardia historically 70-130 bpm). Narrow QRS (unless pre-existing BBB). Retrograde P' (negative in II, III, aVF) appears in one of three places: before the QRS with PR <120 ms, hidden in the QRS, or just after it in the ST segment. Alternatively there is AV dissociation with independent sinus P waves.
checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS Part II statement list (Mason JW et al., Circulation 2007;115:1325) – junctional rhythm/accelerated junctional rhythm statements; 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.2.2 Non-re-entrant junctional tachycardias (non-paroxysmal junctional tachycardia 70-130 b.p.m.; JET with short RP or AV dissociation); Surawicz B, Knilans TK, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed.
checks.note: Mostly correct, but the thresholds differ from the conventional ones: PR <0.12 s rather than <0.10 s, and a 40 bpm lower bound rather than 35 bpm. The current 2004 limits would misclassify retrograde P waves with PR 100-119 ms. Also add the accelerated-junctional and junctional-tachycardia bands and the possibility of AV dissociation. The escape vs premature-beat context is correct.

checks.current_value: Typical (slow-fast) AVNRT, about 90% of cases: abrupt onset and offset; regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, usually about 140-220 bpm (wider range reported); retrograde P' hidden in the QRS or seen at its end as pseudo-r' in V1 and pseudo-S in II, III, aVF (specificity 91-100%, low sensitivity); very short RP (when P' is visible, RP <90 ms on the surface ECG favours AVNRT over AVRT). Atypical (fast-slow) AVNRT: long RP with negative P' in II, III, aVF. Slow-slow AVNRT has an intermediate RP. Vagal manoeuvres terminate only about 19-54% (modified Valsalva about 43%); adenosine terminates most episodes.
checks.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.2.1 AVNRT and section 8.1 narrow QRS differential (pseudo-r'/pseudo-S specificity; RP cut-off 90 ms on surface ECG; vagal manoeuvre efficacy 19-54%, modified Valsalva 43% vs 17% – REVERT trial, Appelboam A et al., Lancet 2015;386:1747); 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline AVNRT section
checks.note: The criteria for typical AVNRT are correct. 'Often ends with vagal manoeuvres' overstates the success rate; quote it as roughly 1 in 3 to 1 in 2 with the modified Valsalva, and note that adenosine is the drug that reliably terminates it. 'P visible in about 50%' cannot be verified against current sources: in typical AVNRT the P' is most often fully hidden and visible as a pseudo-r'/pseudo-S in a minority. Treat that figure as approximate or drop it. Add the atypical long-RP form.

missing_criteria.value: First decide regular or irregular. Irregular: AF, MAT, or flutter/AT with variable block. Regular: locate atrial activity. No visible P' or P' at the end of the QRS: typical AVNRT. Short RP (RP < PR) with P' in the ST segment: orthodromic AVRT (or AT with long PR). Long RP (RP > PR): AT, atypical AVNRT, PJRT, sinus tachycardia. More P' than QRS: AT or flutter (AV-node-independent).
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines (Eur Heart J 2020;41:655), section 8.1 and Figure 'Differential diagnosis of narrow QRS tachycardia'; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline, ECG differential diagnosis figure
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF, V1 (look for P' in ST-T); long rhythm strip

missing_criteria.value: Regular narrow-QRS tachycardia, typically 150 to >220 bpm. Retrograde P' after the QRS, inside the ST-T segment, with a constant RP usually ≥90 ms and less than half the cycle length. Functional BBB on the same side as the pathway may slow the rate. ST depression and QRS alternans are common but nonspecific. Sinus-rhythm ECG may show pre-excitation (manifest pathway) or be normal (concealed pathway).
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.3 Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (orthodromic AVRT description)
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF, V1; compare with baseline sinus ECG

missing_criteria.value: In adults: PR <120 ms, delta wave (slurred initial QRS), QRS ≥120 ms with secondary ST-T changes. WPW syndrome = this pattern plus tachyarrhythmia. Intermittent or abrupt loss of pre-excitation is a low-risk marker.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III: Intraventricular conduction disturbances (Surawicz B et al., Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240), ventricular pre-excitation; 2019 ESC SVT guidelines section 11.3 (risk stratification)

missing_criteria.value: Fast, irregular, broad-QRS tachycardia with beat-to-beat changing QRS width/morphology, often >250 bpm. Shortest pre-excited RR interval ≤250 ms marks a high-risk pathway (risk of VF). AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin, amiodarone IV) are contraindicated.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.3 (pre-excited AF; SPERRI ≤250 ms; acute management recommendations)

missing_criteria.value: Regular wide-QRS tachycardia, fully pre-excited (QRS resembles maximal pre-excitation). Retrograde P' usually within the ST-T. Indistinguishable from VT on morphology alone, so manage as VT/WCT unless known WPW.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.3 (antidromic AVRT)

missing_criteria.entity: Long-RP tachycardias: atypical AVNRT and PJRT
missing_criteria.value: Narrow-QRS tachycardia with RP > PR and deeply negative P' in II, III, aVF. Differential: atypical (fast-slow) AVNRT; PJRT (often incessant, a decremental slow posteroseptal pathway, a cause of tachycardiomyopathy); low/posteroseptal focal AT; sinus tachycardia (P positive inferiorly).
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, sections 11.2.1 (atypical AVNRT, 'long RP tachycardia') and 11.3 (PJRT: deeply inverted retrograde P in II, III, aVF)

missing_criteria.entity: Wide-QRS tachycardia (VT vs SVT with aberrancy/pre-excitation)
missing_criteria.value: Assume VT until proven otherwise, especially with structural heart disease. VT criteria: AV dissociation; fusion or capture beats; precordial concordance; absent RS in all precordial leads or RS interval >100 ms (Brugada); initial R or r >40 ms in aVR (Vereckei); R-wave peak time in II ≥50 ms (Pava). Verapamil is contraindicated in WCT of unknown origin.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 8.2 Wide QRS tachycardia (table of ECG criteria; verapamil recommendation III); 2022 ESC VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld K et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126); Brugada P et al., Circulation 1991;83:1649; Vereckei A et al., Heart Rhythm 2008;5:89
missing_criteria.leads: V1-V6, aVR, II; long rhythm strip for AV dissociation

missing_criteria.entity: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction / variable block
missing_criteria.value: Any regular narrow tachycardia at about 150 bpm should prompt a search for a second F wave (hidden in the QRS or T) in II, III, aVF and V1. Vagal manoeuvres or adenosine raise the AV block and unmask F waves without terminating flutter. Flutter with variable block is irregular but the RR intervals cluster at multiples of a constant F-F cycle, whereas AF has irregular atrial activity of varying rate and morphology.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.1.3 ('2:1 flutter should be considered at a ventricular rate of about 150 b.p.m.') and Table 8 (diagnostic response to vagal manoeuvres/adenosine)

missing_criteria.value: Clinical AF requires ECG documentation: a standard 12-lead ECG, or a single-lead tracing of ≥30 s, showing irregular RR intervals (with intact AV conduction) and no discernible repeating P waves. Device-detected atrial high-rate episodes are not equivalent to clinical AF.
missing_criteria.source: 2024 ESC AF guidelines (Van Gelder IC et al., Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314), diagnosis section; 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline (Joglar JA et al., Circulation 2024;149:e1)

missing_criteria.value: AF with regular RR intervals means AV dissociation: complete AV block with a junctional escape (narrow QRS) or ventricular escape (wide QRS), or an accelerated junctional rhythm. Classically this is digoxin toxicity. It is never 'AF with controlled rate'.
missing_criteria.source: Surawicz B, Knilans TK. Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice, 6th ed. (Saunders/Elsevier 2008), AF and digitalis chapters; 2024 ESC AF guidelines (drug toxicity/bradyarrhythmia in AF)

missing_criteria.entity: Inappropriate sinus tachycardia and sinus nodal re-entrant tachycardia
missing_criteria.value: P morphology and axis identical to sinus (positive in I, II, aVF). IST: sinus rate >100 bpm at rest, mean 24-h rate >90 bpm, out of proportion to demand. Sinus nodal re-entry: paroxysmal onset and offset with sinus-like P waves. Recognising these keeps them from being mislabelled as focal AT.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.0 Sinus tachycardias (IST definition); 2015 HRS Expert Consensus on POTS, IST and VVS (Sheldon RS et al., Heart Rhythm 2015;12:e41-e63)
missing_criteria.leads: II, I, aVF, V1 (compare P with prior sinus ECG)

missing_criteria.entity: Junctional ectopic tachycardia / non-paroxysmal junctional tachycardia
missing_criteria.value: Narrow-QRS tachycardia with short RP or AV dissociation (sinus P waves marching through); gradual onset. Causes include digoxin toxicity, hypokalaemia, myocardial ischaemia, post-cardiac surgery (especially paediatric JET) and congenital forms.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.2.2 Non-re-entrant junctional tachycardias

missing_criteria.value: Negative/isoelectric P' in I and aVL suggests a left atrial origin. Negative P' in V1 suggests a lateral right atrial origin; positive or biphasic P' in V1 suggests a septal RA or LA origin. Negative inferior P' suggests a caudal (low) origin; positive inferior P' suggests a superior origin (e.g. high crista terminalis, superior PVs).
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, section 11.1.1 (P-wave localisation); Kistler PM et al., P-wave morphology in focal atrial tachycardia, J Am Coll Cardiol 2006;48:1010-1017
missing_criteria.leads: I, aVL, II, III, aVF, V1

missing_criteria.value: Termination with the last event a P' (or a QRS without a following P') points to an AV-node-dependent tachycardia (AVNRT, AVRT). Transient AV block with persisting atrial activity unmasks AT or flutter. Gradual slowing and then re-acceleration suggests sinus tachycardia or automatic AT. Record a 12-lead ECG during adenosine. Use caution in pre-excitation (adenosine can precipitate fast AF).
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC SVT guidelines, Table 8 (responses of narrow QRS tachycardia to vagal manoeuvres and adenosine) and key messages

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part III (intraventricular conduction, QRS >=120 ms) and Part I (rhythm statements); 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline (Al-Khatib et al., Circulation 2018;138:e272); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997)
checks.current_value: Premature QRS, usually >=120 ms with bundle-branch-block-like shape, not preceded by a related premature P wave; secondary ST-T opposite to the main QRS deflection; fixed coupling interval for re-entrant/triggered PVCs (coupling variation >80 ms plus fusion beats and a common interectopic denominator suggests parasystole); pause usually fully compensatory
checks.note: Use >=0.12 s rather than >0.12 s. Two caveats: PVCs from the fascicles or septum can be <120 ms, and the pause is fully compensatory only when the sinus node is not reset by retrograde conduction (non-compensatory pause is possible; interpolated PVCs have no pause). Teach the pause as typical, not mandatory.

checks.source: 2019 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS Expert Consensus Statement on Catheter Ablation of Ventricular Arrhythmias (Cronin et al., Heart Rhythm 2020;17:e2), ECG localization section; ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (idiopathic outflow-tract and fascicular VA)
checks.current_value: RBBB-like V1 = left ventricular (or fascicular) origin. LBBB-like V1 = right ventricle OR interventricular septum / LV outflow tract / aortic cusps. LBBB-like + inferior axis = outflow tract; precordial transition at or before V2 (or earlier than the sinus transition) points to LVOT/aortic cusp, transition at V4 or later to RVOT
checks.note: Fine as a first rule of thumb, but the LBBB = RV half is oversimplified. Septal scar VT after MI and LVOT/aortic-cusp PVCs often look LBBB-like. Add axis (inferior vs superior) and the precordial transition to the teaching.

checks.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (PVC burden >=10% and PVC-induced cardiomyopathy); 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline (definitions: NSVT = >=3 consecutive ventricular beats >100 bpm, <30 s); 2014 EHRA/HRS/APHRS Expert Consensus on Ventricular Arrhythmias (Pedersen et al., Europace 2014); Lown & Wolf, Circulation 1971 (historical)
checks.current_value: Keep the descriptive terms bigeminy, trigeminy and couplet. Three or more consecutive ventricular beats at >100 bpm = NSVT (so a 'triplet' is already NSVT). Instead of Lown grades, describe ectopy by Holter burden (% of total beats; >=10% with an unexplained low EF means suspect PVC-induced cardiomyopathy), mono- vs polymorphic, coupling interval (short-coupled <300 ms is high risk) and presence of NSVT
checks.note: The Lown grade numbers match the 1971 original, but the system is now only historical. It did not reliably predict risk, and after CAST, suppressing graded ectopy was shown to be harmful. The '>3 = VT run' threshold also contradicts this cluster's own VT criterion (>=3 beats). It should be >=3.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part I (rhythm statements: ventricular escape beat/rhythm); standard references, e.g. Surawicz & Knilans, Chou's Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice 6th ed.
checks.current_value: Late (post-pause) wide QRS not preceded by a conducted P wave; ventricular escape (idioventricular) rhythm about 20-40 bpm
checks.note: Say 'no related/conducted P wave' rather than 'no P wave'. In complete AV block, dissociated P waves march through the escape rhythm. Rates of 40-~110 bpm are classified as accelerated idioventricular rhythm.

checks.source: 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline (Table of definitions); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines; ACC/AHA/ESC 2006 VA/SCD guidelines (Table 2 classification); ACC/AHA/HRS 2006 Key Data Elements for EP studies (VT = >=3 beats, CL <600 ms)
checks.current_value: VT = >=3 consecutive ventricular beats at >100 bpm (cycle length <600 ms). NSVT ends by itself in <30 s. Sustained VT lasts >30 s OR needs termination earlier because of haemodynamic compromise. Monomorphic VT rate usually ~120-250 bpm (slower on antiarrhythmics). QRS usually >=120 ms (fascicular VT can be ~110-140 ms). Rhythm essentially regular, with small cycle-length variation possible, especially at onset
checks.note: 140-200 bpm is a typical range, not a definition. Rates of 100-140 (slow VT) must not be excluded. The '+/-0.03 s' regularity rule is not a guideline criterion. 'Onset often R-on-T' is misleading for scar-related monomorphic VT, which usually starts with a late-coupled PVC. Short-coupled R-on-T initiation belongs to ischaemic polymorphic VT/VF and idiopathic VF. Torsades starts after a pause (short-long-short).

checks.source: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for Adult SVT (Page et al., Circulation 2016;133:e506), wide-complex tachycardia section; ESC 2019 SVT guidelines (Brugada et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:655), table of ECG criteria favouring VT; Brugada P et al., Circulation 1991;83:1649
checks.current_value: VA/AV dissociation (ventricular rate > atrial rate) occurs in roughly half of VTs but is visible on the surface ECG in only ~20-30%; about a third of VTs have 1:1 or Wenckebach retrograde VA conduction (retrograde P after the QRS, on the ST segment). A capture beat is a narrow, normally conducted QRS; a fusion beat is intermediate. Both are near-diagnostic of VT but uncommon, especially at fast rates
checks.note: Correct. Add that absence of visible dissociation does not exclude VT. AV dissociation with V > A is highly specific for VT.

checks.source: Wellens HJ, Bar FW, Lie KI, Am J Med 1978;64:27; ESC 2019 SVT guidelines (Brugada et al.), wide-QRS tachycardia criteria; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline; 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline
checks.current_value: Favour VT if any of these are present: prior MI or structural heart disease (strongest clinical predictor); extreme/'northwest' axis (-90 to +/-180 degrees); QRS >140 ms with RBBB-like or >160 ms with LBBB-like pattern; precordial concordance (negative concordance highly specific; positive concordance also occurs with antidromic AVRT over a left-posterior pathway); morphology identical to PVCs recorded in sinus rhythm. If in doubt, manage as VT
checks.note: Still taught. Caveats: the QRS-width criteria are unreliable with class IC/III drugs, hyperkalaemia, pre-existing BBB or pre-excitation. Fascicular VT can be relatively narrow.

checks.source: Brugada P, Brugada J, Mont L et al., Circulation 1991;83:1649-1659; Kindwall KE et al., Am J Cardiol 1988;61:1279 (LBBB-type criteria); ESC 2019 SVT guidelines (lists RS >100 ms and absence of RS as VT criteria); Jastrzebski M et al., Europace 2012 (comparative validation)
checks.current_value: Step 1: no RS complex in any of V1-V6 -> VT. Step 2: R-onset to S-nadir >100 ms in ANY precordial lead -> VT. Step 3: AV dissociation -> VT. Step 4: VT morphology criteria met in both V1/V2 and V6 -> VT; otherwise SVT with aberrancy. For LBBB-like WCT in V1/V2: r >30 ms, r-onset to S-nadir >60 ms, or a notched S downstroke favour VT
checks.note: Still the reference stepwise algorithm. Specify 'in any precordial lead' for step 2. Independent validations show lower specificity (about 60-75%) than the original 96%, and the algorithm is less reliable with pre-excitation and antiarrhythmic drugs. Teach it alongside the aVR and lead-II algorithms (see missing criteria).

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part I (accelerated idioventricular rhythm statement); ESC 2017 STEMI guidelines (Ibanez et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:119) and ESC 2023 ACS guidelines (reperfusion arrhythmias, benign, no specific therapy)
checks.current_value: Three or more consecutive ventricular beats at about 40/50-110/120 bpm (definitions vary), often close to the sinus rate, with fusion and capture beats as it competes with sinus rhythm. Usually benign and self-limited. Common after reperfusion but NOT a specific marker of successful reperfusion (ST-segment resolution is the better marker)
checks.note: 60-120 bpm falls inside the accepted range, but the lower bound is not standardized: many sources use 40 or 50. For grading in the app, accept roughly 50-110. Soften 'marker of reperfusion' to 'frequently associated with reperfusion'.

checks.source: Drew BJ et al., AHA/ACCF Scientific Statement: Prevention of Torsade de Pointes in Hospital Settings, Circulation 2010;121:1047-1060; ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (LQTS section); 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline
checks.current_value: Polymorphic VT whose QRS amplitude and polarity twist around the isoelectric line (a cycle every ~5-20 beats), rate ~160-240 (up to 250) bpm, occurring with marked QT prolongation and often QT-U distortion. QTc >500 ms (or a rise of >=60 ms from baseline on a QT-prolonging drug) is the high-risk threshold. Typical onset is pause-dependent: a short-long-short RR sequence, with the triggering PVC landing near the peak of the T/U wave of the post-pause beat. Often self-terminating but can degenerate into VF
checks.note: 'QT >0.60 s' is not a current criterion. The threshold is a rate-corrected QTc >500 ms. The trigger should be taught as the short-long-short (pause-dependent) sequence rather than a generic 'PVC on T'. LQT1 is adrenergic-dependent. Rare short-coupled TdP has a normal QT.

checks.source: ACC/AHA/ESC 2006 Guidelines for Management of Patients With Ventricular Arrhythmias and Prevention of SCD (Zipes et al., Circulation 2006;114:e385), Table 2 ECG classification; WHO ICD-11 BC71.1 (VF definition); ERC 2021 / AHA 2020 resuscitation guidelines (fine VF vs asystole)
checks.current_value: Ventricular flutter: regular (cycle-length variability <=~30 ms), monomorphic sine-wave tachycardia at about 300 bpm (cycle length ~200 ms), with no isoelectric interval and no separable QRS or T. VF: rapid (usually >300 bpm, CL <=180 ms), grossly irregular activity with varying cycle length, morphology and amplitude. Coarse or fine; fine VF can mimic asystole, so check another lead and the gain
checks.note: 'About 200/min' understates the flutter rate, which current definitions put at about 300/min. The book's figure may confuse the ~200 ms cycle length with rate. Accept roughly 250-350/min. The VF description is still correct.

checks.source: 2013 HRS/EHRA/APHRS Expert Consensus on Inherited Primary Arrhythmia Syndromes (Priori et al., Heart Rhythm 2013;10:1932); 2016 J-Wave Syndromes Expert Consensus Conference report, Shanghai score (Antzelevitch et al., Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295 / Europace 2017); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Brugada syndrome section)
checks.current_value: Type 1 Brugada ECG pattern: coved ST elevation >=2 mm (0.2 mV) followed by a negative T wave in >=1 right precordial lead (V1 and/or V2), recorded in the 4th, 3rd or 2nd intercostal space. A spontaneous type 1 pattern in a patient without other heart disease establishes the diagnosis. A type 1 pattern induced by drug or fever needs added clinical features (arrhythmic syncope, aborted SCD/VF, family history of BrS or of unexplained SCD <45 y, nocturnal agonal respiration). The type 2 (saddleback) pattern is not diagnostic alone. It is a pseudo-RBBB: no broad terminal S in I/V6
checks.note: The 1992 'RBBB + persistent ST elevation + sudden death' description is superseded. Today the ECG pattern (type 1 coved, >=2 mm) is separated from the syndrome (pattern plus clinical features), and high intercostal leads are allowed. Teach Brugada phenocopies and the sodium-channel-blocker challenge.

missing_criteria.value: VT if in aVR: initial dominant R wave; or initial r or q >40 ms; or notch on the descending limb of a negative-onset QRS; or vi/vt <=1 (ventricular activation velocity in the initial 40 ms vs the terminal 40 ms)
missing_criteria.source: Vereckei A et al., Heart Rhythm 2008;5:89-98; ESC 2019 SVT guidelines (Brugada et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:655), WCT criteria table

missing_criteria.value: R-wave peak time (QRS onset to first change of polarity) >=50 ms in lead II favours VT
missing_criteria.source: Pava LF et al., Heart Rhythm 2010;7:922-926; ESC 2019 SVT guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Differential includes SVT with aberrancy/pre-existing BBB, pre-excited AF (fast, broad, irregular, varying QRS width, rates may exceed 250 bpm), antidromic AVRT, paced rhythm, hyperkalaemia or sodium-channel-blocker toxicity (very wide, sine-like), and motion/tremor artefact (narrow QRS marching through the artefact). If the diagnosis is uncertain, treat as VT
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2019 SVT guidelines; 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS SVT guideline; 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline

missing_criteria.value: NSVT: >=3 beats >100 bpm, <30 s. Sustained: >30 s or terminated earlier for haemodynamic compromise. Monomorphic (single stable QRS morphology) vs polymorphic (beat-to-beat changing QRS). Electrical storm: >=3 episodes of sustained VT/VF or appropriate ICD therapies within 24 h
missing_criteria.source: 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline (definitions); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Polymorphic VT without QT prolongation is usually ischaemic (acute coronary syndrome) or short-coupled idiopathic VF. Treat with revascularisation/antiarrhythmics, not magnesium/pacing as for TdP. Measure the QT on the sinus beats before the episode
missing_criteria.source: 2017 AHA/ACC/HRS VA/SCD guideline; ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines; Drew et al., AHA/ACCF 2010 TdP statement

missing_criteria.value: Beat-to-beat alternation of the QRS axis/polarity in the frontal plane (often RBBB with alternating left/right axis). Suggests digoxin toxicity, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (exercise-induced) or Andersen-Tawil syndrome
missing_criteria.source: 2013 HRS/EHRA/APHRS Expert Consensus on Inherited Primary Arrhythmia Syndromes; ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (CPVT section)

missing_criteria.value: RBBB-like with left superior axis (left posterior fascicle, most common) or right/inferior axis (left anterior fascicle). Relatively narrow QRS (~110-140 ms) with RS in precordial leads, so it is often mistaken for SVT with aberrancy. Verapamil-sensitive, structurally normal heart
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (idiopathic VA); 2019 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS catheter-ablation consensus (Cronin et al.)

missing_criteria.value: LBBB-like with inferior axis (tall R in II, III, aVF). Precordial transition at V4 or later suggests RVOT; transition at or before V2, or earlier than the sinus-rhythm transition (V2 transition ratio >=0.6), suggests LVOT/aortic cusp. Most common idiopathic VA
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines; 2019 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS catheter-ablation consensus; Betensky BP et al., JACC 2011;57:2255

missing_criteria.value: PVC burden >=10% of beats on Holter with an unexplained reduced LVEF raises suspicion of PVC-induced cardiomyopathy. Higher-risk features: short coupling interval (<300 ms, R-on-T, risk of idiopathic VF/short-coupled TdP), QRS >150-160 ms, non-outflow-tract origin, polymorphic PVCs, and exercise-induced increase
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines; 2014 EHRA/HRS/APHRS Expert Consensus on Ventricular Arrhythmias

missing_criteria.value: Congenital LQTS diagnosed with QTc >=480 ms on repeated 12-lead ECGs, or LQTS (Schwartz) score >3. QTc >=460 ms with unexplained syncope can also qualify. For drug-induced risk, QTc >500 ms or an increase >=60 ms from baseline is high risk. Measure in the lead with the longest QT (II or V5) using the tangent method. Prefer Fridericia over Bazett at high heart rates
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (LQTS); Drew et al., AHA/ACCF 2010 TdP statement; AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 ECG Standardization Part IV (ST/T/U and QT)

missing_criteria.value: Diagnose SQTS with QTc <=360 ms plus a pathogenic mutation, a family history of SQTS, or survival of VT/VF without heart disease. Consider it with QTc <=320 ms alone. Short, tall, peaked T waves
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines; 2013 HRS/EHRA/APHRS inherited arrhythmia consensus

missing_criteria.value: J-point elevation >=1 mm (0.1 mV) with a notch or slur at the end of the QRS in >=2 contiguous inferior and/or lateral leads. Early repolarization syndrome = this pattern in a survivor of otherwise unexplained VF/polymorphic VT
missing_criteria.source: Macfarlane PW et al., The Early Repolarization Pattern: consensus paper, JACC 2015;66:470; 2016 J-Wave Syndromes Expert Consensus (Antzelevitch et al.); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF, I, aVL, V4-V6

missing_criteria.value: Type 2 (saddleback): ST elevation >=0.5 mm (usually >=2 mm J-point) with concave-up ST and positive or flat T in V1/V2 (beta angle >58 degrees, base of the triangle 5 mm below the r' apex >=3.5 mm). Not diagnostic alone; may convert to type 1 with fever, sodium-channel blockers or high-ICS leads. Record V1-V2 in the 2nd-3rd ICS when suspected. Phenocopies (e.g. RV ischaemia, hyperkalaemia, pectus) must be excluded
missing_criteria.source: Bayes de Luna A et al., Current electrocardiographic criteria for diagnosis of Brugada pattern: a consensus report, J Electrocardiol 2012;45:433; 2016 J-Wave Syndromes Expert Consensus; ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Inverted T waves V1-V3 or beyond in individuals >14 y without complete RBBB (major). Epsilon wave (major in the 2010 Task Force criteria, minor in the 2020 Padua criteria). Terminal activation duration >=55 ms in V1-V3. VT with LBBB morphology and superior axis (major) or inferior axis (minor). >500 PVCs/24 h
missing_criteria.source: Marcus FI et al., 2010 Task Force Criteria, Circulation 2010;121:1533; Corrado D et al., 2020 Padua criteria, Int J Cardiol 2020;319:106; ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines

missing_criteria.value: Low-amplitude (fine) VF can look like asystole. Confirm 'flat line' in at least two leads with adequate gain and check lead connections before calling asystole
missing_criteria.source: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021 (Adult Advanced Life Support); 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Recommendations for Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part IV: ST segment, T and U waves, QT interval (Rautaharju et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241); Drew BJ et al., AHA/ACCF Scientific Statement on Prevention of Torsade de Pointes in Hospital Settings (Circulation 2010;121:1047); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997) for congenital LQTS/SQTS; CredibleMeds QTdrugs list for drug classification
checks.current_value: Long QT. Drugs: class Ia (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) and class III antiarrhythmics (sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide, amiodarone; amiodarone lengthens QT a lot but rarely causes TdP). Non-cardiac drugs: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol), methadone, ondansetron, tricyclics, citalopram, azole antifungals (check CredibleMeds). Electrolytes: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia. Other causes: bradycardia or high-grade AV block, acute ischaemia, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy or heart failure, intracranial events (e.g. SAH), hypothermia, hypothyroidism, starvation/anorexia, congenital LQTS; female sex is a risk factor. Short QT: hypercalcaemia, digoxin, hyperkalaemia (modest, variable), hyperthermia, acidosis, congenital SQTS.
checks.note: Nothing listed is wrong, but the list leaves out the causes students most need: hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, non-cardiac QT-prolonging drugs, class III agents other than amiodarone, bradycardia, and congenital LQTS/SQTS. In hypokalaemia the 'long QT' is often really a QU interval (T–U fusion), and this should be taught explicitly. The hyperkalaemia effect on QT is small and inconsistent; peaked T waves are the teaching point.

checks.source: Drew BJ et al., AHA/ACCF Scientific Statement on Prevention of Torsade de Pointes in Hospital Settings (Circulation 2010;121:1047); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997); AHA 2023 Focused Update on poisoning-related cardiac arrest/toxicity (Lavonas et al., Circulation 2023;148:e149)
checks.current_value: Definition: TdP is polymorphic VT with a QRS axis that twists around the baseline, occurring with QT prolongation. It is often started by a pause-dependent short–long–short sequence, with large, distorted T–U waves in the beat after the pause. Acquired causes: QT-prolonging drugs (class Ia; class III such as sotalol, dofetilide and ibutilide; non-cardiac drugs such as macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, methadone, ondansetron and tricyclics), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia, complete AV block or long pauses. Added risk: female sex, heart failure/LVH, recent conversion from AF, drug interactions, renal or hepatic impairment. Congenital: LQTS. Risk is high at QTc >500 ms or a rise of >60 ms from baseline.
checks.note: 'Ischaemia' is misleading as a cause of TdP. Polymorphic VT in acute ischaemia usually happens with a normal QT and should not be called torsades, because treatment differs (revascularisation, not magnesium or overdrive pacing). Class III drugs and non-cardiac drugs, now the main acquired causes, are missing. Advanced AV block is correct, through the bradycardia/pause mechanism.

checks.source: Gibbons RJ et al., ACC/AHA 2002 Guideline Update for Exercise Testing (digoxin causes exercise-induced ST depression in roughly 25–40% of healthy subjects); Fletcher GF et al., AHA Exercise Standards for Testing and Training (Circulation 2013;128:873); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241)
checks.current_value: 'Digoxin effect' at therapeutic levels: sagging/scooped ('reverse tick') ST depression, clearest in leads with tall R waves; low, flat or inverted T; shortened QT; sometimes a more prominent U wave and a mildly longer PR. It can mimic strain or ischaemia and lowers the specificity of exercise ST depression, which can be a false positive. It shows drug exposure, not toxicity.
checks.note: Correct. Teach the characteristic scooped morphology and the short QT so students can tell it apart from ischaemic or strain-type ST depression. Teach separately that digoxin effect is not digoxin toxicity (see missing criteria).

checks.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for acute pulmonary embolism (Konstantinides et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:543): RV-strain signs (T inversion V1–V4, QR in V1, S1Q3T3, incomplete/complete RBBB) mainly in more severe PE; sinus tachycardia may be the only abnormality in milder cases; atrial arrhythmias such as AF can occur. Shopp JD et al., meta-analysis of ECG findings and outcome in PE (Am J Cardiol 2015). Context: the 2026 AHA/ACC multisociety acute PE guideline (Creager et al., Circulation 2026;153:e977) bases its A–E categories on clinical severity, biomarkers and RV imaging; I did not verify its ECG wording.
checks.current_value: The ECG is insensitive and nonspecific for PE: it neither rules PE in nor out, and its main uses are excluding other diagnoses and grading severity. Sinus tachycardia is the most frequent abnormality. Signs of RV strain/overload: T inversion in V1–V4 (± inferior leads), the most frequent finding in severe PE; S1Q3T3; new incomplete or complete RBBB; QR in V1; right axis shift; ST elevation in aVR/V1. Atrial arrhythmias such as AF can occur. The ECG can be normal, often in roughly 10–25% depending on the series. Changes are often transient. RV-strain findings are linked to worse outcomes.
checks.note: The listed findings and approximate frequencies fall within published ranges, though prevalence varies widely by series and severity. The list omits sinus tachycardia (the most common finding), QR in V1, AF and the prognostic value of RV-strain signs. Add these, present percentages as approximate ranges, and state clearly that S1Q3T3 is neither sensitive nor specific.

checks.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Recommendations Part V: ECG changes associated with cardiac chamber hypertrophy (Hancock EW et al., Circulation 2009;119:e251), which prefers the term 'right atrial abnormality' and reviews RVH criteria; 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines for pulmonary hypertension (Humbert et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618), table of ECG abnormalities suggesting PH
checks.current_value: Chronic lung disease / chronic cor pulmonale. Right atrial abnormality: P ≥0.25 mV in II, III, aVF with a vertical P axis (more than about +70°). Right axis deviation or an S1S2S3 pattern. Low QRS voltage in the limb leads (emphysema). Poor R-wave progression with persistent S waves to V5–V6 (clockwise rotation). RVH signs: R/S ≥1 in V1, qR in V1, R in V1 + S in V5/V6 >1.05 mV. RV strain: ST depression/T inversion in V1–V3 and inferior leads. Incomplete or complete RBBB. Atrial arrhythmias such as multifocal atrial tachycardia and AF. A normal ECG does not exclude pulmonary hypertension.
checks.note: The three-item combination is incomplete and gives RBBB more weight than it deserves. Right axis deviation, poor R progression with deep lateral S waves, and RVH/RV-strain signs are the core teaching. 'P pulmonale' has low sensitivity and specificity; current standards call it 'right atrial abnormality'.

checks.source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies (Arbelo et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503); 2024 AHA/ACC/AMSSM/HRS/PACES/SCMR Guideline for HCM (Ommen et al., Circulation 2024;149:e1239); ESC 2014 HCM guidelines (pathological Q-wave definition)
checks.current_value: The ECG is abnormal in most HCM patients (normal in only a small minority), so it is a sensitive screening tool. Findings: LVH voltage with repolarisation abnormalities (ST depression, T inversion, often lateral). Deep, narrow pathological Q waves (>3 mm deep and/or >40 ms) in inferior (II, III, aVF) and/or lateral (I, aVL, V4–V6) leads, from septal hypertrophy. Left atrial abnormality. Giant negative T waves (≥10 mm) in V2–V5 in apical HCM. Fascicular block is possible. LBBB is uncommon in untreated HCM and seen mainly after myectomy; RBBB is seen after alcohol septal ablation. AF. Red flags for phenocopies: short PR/pre-excitation (PRKAG2, Danon, Pompe) and low voltage despite thick walls (amyloid).
checks.note: The core description is correct. Add giant negative T waves in apical HCM and LA abnormality, and note that LBBB is uncommon unless the patient has had septal reduction therapy.

checks.source: Macfarlane PW et al., The Early Repolarization Pattern: A Consensus Paper (J Am Coll Cardiol 2015;66:470); Antzelevitch C et al., J-Wave Syndromes Expert Consensus Conference Report (Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295; Shanghai score); ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997); AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part VI (Wagner GS et al., Circulation 2009;119:e262); 2017 International criteria for ECG interpretation in athletes (Sharma S et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057)
checks.current_value: Early repolarisation pattern (ERP): a notch (J wave) or slur at the end of the QRS on the downslope of a prominent R wave. The notch/slur peak or onset (Jp) is ≥0.1 mV in ≥2 contiguous inferior and/or lateral leads (V1–V3 excluded), with QRS <120 ms. ST elevation is not required. Concave ST elevation in V1–V4 alone, common in healthy young men, is 'normal (male-pattern) ST elevation', not ERP; its limits are age- and sex-specific (in V2–V3: <2.5 mm men <40 y, <2 mm men ≥40 y, <1.5 mm women). ERP is a normal finding in athletes. Higher-risk ERP features: Jp ≥0.2 mV, inferior or global distribution, horizontal/descending ST after the J point. Early repolarisation syndrome = ERP in a patient resuscitated from unexplained VF/polymorphic VT.
checks.note: The 2004 definition (precordial ST elevation with tall T waves) is now classified as normal variant ST elevation, not ERP. The modern definition rests on the inferolateral J-point notch or slur. Students must also learn to separate benign ST elevation from STEMI, pericarditis and Brugada pattern.

missing_criteria.value: Rough sequence as K rises: tall, narrow-based, symmetric 'tented' T waves; then PR prolongation with flattening or loss of P waves; then QRS widening (bizarre morphology, possible pseudo-STEMI or Brugada-like pattern); then sine-wave pattern, bradycardia, high-grade AV block, VF or asystole. The ECG correlates poorly with serum K and can be near-normal even when K is dangerously high. Any ECG change in hyperkalaemia is an emergency.
missing_criteria.source: KDIGO Controversies Conference on potassium (Clase CM et al., Kidney Int 2020;97:42); UK Kidney Association Clinical Practice Guideline on Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (2023); AHA 2020 ACLS guidelines, special circumstances (electrolyte-related arrest)
missing_criteria.leads: T peaking clearest in V2–V4, II, III

missing_criteria.value: ST depression, flattening or inversion of the T wave, prominent U wave (often taller than the T in V2–V3), T–U fusion giving an apparent long QT (really QU). Raises the risk of TdP and digoxin toxicity; often coexists with hypomagnesaemia.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241, U-wave section); Drew BJ et al., AHA/ACCF TdP prevention statement (Circulation 2010;121:1047)

missing_criteria.value: Hypocalcaemia lengthens the QT by lengthening the ST segment; the T wave keeps a normal width. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT through a short or absent ST segment (T wave seems to start at the end of the QRS); J (Osborn)-like waves occasionally appear in severe cases.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241); Antzelevitch C et al., J-wave syndromes consensus (Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295) for J waves of non-ischaemic cause
missing_criteria.leads: All leads; measure QT in the lead with the longest QT

missing_criteria.value: Measure from the earliest QRS onset to the latest T end (tangent method), leaving out a separate U wave, in the lead with the longest QT (often II or V5). Bazett over-corrects at high heart rates and under-corrects at low ones; prefer Fridericia, Framingham or regression formulas. Prolonged: QTc ≥450 ms in men, ≥460 ms in women. Short: about ≤390 ms. High TdP risk: QTc >500 ms or a rise of >60 ms from baseline. Athlete referral thresholds: QTc ≥470 ms (men), ≥480 ms (women). With QRS ≥120 ms, use the JT interval or an adjusted QT.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part IV (Rautaharju et al., Circulation 2009;119:e241); Drew BJ et al., Circulation 2010;121:1047; 2017 International criteria for ECG interpretation in athletes (Sharma et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057)

missing_criteria.value: Diagnose with QTc ≥480 ms on repeated 12-lead ECGs, or an LQTS (Schwartz) risk score >3. Consider it at QTc ≥460 ms with unexplained syncope. Typical T-wave patterns by genotype: LQT1 broad-based T; LQT2 low-amplitude, notched or bifid T; LQT3 long isoelectric ST with a late, peaked T.
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 Guidelines for VA and prevention of SCD (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997); 2013 HRS/EHRA/APHRS Expert Consensus on inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes (Priori et al., Heart Rhythm 2013;10:1932)
missing_criteria.leads: Repeated 12-lead ECGs; lateral and precordial leads for T morphology

missing_criteria.value: Diagnose with QTc ≤360 ms plus one or more of: a pathogenic mutation, a family history of SQTS, or survival of VT/VF without structural heart disease. Consider it at QTc ≤320 ms. Tall, peaked, symmetric T waves with little or no ST segment. Exclude secondary causes first (hypercalcaemia, digoxin, hyperthermia).
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997)

missing_criteria.value: Type 1 (diagnostic) pattern: coved ST elevation ≥2 mm (0.2 mV) followed by a negative T wave in ≥1 right precordial lead (V1–V2) recorded in the 2nd, 3rd or 4th intercostal space, either spontaneous or induced by a sodium-channel blocker. Type 2 (saddleback) is not diagnostic. A drug-induced type 1 pattern alone is not enough for a diagnosis; it also needs arrhythmic syncope, documented VF/polymorphic VT or a family history. Fever, hyperkalaemia and sodium-channel-blocker toxicity can produce phenocopies.
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997); Antzelevitch C et al., J-wave syndromes consensus / Shanghai score (Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295); Bayés de Luna A et al., Current electrocardiographic criteria for diagnosis of Brugada pattern: a consensus report (J Electrocardiol 2012;45:433)
missing_criteria.leads: V1–V2, including high intercostal spaces (2nd–3rd ICS)

missing_criteria.value: J-point elevation in V2–V3 is normal up to <2.5 mm in men <40 y, <2 mm in men ≥40 y and <1.5 mm in women; in other leads up to <1 mm. Concave elevation within these limits in a healthy young person is a normal variant. Above them, in the right clinical setting, it meets STEMI voltage criteria. The 2004 'early repolarisation' description belongs here.
missing_criteria.source: AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 Part VI: acute ischaemia/infarction (Wagner GS et al., Circulation 2009;119:e262); Fourth Universal Definition of MI (Thygesen K et al., Eur Heart J 2019;40:237); ESC 2023 ACS guidelines (Byrne RA et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720)

missing_criteria.value: ERS = J-point elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous inferior and/or lateral leads in a patient resuscitated from otherwise unexplained VF/polymorphic VT. In an asymptomatic person, ERP is a benign finding that needs no further testing. Higher-risk features: Jp ≥2 mm, inferior or global distribution, horizontal or descending ST segment, dynamic J waves.
missing_criteria.source: ESC 2022 VA/SCD guidelines (Zeppenfeld et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997); Macfarlane PW et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2015;66:470; Antzelevitch C et al., Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295
missing_criteria.leads: II, III, aVF, I, aVL, V4–V6

missing_criteria.value: Normal training-related findings: isolated QRS voltage criteria for LVH/RVH, incomplete RBBB, ERP/ST elevation, sinus bradycardia ≥30 bpm, sinus arrhythmia, ectopic atrial or junctional rhythm, first-degree AV block, Mobitz I, T inversion V1–V3 under age 16 (juvenile pattern), and T inversion V1–V4 in Black athletes when preceded by J-point elevation and convex ST elevation. Abnormal: T inversion ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads beyond those (lateral or inferolateral), ST depression ≥0.5 mm, pathological Q (Q/R ≥0.25 or ≥40 ms), LBBB, QRS ≥140 ms, epsilon wave, pre-excitation, QTc ≥470 ms (men)/≥480 ms (women), Brugada type 1, HR <30 bpm, PR ≥400 ms, Mobitz II or third-degree AV block, ≥2 PVCs per tracing, atrial tachyarrhythmias. Borderline (two or more call for work-up): LAD, RAD, LA or RA enlargement, complete RBBB.
missing_criteria.source: International criteria for ECG interpretation in athletes (Sharma S, Drezner JA et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057; Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466)

missing_criteria.value: Low QRS voltage (all limb leads <0.5 mV), or voltage disproportionately low for the LV wall thickness seen on echo (voltage–mass discordance). Pseudo-infarct pattern: Q/QS in V1–V3 without infarction. AV or intraventricular conduction disease; AF. A normal-voltage ECG does not exclude amyloidosis.
missing_criteria.source: ESC Working Group position statement on diagnosis and treatment of cardiac amyloidosis (Garcia-Pavia P et al., Eur Heart J 2021;42:1554); ESC 2023 cardiomyopathy guidelines (Arbelo et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503); 2023 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on cardiac amyloidosis (Kittleson MM et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2023;81:1076)

missing_criteria.value: T inversion in V1–V3 or beyond in people over 14 years without complete RBBB (major criterion). Epsilon wave: a small terminal deflection after the QRS in V1–V3 (major in the 2010 Task Force criteria, downgraded to minor in the 2020 Padua criteria). Terminal activation duration ≥55 ms in V1–V3. Low limb-lead voltage. PVCs or VT with LBBB morphology (superior axis suggests RV origin). Padua 2020 adds left-ventricular criteria: inferolateral T inversion and low voltage.
missing_criteria.source: Marcus FI et al., 2010 Task Force Criteria (Circulation 2010;121:1533); Corrado D et al., 2020 Padua criteria (Int J Cardiol 2020;319:106); ESC 2023 cardiomyopathy guidelines (Arbelo et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3503)

missing_criteria.value: Pericarditis: new, widespread concave ST elevation without reciprocal depression (except in aVR and often V1), plus PR depression with PR elevation in aVR. Stages evolve over days to weeks (ST normalises before T inversion, unlike infarction). New widespread STE or PR depression is one of the clinical diagnostic criteria (with pain, rub and effusion). Large effusion or tamponade: low QRS voltage, electrical alternans, sinus tachycardia.
missing_criteria.source: 2015 ESC Guidelines for pericardial diseases (Adler Y et al., Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921); 2025 ESC Guidelines for the management of myocarditis and pericarditis (Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952)
missing_criteria.leads: Diffuse limb and precordial leads; aVR for reciprocal PR elevation/ST depression

missing_criteria.value: Sinus tachycardia; QRS ≥100 ms (seizure risk) and ≥160 ms (ventricular arrhythmia risk); terminal R in aVR ≥3 mm or R/S in aVR ≥0.7; rightward terminal 40-ms QRS axis; QT prolongation; Brugada-like pattern. QRS widening is treated with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate.
missing_criteria.source: AHA 2023 Focused Update on management of patients with cardiac arrest or life-threatening toxicity due to poisoning (Lavonas EJ et al., Circulation 2023;148:e149); Boehnert MT, Lovejoy FH, N Engl J Med 1985;313:474; Liebelt EL et al., Ann Emerg Med 1995;26:195
missing_criteria.leads: aVR, I, limb leads for QRS duration

missing_criteria.value: Toxicity combines increased automaticity with depressed conduction. Arrhythmias: frequent PVCs or ventricular bigeminy, atrial tachycardia with AV block, accelerated junctional rhythm, 'regularised' AF (AF with complete AV block and a junctional escape), bidirectional VT, high-grade AV block or severe sinus bradycardia. Worsened by hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypercalcaemia and renal failure. Treat life-threatening toxicity with digoxin-specific Fab. 'Digoxin effect' (scooped ST) does not indicate toxicity.
missing_criteria.source: AHA 2023 Focused Update on poisoning-related cardiac arrest/toxicity (Lavonas EJ et al., Circulation 2023;148:e149)

missing_criteria.value: Osborn (J) waves: a positive hump at the J point, larger at lower temperatures. Sinus bradycardia; prolonged PR, QRS and QT; AF with slow ventricular response; shivering artefact. Risk of VF and asystole rises sharply below about 28–30 °C. The J waves resolve with rewarming.
missing_criteria.source: Antzelevitch C et al., J-wave syndromes expert consensus (Heart Rhythm 2016;13:e295); Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for Out-of-Hospital Evaluation and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia: 2019 Update (Dow J et al., Wilderness Environ Med 2019;30:S47)

missing_criteria.value: Acute phase: ST elevation, often anterior and extending beyond one coronary territory, with less reciprocal depression; sometimes ST depression only. Later: deep, widespread T inversion with QTc prolongation over days, then gradual resolution. The ECG cannot reliably tell takotsubo from STEMI, so coronary angiography is needed.
missing_criteria.source: International Expert Consensus Document on Takotsubo Syndrome, Part I (Ghadri JR et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:2032); ESC 2023 ACS guidelines (Byrne RA et al., Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720), MINOCA differential

missing_criteria.parameter: Most frequent finding and RV-strain markers
missing_criteria.value: Sinus tachycardia is the most common abnormality and may be the only one in milder PE. In more severe PE, RV-strain signs appear: T inversion in V1–V4 (± III, aVF), QR in V1, S1Q3T3, incomplete or complete RBBB, ST elevation in aVR/V1. AF or atrial flutter can occur. These signs are associated with RV dysfunction and worse outcome. The ECG neither confirms nor excludes PE; diagnosis relies on clinical probability, D-dimer and CTPA.
missing_criteria.source: 2019 ESC Guidelines for acute pulmonary embolism (Konstantinides SV et al., Eur Heart J 2020;41:543); 2026 AHA/ACC multisociety Guideline for evaluation and management of acute PE in adults (Creager MA et al., Circulation 2026;153:e977), risk stratification context only; its ECG wording not verified
missing_criteria.leads: V1–V4, III, aVF, aVR, I (S wave)

checks.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. New normal limits for the paediatric electrocardiogram. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Table 2, digital 1200 Hz ECGs, n=1912); Fleming S et al. Lancet 2011;377:1011-1018 (heart-rate centiles 0-18 y); Saarel EV et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2018;11:e005808
checks.current_value: Heart rate: median about 150-160 bpm in the first 3 months (Rijnbeek 1-3 mo about 152-154), falling to a median of about 73-80 bpm at 12-16 y (normal range roughly 50-110). PR is age-dependent and must be read against age-specific limits: median about 100 ms in the first months (98th centile about 120-135 ms), about 115-120 ms at 1-5 y (98th about 150 ms), about 135-140 ms at 12-16 y (98th about 175-180 ms). First-degree AV block in a child = PR above the age-specific 98th centile, not >200 ms and not a single paediatric value.
checks.note: The heart-rate trend is right, but 'about 85 at 12-15 y' is a little high versus modern medians (about 73-80). The single PR figure 0.12 s (0.11-0.14) for all children is the problem: a 0.14 s PR is above the upper limit in a neonate but normal in an adolescent. Values read from the rotated tables in Rijnbeek 2001 are approximate; anchor to the paper.

checks.source: Park MK, Salamat M. Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners, 7th ed. Elsevier 2021 (QRS axis by age table, same bands); Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Table 2); Schwartz PJ et al. ESC Task Force: Guidelines for the interpretation of the neonatal electrocardiogram. Eur Heart J 2002;23:1329-1344
checks.note: The age bands and ranges match what Park's textbook still teaches. In Rijnbeek's digital data, neonatal medians are about +100 to +110° and after 3-6 months about +65 to +70°. The 2nd centiles after 3-6 months dip slightly below 0° (to about -20° in some groups), so 'lower limit about 0°' is a rough guide only. The teaching point still holds: a superior/left axis (< -30°, 'northwest' or -30 to -150°) in an infant points to AVSD (primum or complete), tricuspid atresia, Noonan syndrome, or some inlet VSDs. LVH alone rarely causes LAD in children.

checks.source: Sharma S, Drezner JA et al. International recommendations for electrocardiographic interpretation in athletes. J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057-1075 / Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466-1480 (juvenile pattern); Schwartz PJ et al. ESC neonatal ECG guidelines, Eur Heart J 2002;23:1329-1344; Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021
checks.current_value: T in V1 can be upright at birth and normally inverts within the first week. From then until adolescence, an upright T in V1 (when the R wave is dominant) is a sign of RV hypertrophy. Anterior T inversion in V1-V3 ('juvenile pattern') is normal up to age 16. From 16 y, T inversion in 2 or more contiguous anterior leads beyond V2 needs evaluation (exception: black athletes with J-point/convex ST elevation in V1-V4). R > S in V1, RV dominance and a rightward axis are normal in the newborn and regress over the first months to years.
checks.note: The newborn RV-dominance part is current. The upper age bound '6-12 y' is too early: it would make a learner call normal V1-V3 T inversion at 13-15 y abnormal. Modern teaching uses the <16 y juvenile-pattern rule.

checks.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Tables 5-6, R and S amplitudes by age and sex); Saarel EV et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2018;11:e005808; Bratincsák A et al. Electrocardiogram standards for children and young adults using Z-scores. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2020;13:e008253
checks.current_value: Use digital-era, sex-specific age norms. Rijnbeek (approximate, median (98th centile) in mm): R V1 about 11 (20-22) at 0-1 mo, about 12-13 (21-22) at 1-6 mo, about 10-11 (19-21) at 6 mo-3 y, about 6 (13-15) at 5-8 y, about 4-5 (11-12) at 12-16 y. S V1 about 7 (14-15) in the neonate, rising to about 12-13 (21-25) at 5-16 y. R V2 about 18 (26) in the neonate, falling to about 9-10 (19) at 12-16 y.
checks.note: These figures appear to be the classic analog-era Park/Guntheroth table (same age bands), which Park's textbook still prints, so it is acceptable as a rough guide. Digital high-bandwidth norms differ, though: for example, the neonatal R V1 upper limit is about 20-22 mm rather than 25. Precordial voltage criteria for hypertrophy in children have low sensitivity against echo and must not be graded as definitive. Exact digits are hard to read from a low-resolution scan; verify against the source.

checks.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Tables 5-6); Saarel EV et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2018;11:e005808; Bratincsák A et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2020;13:e008253; Rivenes SM et al. Am Heart J 2003;145:716-723 (poor ECG accuracy for paediatric LVH)
checks.current_value: Digital-era norms (Rijnbeek, approximate, median (98th) mm): R V6 about 10 (16-18) at 0-1 mo, about 15-17 (22-28) at 1-6 mo, about 17-19 (27-30) at 6 mo-5 y, about 20-22 (30-32) at 5-12 y, about 17-20 (25-30) at 12-16 y (girls lower). S V6 98th centile about 8-12 mm in infancy and about 8-9 mm in older children.
checks.note: The book's upper limits (R V6 20-24 mm; S V6 4-7 mm) are well below the modern 98th centiles. A grader using them would over-call LVH (R V6) and RVH (S V6) in normal children. Teach voltage as one clue alongside axis, T-wave and Q-wave changes, and confirm hypertrophy by echo.

checks.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Table 5: limb-lead R amplitudes); Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021 (R/S voltage table)
checks.current_value: Broadly compatible with modern data for leads I, III, aVF and aVR. Rijnbeek R in II is about 6 mm (98th 13) in the neonate and about 11-14 mm (98th 20-25) from 3 months to 16 y.
checks.note: An adult mean R in lead II of 19 mm is implausible; adult means are about 9-13 mm, so this is likely a scan or print error (perhaps 9 (25)). It must be checked before use. The adult aVF entry 5 (23), with a mean far below the upper limit, also looks odd. Limb-lead voltage is rarely used diagnostically in children apart from R in aVR (RVH) and the frontal axis.

checks.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021 (P axis and atrial situs); Momma K, Takao A, Shibata T. Characteristics and natural history of abnormal atrial rhythms in left isomerism. Am J Cardiol 1990;65:231-236; Wren C, Macartney FJ, Deanfield JE. Cardiac rhythm in atrial isomerism. Am J Cardiol 1987;59:1156-1158; Kligfield P et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for standardization and interpretation of the ECG Part I. Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324
checks.current_value: Situs solitus: P axis 0 to +90° (P up in I and II/aVF, down in aVR). Situs inversus: P axis +90 to +180° (P negative in lead I, upright in aVR, negative in aVL); with mirror-image dextrocardia, P, QRS and T are all inverted in lead I and R falls across V1-V6, which separates it from LA/RA lead reversal (normal precordial progression). Isomerism: right isomerism (bilateral sinus nodes) can have a normal, about +90° or alternating P axis. Left isomerism (absent or hypoplastic sinus node) usually shows an ectopic or low atrial rhythm with a superior or shifting P axis, slow atrial rates and a risk of congenital AV block. P polarity alone cannot reliably diagnose isomerism.
checks.note: The solitus and inversus statements are current, though inversus should lead with P inversion in lead I. A single isomerism rule ('P negative in aVR and aVL', implying an axis near +90°) fits some right isomerism but not left isomerism, so it should not be taught as a general rule.

checks.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021; Heller J et al. 'Crochetage' (notch) on R wave in inferior limb leads: a new independent electrocardiographic sign of atrial septal defect. J Am Coll Cardiol 1996;27:877-882; Surawicz B et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part III. Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines for adult congenital heart disease. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645
checks.note: Core pattern is current: right axis (about +90 to +180°), RV volume overload with rsR' in V1 (incomplete RBBB pattern) in most patients, and PR prolongation in a minority (more frequent with age, large shunts and familial NKX2-5 ASD). Additions: (1) the crochetage sign, a notch near the R-wave apex in inferior leads (about 73% sensitivity; specificity 92% or higher when present in all three inferior leads or with iRBBB); (2) per AHA Part III, rsr' with normal QRS duration in V1-V2 is a normal variant in children, so iRBBB requires age-specific QRS duration; (3) adults may develop atrial flutter or fibrillation; (4) a normal ECG does not exclude ASD; (5) with pulmonary hypertension, expect RVH with qR in V1 and RV strain.

checks.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021; MSD Manual Professional, Atrioventricular septal defect (ECG: superior axis, frequent first-degree AV block, RVH/LVH, occasional RBBB); Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC ACHD guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645
checks.current_value: Teach the superior QRS axis (about -30 to -150°, counterclockwise frontal loop) as the hallmark of both partial (primum) and complete AVSD. It is present in the large majority and reflects the displaced AV node/His bundle and early posterior-inferior LV activation. Next teach first-degree AV block (frequent, not universal), RV volume overload with rsR'/RBBB pattern in V1, and in complete AVSD LVH or biventricular hypertrophy. Late complete AV block can occur.
checks.note: The triad (first-degree AV block + LAD + RBBB) remains standard teaching. However, I could not verify the 93% first-degree AV block figure for the complete form from a current source; it may belong to the superior axis rather than to PR prolongation. Do not teach the percentage until it is verified.

checks.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC ACHD guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645; Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC Guideline for adults with congenital heart disease. Circulation 2019;139:e698-e800
checks.note: Current. Small VSD or PDA: normal ECG. Moderate: LV volume overload (LVH, often with LA enlargement). Large: biventricular hypertrophy, often with Katz-Wachtel large equiphasic mid-precordial QRS complexes, plus LAE. With pulmonary vascular disease or Eisenmenger physiology: RVH only, with loss of LV forces. A frontal axis of about +45 to +90° in PDA is consistent with a normal-for-age axis. A superior axis with a VSD should raise the question of an inlet/AV-canal-type defect, but is not specific for it.

checks.source: Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC Guidelines for adult congenital heart disease. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645; Baumgartner H et al. EAE/ASE Echocardiographic assessment of valve stenosis. J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2009;22:1-23; Feltes TF et al. Indications for cardiac catheterization and intervention in pediatric cardiac disease: AHA scientific statement. Circulation 2011;123:2607-2652; Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC ACHD guideline. Circulation 2019;139:e698-e800
checks.current_value: The ECG cannot quantify the PS gradient. It shows qualitative RV pressure overload: right axis for age, tall R or qR in V1, upright T in V1 in a child, RA enlargement, and an RV strain pattern in severe cases; the degree of RVH broadly parallels RV pressure. Severity is graded by Doppler echo: mild = peak velocity <3 m/s (peak gradient <36 mmHg); moderate = 3-4 m/s (36-64 mmHg); severe = >4 m/s (>64 mmHg). A normal ECG does not exclude significant PS.
checks.note: The threshold-to-gradient rules (axis >+120° means 80 mmHg or more; R V1 >20 mm means more than 50 mmHg, and so on) come from the catheter era. R V1 height correlates only loosely with the transvalvular gradient, and quoted multiplier rules ('R V1 x 4 or x 5 ≈ RV systolic pressure') vary between sources and are not guideline criteria.

checks.source: Otto CM et al. 2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the management of valvular heart disease. Circulation 2021;143:e72-e227; Vahanian A et al. 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for valvular heart disease. Eur Heart J 2022;43:561-632; Feltes TF et al. AHA scientific statement on pediatric catheterization/intervention. Circulation 2011;123:2607-2652; Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021
checks.current_value: The ECG is often normal in mild or moderate congenital AS. LVH, with or without ST depression and T inversion in V5-V6 ('strain'), suggests severe obstruction. A normal ECG does not exclude severe AS, and ECG findings correlate poorly with the gradient. Severity is graded by echo (severe: peak velocity of 4 m/s or more, mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more). In children, ischaemic ST-T changes at rest or on exercise lower the threshold for balloon valvotomy: per the AHA 2011 statement, a catheter peak gradient of 50 mmHg or more, or 40 mmHg or more with symptoms or ischaemic ECG changes.
checks.note: The qualitative ECG description (left precordial R increase, delayed intrinsicoid deflection, may be normal) is still valid. Only the 'strain if >80 mmHg' threshold is superseded. Gradient thresholds in the current value are as I recall them from the cited guidelines; confirm the exact numbers before quoting them in the app.

checks.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021; Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC ACHD guideline, Circulation 2019;139:e698-e800; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC ACHD guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645; Brugada J et al. 2019 ESC Guidelines for SVT, Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720
checks.note: All four clues are still taught. Tricuspid atresia: superior/left axis (mainly with normally related great arteries), LVH or LV dominance with poor RV forces, and RA or biatrial enlargement. D-TGA: often normal for age at birth; RVH appears, and an upright T in V1 after the first days of life may be the only sign. Ebstein: tall 'Himalayan' P waves, RBBB pattern with low-voltage or fragmented right precordial QRS, first-degree AV block, and right-sided accessory pathways/WPW in a substantial minority (often multiple pathways); RVH is typically absent. TAPVC: RAE, RVH (often rsR' in V1) and right axis.

checks.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC ACHD guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645; Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC ACHD guideline, Circulation 2019;139:e698-e800
checks.current_value: Coarctation is age-dependent. Symptomatic neonates and young infants show RVH or an RBBB pattern, reflecting the RV's fetal systemic workload. Older children and adults show either a normal ECG or LVH (with or without strain), in proportion to the severity and duration of upper-body hypertension. Overall the ECG is nonspecific and diagnosis rests on blood pressure gradients and imaging.
checks.note: Not wrong, but incomplete. The criterion omits LVH, which is the main ECG finding beyond infancy. An axis of about +70° and incomplete RBBB in one third are not useful teaching discriminators.

missing_criteria.value: Complete RBBB/LBBB: QRS >100 ms at 4-16 y and >90 ms under 4 y (adults 120 ms or more). Incomplete RBBB: 90-100 ms at 4-16 y and about 86-90 ms in younger children (secondary summaries disagree on whether the younger band is <4 y or <8 y; check the primary text). In children, an rsr' in V1-V2 with normal QRS duration is a normal variant.
missing_criteria.source: Surawicz B et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG, Part III: intraventricular conduction disturbances. Circulation 2009;119:e235-e240 (J Am Coll Cardiol 2009;53:976-981)

missing_criteria.value: Median QRS is about 65-70 ms in infants, rising to about 85-90 ms at 12-16 y. The 98th centile is about 80-85 ms in infancy and about 105-110 ms in adolescent boys (girls slightly lower).
missing_criteria.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Table 2); Saarel EV et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2018;11:e005808

missing_criteria.value: SVT is likely when HR is 220 bpm or more in infants (180 or more in children), with abrupt onset, a fixed R-R interval, absent or retrograde P waves and no beat-to-beat variability. Sinus tachycardia is usually below these rates, with visible upright P waves in II/aVF and rate variability.
missing_criteria.source: Topjian AA et al. 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC, Part 4: Pediatric Basic and Advanced Life Support. Circulation 2020;142(suppl 2):S469-S523; Brugada J et al. 2019 ESC SVT guidelines. Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720

missing_criteria.entity: Long QT in neonates and children
missing_criteria.value: The paediatric QTc (Bazett) 98th centile is about 450-460 ms. A neonatal QTc above about 470 ms strongly suggests congenital LQTS (above 440 ms warrants a repeat ECG). LQTS is diagnosed with QTc of 480 ms or more on repeated ECGs, or an LQTS risk score above 3; QTc of 460 ms or more with arrhythmic syncope also qualifies. Bazett over-corrects at high infant heart rates, so measure in lead II or V5.
missing_criteria.source: Schwartz PJ et al. ESC Task Force guidelines for the interpretation of the neonatal ECG. Eur Heart J 2002;23:1329-1344; Schwartz PJ et al. Prevalence of the congenital long-QT syndrome. Circulation 2009;120:1761-1767; Zeppenfeld K et al. 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias and prevention of SCD. Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126

missing_criteria.value: RVH: R in V1 or S in V6 above the age-specific 98th centile; upright T in V1 with R dominance after the first week and before adolescence; qR in V1; right axis for age; tall R in aVR. LVH: R in V6 or S in V1 above age-specific limits, LV strain, or deep Q in V5-V6 with tall T (volume overload). Use digital-era age and sex norms. Sensitivity for echo-defined LVH is low, so the ECG should not be used to exclude hypertrophy.
missing_criteria.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711; Rivenes SM et al. Usefulness of the pediatric electrocardiogram in detecting left ventricular hypertrophy. Am Heart J 2003;145:716-723; Bratincsák A et al. Circ Arrhythm Electrophysiol 2020;13:e008253; Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021

missing_criteria.value: Deep inferior Q waves are normal in young children: the 98th centile in lead III is about 7-8 mm between 6 months and 3 y, and in V6 about 4-6 mm. Do not call these infarction. Pathological Q waves in infants (I/aVL, V5-V6) suggest ALCAPA, cardiomyopathy or myocarditis, and in V1 suggest severe RVH or ccTGA.
missing_criteria.source: Rijnbeek PR et al. Eur Heart J 2001;22:702-711 (Q-wave amplitude table); Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021

missing_criteria.value: Anterior T inversion in V1-V3 is normal under 16 years of age. From 16 y, T inversion in 2 or more contiguous leads beyond V2 is abnormal (except black athletes with J-point elevation and convex ST elevation preceding T inversion in V1-V4, and biphasic T only in V3).
missing_criteria.source: Sharma S et al. International recommendations for electrocardiographic interpretation in athletes. J Am Coll Cardiol 2017;69:1057-1075 / Eur Heart J 2018;39:1466-1480

missing_criteria.value: A notch near the apex of the R wave in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). It is seen in about 73% of secundum ASDs, and specificity is 92% or higher when present in all three inferior leads or combined with incomplete RBBB. It is independent of RBBB and more frequent with larger shunts.
missing_criteria.source: Heller J et al. 'Crochetage' (notch) on R wave in inferior limb leads: a new independent electrocardiographic sign of atrial septal defect. J Am Coll Cardiol 1996;27:877-882

missing_criteria.value: An ectopic or low atrial rhythm with a leftward or superior P axis (less than about +30°; P negative or flat in III/aVF) is frequent, unlike secundum ASD. This is combined with RV volume overload (rsR' in V1).
missing_criteria.source: Park's Pediatric Cardiology for Practitioners 7th ed. 2021; Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC ACHD guideline. Circulation 2019;139:e698-e800

missing_criteria.value: Unrepaired: right axis (about +120 to +150°), RVH with a tall R in V1 and an abrupt change to rS in V2, and sometimes RAE. Repaired: an RBBB pattern is expected. A QRS duration of 180 ms or more (or progressive widening) is a marker of risk for sustained VT and sudden death.
missing_criteria.source: Gatzoulis MA et al. Risk factors for arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death late after repair of tetralogy of Fallot: a multicentre study. Lancet 2000;356:975-981; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC ACHD guidelines. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645
missing_criteria.leads: V1, V2, all leads for QRS duration

missing_criteria.value: Septal activation is reversed: Q waves appear in V1 (or V4R) and often III/aVF, with no septal q in V5-V6. Progressive AV block develops (about 2% per year; complete heart block is common by adulthood). WPW may occur with Ebstein-like left AV valve.
missing_criteria.source: Huhta JC et al. Complete atrioventricular block in patients with atrioventricular discordance. Circulation 1983;67:1374-1377; Stout KK et al. 2018 AHA/ACC ACHD guideline. Circulation 2019;139:e698-e800

missing_criteria.value: AV dissociation with a narrow-QRS junctional escape, often linked to maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (neonatal lupus). Pacing is indicated with symptoms, a wide-QRS escape rhythm, complex ventricular ectopy, ventricular dysfunction, or a low ventricular rate (infants below about 50-55 bpm, or below about 70 bpm with structural heart disease). QT prolongation is also a concern.
