missing_criteria.source: Shah MJ et al. 2021 PACES expert consensus statement on the indications and management of cardiovascular implantable electronic devices in pediatric patients. Heart Rhythm 2021;18:1888-1924; Epstein AE et al. 2012 ACCF/AHA/HRS focused update on device-based therapy. Circulation 2013;127:e283-e352

missing_criteria.value: Recognise a short PR for age, a delta wave and wide QRS. A low-risk pathway is suggested by intermittent pre-excitation or abrupt loss of pre-excitation with exercise. Otherwise, asymptomatic children of about 8 y and older are risk-stratified with electrophysiology studies (SPERRI of 250 ms or less = high risk). WPW is common with Ebstein anomaly and ccTGA.
missing_criteria.source: Cohen MI et al. PACES/HRS Expert consensus statement on the management of the asymptomatic young patient with a WPW ECG pattern. Heart Rhythm 2012;9:1006-1024; Brugada J et al. 2019 ESC SVT guidelines. Eur Heart J 2020;41:655-720

missing_criteria.entity: ALCAPA (anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery)
missing_criteria.value: In an infant with LV dysfunction: deep and wide Q waves (about 3 mm or more deep and 30 ms or more wide) in I and aVL, with or without V5-V6, plus anterolateral ST-T changes. This separates ALCAPA from myocarditis or dilated cardiomyopathy.
missing_criteria.source: Johnsrude CL et al. Differentiating anomalous left main coronary artery originating from the pulmonary artery in infants from myocarditis and dilated cardiomyopathy by electrocardiogram. Am J Cardiol 1995;75:71-74

missing_criteria.value: Mirror-image dextrocardia: P, QRS and T inverted in lead I, an upright P in aVR, and R amplitude decreasing from V1 to V6; right-sided chest leads restore normal progression. LA/RA reversal: lead I is inverted but precordial progression is normal.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield P et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations Part I. Circulation 2007;115:1306-1324; Batchvarov VN et al. Incorrect electrode cable connection during electrocardiographic recording. Europace 2007;9:1081-1090

missing_criteria.value: Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (often 2:1 conduction with hidden flutter waves at deceptively 'normal' ventricular rates) after Fontan, Mustard/Senning or ASD/TOF repair. Junctional ectopic tachycardia early after surgery: narrow QRS with VA dissociation and ventricular rate above atrial rate. Sinus node dysfunction after atrial-level surgery.
missing_criteria.source: Khairy P et al. PACES/HRS Expert consensus statement on the recognition and management of arrhythmias in adult congenital heart disease. Heart Rhythm 2014;11:e102-e165; Baumgartner H et al. 2020 ESC ACHD guidelines. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645

checks.source: Mason JW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part II: Electrocardiography Diagnostic Statement List. Circulation 2007;115:1325-32 (lists 'ventricular-paced rhythm' and separately 'ventricular pacing of non-right-ventricular-apical origin'); Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and CRT, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-520; Barold SS, Herweg B. Usefulness of the 12-lead ECG in the follow-up of patients with cardiac resynchronization devices, Parts I-II, Cardiol J 2011
checks.current_value: RV apical pacing: stimulus artifact followed by a wide QRS (typically >=140-180 ms) with LBBB-like morphology (QS/rS in V1; predominantly negative QRS in most or all precordial leads, often including V5-V6), left superior axis (negative QRS in II, III, aVF), and secondary ST-T changes discordant to the QRS.
checks.note: Still correct for the apex, but the course should add: (1) RV septal / outflow-tract pacing (now common) gives an LBBB-like QRS with normal or inferior axis (positive II, III, aVF); (2) a dominant R in V1 during intended RV pacing warrants checking lead position (LV via PFO/ASD, coronary sinus, arterial) although it can occur benignly with high V1-V2 placement; (3) biventricular (CRT) and conduction-system (His/LBBA) pacing produce different, narrower morphologies (see missing criteria). Teach that the pacing spike itself may be tiny with bipolar leads.

checks.source: Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and CRT (device follow-up section), Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-520; Kusumoto FM et al. 2017 HRS expert consensus statement on cardiovascular implantable electronic device lead management and extraction, Heart Rhythm 2017;14:e503-51; Ellenbogen KA et al. Clinical Cardiac Pacing, Defibrillation and Resynchronization Therapy, 5th ed. 2017
checks.current_value: Safety margin: output about 2x the voltage threshold (or ~3x pulse-width threshold); automatic capture-management algorithms allow smaller margins. Typical normal pacing impedance roughly 200/300-1000/1500 ohm (lead-dependent; high-impedance leads higher); an abrupt change >30% from baseline is significant. Abnormally high impedance = conductor fracture or loose set-screw/connector (intermittent/no output, loss of capture, noise oversensing). Abnormally low impedance = insulation breach (current leak with loss of capture, oversensing, accelerated battery drain).
checks.note: Content is accurate but is interrogation data, not something read on the surface ECG. For an ECG course, frame it via the ECG consequences: missing spikes/pauses (no output or oversensing of make-break noise) and spikes without capture. Insulation failure also causes loss of capture and oversensing, not only battery drain. Keep as background, not a grading item.

checks.source: Crossley GH et al. The Heart Rhythm Society/American Society of Anesthesiologists 2011 Expert Consensus Statement on the perioperative management of patients with ICDs, pacemakers and arrhythmia monitors, Heart Rhythm 2011;8:1114-54; ASA Practice Advisory for the perioperative management of patients with CIEDs, Anesthesiology 2020;132:225-52; manufacturer technical manuals (e.g., Abbott magnet-rate/ERI reference sheet)
checks.current_value: Pacemaker + magnet: usually asynchronous pacing (AOO/VOO/DOO) at a manufacturer-specific magnet rate. Medtronic about 85 ppm, with the first 3 pulses at 100 ppm (threshold margin test with reduced output on the 3rd); Boston Scientific and Abbott about 100 ppm; Biotronik a brief asynchronous run (about 10 cycles) then back to programmed behaviour. The magnet rate drops at elective replacement indicator (ERI). The response is programmable and may be off or delayed, and some leadless devices have no magnet response. ICD + magnet: suspends tachyarrhythmia detection/therapy but does NOT make bradycardia pacing asynchronous.
checks.note: 'First 3 pulses at 100 bpm' is one manufacturer's (Medtronic) behaviour presented as universal. Teach the principle (asynchronous pacing, fixed rate, spikes ignoring intrinsic beats, rate falls at ERI), the ICD exception, and 'check the device/manufacturer'.

checks.source: Bernstein AD et al. The revised NASPE/BPEG generic code for antibradycardia, adaptive-rate and multisite pacing, PACE 2002;25:260-4; Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and CRT, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-520; Mason JW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part II statement list, Circulation 2007;115:1325-32 (atrial-paced, atrial-sensed ventricular-paced, AV dual-paced statements)
checks.current_value: DDD has 4 operating states: AP-VP (AV sequential), AP-VS (atrial paced, intrinsic conduction), AS-VP (P-tracking: sensed P then paced QRS after the programmed AV delay), AS-VS (fully inhibited). PVARP is automatically extended after a PVC to avoid tracking a retrograde P (pacemaker-mediated tachycardia prevention). In atrial tachyarrhythmias the device mode-switches to a non-tracking mode (e.g., DDIR/VDIR).
checks.note: Correct. A modern course should add upper-rate behaviour (pacemaker Wenckebach, 2:1 block), PMT recognition, ventricular safety pacing, and algorithms that minimise RV pacing (AV hysteresis/search, MVP-type AAI<->DDD switching that allows single non-conducted P waves) so that normal behaviour is not called malfunction.

checks.source: Kusumoto FM et al. 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay, Circulation 2019;140:e382-e482 (doi 10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628); Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and CRT, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-520 (and ESC 2021 Essential Messages)
checks.current_value: After excluding reversible/physiological causes (drugs, hyperkalaemia, acute ischaemia, Lyme, hypothyroidism, sleep apnoea, high vagal tone): acquired third-degree, high-degree (advanced) or Mobitz II second-degree AV block -> permanent pacing Class I REGARDLESS of symptoms (ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 Class 1; ESC 2021 Class I, also infra-His 2:1 block). Permanent AF with AV block/slow ventricular response -> ventricular pacing Class I. Mobitz I or 2:1 at AV-nodal level and first-degree AV block: pace only when symptoms are clearly attributable (IIa; e.g., ESC IIa for marked first-degree block, typically PR >300 ms, with pacemaker-syndrome-like symptoms). Asymptomatic first-degree or nodal Mobitz I: Class III (no benefit/harm). Alternating bundle branch block: Class I.
checks.note: The book reflects ACC/AHA/NASPE 1998-2002 classes, in which asymptomatic complete block and Mobitz II were IIa and 'asystole >=3 s / escape <40 bpm' were gating criteria. Both current guidelines upgraded Mobitz II, high-grade and complete AV block to Class I irrespective of symptoms. The 3-s / 6-s pause thresholds now appear mainly in the syncope/reflex context (ESC 2021: dual-chamber pacing for recurrent syncope >40 y with symptomatic pauses >3 s or asymptomatic >6 s).

missing_criteria.value: Position I = chamber paced, II = chamber sensed (A/V/D/O), III = response to sensing (I inhibit, T trigger, D dual, O none), IV = rate modulation (R), V = multisite pacing. Learners must map VVI, AAI, DDD, VDD, DDDR, VOO/DOO (magnet) to expected ECG behaviour.
missing_criteria.source: Bernstein AD et al. Revised NASPE/BPEG generic code, PACE 2002;25:260-4

missing_criteria.parameter: Detection and appearance on the ECG
missing_criteria.value: Bipolar pacing spikes are often tiny or invisible on the surface ECG; unipolar spikes are large. Digital electrocardiographs need high-rate pacemaker-pulse detection and may display marker spikes, or miss or falsely insert them, so a 'spike' on a filtered tracing may be an annotation. Always look at several leads for a spike before an atrial or ventricular complex.
missing_criteria.source: Kligfield P et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Recommendations for the Standardization and Interpretation of the ECG, Part I, Circulation 2007;115:1306-24 (pacemaker pulse detection); IEC 60601-2-25

missing_criteria.value: A pacing stimulus delivered outside the tissue's refractory period that is not followed by a P wave (atrial) or QRS (ventricular). Causes: threshold rise, lead dislodgement or fracture, hyperkalaemia, antiarrhythmic drugs, MI or fibrosis, battery depletion. Do not call a spike falling in the refractory period (e.g., just after an intrinsic QRS during undersensing) a capture failure.
missing_criteria.source: Mason JW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part II statement list, Circulation 2007;115:1325-32 ('failure to capture, atrial/ventricular'); Ellenbogen KA et al. Clinical Cardiac Pacing, Defibrillation and Resynchronization Therapy, 5th ed. 2017

missing_criteria.value: Pacing spikes appear inappropriately after intrinsic P waves or QRS complexes, i.e., the device behaves as if it did not see them; the intervals do not reset. Differentiate from magnet/asynchronous mode, functional undersensing in blanking/refractory periods (e.g., PVC in PVARP), and fusion/pseudofusion.
missing_criteria.source: Mason JW et al. AHA/ACCF/HRS Part II statement list, Circulation 2007;115:1325-32 ('failure to inhibit'); Ellenbogen KA et al. 5th ed. 2017

missing_criteria.value: Pauses longer than the lower-rate interval without spikes and without intrinsic activity, because the device sensed non-cardiac or far-field signals (myopotentials, EMI, T-wave, far-field R, crosstalk, lead-fracture noise). Rule out normal features before calling oversensing: rate hysteresis, sleep/rest rate, and RV-pacing-avoidance algorithms.
missing_criteria.source: Mason JW et al. Part II statement list, Circulation 2007 ('failure to pace'); Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC pacing guidelines; Ellenbogen KA et al. 5th ed. 2017

missing_criteria.value: Fusion beat: a QRS shaped by both the paced and the intrinsic wavefronts, intermediate in morphology. Pseudofusion beat: the spike falls on an intrinsic QRS that it does not change. Both are normal timing coincidences when the intrinsic rate is close to the pacing rate. They are not malfunctions.
missing_criteria.source: Ellenbogen KA et al. Clinical Cardiac Pacing, Defibrillation and Resynchronization Therapy, 5th ed. 2017; Barold SS, Stroobandt RX, Sinnaeve AF. Cardiac Pacemakers and Resynchronization Step-by-Step
missing_criteria.leads: Any; best seen in V1, II

missing_criteria.value: Atrial rates above the upper tracking rate cause pacemaker Wenckebach (progressive lengthening of the AS-VP interval with a dropped beat) or fixed 2:1 block when the P-P interval is shorter than the total atrial refractory period. PMT (endless-loop tachycardia) is a regular ventricular-paced tachycardia at or near the upper tracking rate, sustained by retrograde P waves (often triggered by a PVC or loss of atrial capture). A magnet terminates it.
missing_criteria.source: Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC pacing guidelines; Ellenbogen KA et al. 5th ed. 2017
missing_criteria.leads: Rhythm strip; look for retrograde P in II, III, aVF

missing_criteria.value: Effective BiV pacing typically gives a narrower paced QRS than baseline, a dominant R in V1 (RBBB-like), and a negative or QS QRS in lead I (right axis). Reversion to an LBBB-like pattern (negative V1, positive I, wider QRS) suggests loss of LV capture. Loss of RV capture gives a wide RBBB-like QRS with a QS in I. CRT candidacy: LBBB with QRS >=150 ms is Class I (130-149 ms IIa).
missing_criteria.source: Barold SS, Herweg B. Usefulness of the 12-lead ECG in the follow-up of patients with cardiac resynchronization devices, Parts I-II, Cardiol J 2011;18:476-86 and 610-24; Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and CRT

missing_criteria.entity: Conduction system pacing (His bundle / left bundle branch area)
missing_criteria.value: His pacing: selective capture = isoelectric interval after the spike with a native-like QRS; non-selective capture = pseudo-delta wave fused to the spike with a narrow QRS. LBBA pacing: paced QRS with RBBB-like V1 (qR/rSR'). LBB capture is supported by a stimulus-to-V6 R-wave peak time <75 ms (narrow baseline QRS or isolated RBBB) or <80 ms (LBBB/IVCD), a V6-V1 interpeak interval >44 ms, or a sudden V6 RWPT change during threshold testing.
missing_criteria.source: Burri H et al. EHRA clinical consensus statement on conduction system pacing implantation, Europace 2023;25:1208-36 (endorsed by APHRS, CHRS, LAHRS); Chung MK et al. 2023 HRS/APHRS/LAHRS guideline on cardiac physiologic pacing, Heart Rhythm 2023

missing_criteria.entity: Acute MI in ventricular paced rhythm
missing_criteria.value: RV pacing hides acute MI in the same way as LBBB. Apply Sgarbossa-type rules: concordant ST elevation >=1 mm in leads with positive QRS; concordant ST depression >=1 mm in V1-V3 (V4-V6 can be included in paced rhythm); excessively discordant ST elevation, best judged as a proportion (Smith-modified ST/S ratio <=-0.25) rather than the original >=5 mm. In paced rhythm the modified criteria had about 81% sensitivity and 96% specificity for occlusion MI. If symptoms persist, the patient goes to a primary PCI strategy.
missing_criteria.source: Thygesen K et al. Fourth Universal Definition of MI 2018, Circulation 2018;138:e618-51; Byrne RA et al. 2023 ESC Guidelines for ACS, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720-826 (atypical ECG presentations incl. paced rhythm); Dodd KW et al. Ann Emerg Med 2021;78:517-29; Kontos MC et al. 2022 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on chest pain in the ED, JACC 2022
missing_criteria.leads: All 12 leads; concordant ST depression V1-V6

missing_criteria.value: After a period of ventricular pacing (or intermittent LBBB/WPW), intrinsic beats can show deep T-wave inversion following the vector of the paced QRS. This mimics anterior ischaemia. Favouring memory over LAD ischaemia: positive T in aVL, positive or isoelectric T in I, and maximal precordial T inversion greater than the T inversion in III (all three criteria together: high sensitivity and specificity).
missing_criteria.source: Shvilkin A et al. Vectorcardiographic and electrocardiographic criteria to distinguish new and old LBBB/cardiac memory from ischemia, Heart Rhythm 2005;2:1072-8 (cardiac memory criteria); Rosenbaum MB et al. Am J Cardiol 1982;50:213-22

missing_criteria.value: Hyperkalaemia (typically K >7 mEq/L) and class IC drugs widen the paced QRS and increase stimulus-to-QRS latency, raise thresholds, and can cause Wenckebach-type or 2:1 exit block up to complete loss of capture. The atrium is affected before the ventricle. An unusually wide paced QRS (>200 ms) should prompt checking potassium and drugs.
missing_criteria.source: Barold SS, Herweg B. The effect of hyperkalaemia on cardiac rhythm devices, Europace 2014;16:467-76
missing_criteria.leads: Rhythm strip; all leads for QRS width

missing_criteria.value: With VVI pacing, look for retrograde P waves in the ST segment or T wave after each paced QRS (inverted in II, III, aVF). VA conduction causes pacemaker syndrome and can trigger PMT in tracking modes. This is a reason to prefer AV-synchronous pacing in patients in sinus rhythm.
missing_criteria.source: Glikson M et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and CRT (mode selection, pacemaker syndrome)

missing_criteria.parameter: Ventricular safety pacing and RV-pacing-minimisation algorithms
missing_criteria.value: Ventricular safety pacing: a signal sensed early after an atrial pace triggers a ventricular stimulus at a short AV delay (about 100-120 ms), often falling on an intrinsic QRS.
